generalized-star-height-problem.what_happened: Three manuscripts in the family claim the same kind of result with different numerical bounds. 'Generalized Star Height at Most Three' (Theorem 1.1) claims that every regular language L over every finite alphabet Σ has h_Σ(L) ≤ 3, where h_Σ(L) is the least height of a generalized expression over Σ built from 0, 1, the letters, union, concatenation, complement relative to Σ*, and Kleene star. 'Generalized Star Height at Most Four' (Theorem 1.1) claims the same with h_Σ(L) ≤ 4. 'Finite Monoid Computations and a Uniform Generalized Star-Height Bound' (Theorem 1.1) claims the same with h_Σ(L) ≤ 13. Height is the maximum over union and concatenation, unchanged by complement, and one more than the body under star, so the bounds are on star nesting depth. The method is shared in outline: a word is cut into a prefix code of episodes plus a remainder; each episode acts on a finite F₂-vector space by an affine update; and the transition-monoid value of an episode sequence is expressed by a split identity that cuts each episode into a prefix test and a suffix test, raising the height bound from a skip bound H to at most max{2, H+1}. The papers differ in how the cut is decoded. The 13-paper uses prediction trials and full decision histories, with twelve split applications in all. The 4-paper uses an affine correction that hides one interval product, a finite tag clock and several marker scales, with heights 0→2→3→4. The 3-paper uses a robust tag clock, markers with periodic continuations, and shift tables in two splits, with heights 0→2→3. In each, the final expression is a finite union of concatenations A_d B_f, where A_d (the episode part) has the claimed height and B_f (the incomplete remainder) has height at most one.
generalized-star-height-problem.delivers: Together the claims give the uniform-boundedness answer to the question as worded: a single finite N, strongest in the family at N = 3, such that every regular language over every finite alphabet has a generalized expression over that same alphabet of star height at most N. The bound does not depend on the alphabet, the language, or the size of the recognising DFA. Restrictions: 'regular' means accepted by a DFA; complement is taken relative to the same Σ*, so the 'generalized' operator is complement relative to the free monoid on the alphabet; complement adds no star height. The manuscripts describe this as an affirmative answer to the uniform-boundedness question (13-paper introduction; 3-paper introduction). The theorem matches the list's question on the uniform reading, which is problem_asks item (1). The manuscripts do not claim to settle the problem as a whole, and they state that the question of whether height one always suffices is a separate one that their bounds do not decide.
generalized-star-height-problem.remains: (a) Whether height one always suffices, that is, whether some regular language has generalized star height greater than one. All three papers state that their bounds do not decide this. (b) The exact value of h_Σ(L) for particular languages; the 13-paper says computing the minimum is a further question. (c) Quantitative size bounds on the finite parameters and on expression length, which are not claimed: the 4-paper says it 'assert[s] no useful bound on their sizes or on expression length', and the 3-paper says its bound comes without a bound on expression size or running time. If the claims are correct, nothing remains open in the uniform-bound reading of the question.

machine_checked.scope:
Generalized star height measures the nesting of Kleene stars in regular expressions that also allow Boolean operations. The formalization proves that every regular language over a finite alphabet has a generalized expression over the same alphabet of star height at most three. This is stronger than the bound of thirteen in the accompanying finite-monoid paper. The selected statement asserts the uniform expression bound, without separately encoding every construction step of that paper.

The formalization proves that every regular language over a finite alphabet has a generalized regular expression over that same alphabet with star height at most three. Generalized expressions allow Boolean operations as well as concatenation and Kleene star. The bound of three implies the accompanying paper's bound of four; the selected statement concerns the expression bound itself.

Generalized star height measures the nesting of Kleene stars in regular expressions that also allow Boolean operations. The formalization proves that every regular language over a finite alphabet has a generalized regular expression over that same alphabet of star height at most three. Complements are taken in the same free monoid. This is the paper's uniform bound.

generalized-star-height-problem.doubts: Read in part only. The three build folders were searched for hedging language, but most sections were not read in full: 13-paper algebra, clock, geometry, outer, aligned and parameters; 4-paper clock, scales, episodes, splits, and the start of compilation; 3-paper clock, markers, schedule, episodes, decoder, and the outer and inner splits. Within the text read: the 4-paper's introduction says its finite choices 'can be found by exhaustive search; we assert no useful bound on their sizes or on expression length'. The 3-paper's component-language proposition is closed by the summary 'We have checked every allowed source of data' rather than itemised checks. The 3-paper's provisional-clock and rational-approximation step is described only in summary in its introduction. The 13-paper says its bound of 13 records the depth of its own method and that the stronger companion bounds replace no step; each paper says it proves its own needed lemmas and uses no companion's numerical theorem. No step is flagged as sketched, and no hedge is placed on a main theorem. The headline claim answers a question that the manuscripts' own citations present as open: Straubing (2002) is cited as distinguishing the two questions, Place and Zeitoun (2017) record that no language of generalized height above one was then known, and Cotumaccio (2025) still lists the problem as open. These are facts about how strong the claim is, not a judgment on whether it holds.
generalized-star-height-problem.direction: proves the uniform bound (N = 3; the family's companions claim 4 and 13 as weaker results); does not address whether height one suffices

banachs-problem.what_happened: One manuscript, 'A smooth three-torus diffeomorphism with simple Lebesgue spectrum' (OpenAI, dated September 23, 2026). Its Theorem 1.1 (thm:main) claims that there exist a C^∞ volume-preserving diffeomorphism T of the three-torus T³ (with normalized standard volume) and a real function f in the mean-zero space L²_0(T³) such that the bilateral orbit {f∘Tⁿ : n∈Z} is an orthonormal basis of all of L²_0. The same theorem derives that T is ergodic and that the Koopman operator U_T on L²_0 is unitarily equivalent to multiplication by w on L²(S¹, m), which is simple Lebesgue spectrum. The proof is an inductive limit. It builds smooth volume-preserving maps S_n, which are twists (θ,u,a) ↦ (θ+φ(u),u,a) reached through volume-preserving coordinate passages, with observables f_n whose spectral density is made exactly one by a whitening step (§5). The sequence converges in C^∞ to T, and completeness of the orbit comes from approximating a dense family of test functions by Laurent polynomials in U applied to f_n. Section 6 (Corollary 'dynamical-profile') adds mixing, zero entropy and vanishing Lyapunov exponents. Its mixing of order k≥3 depends on a separate OpenAI preprint, 'Rokhlin's multiple-mixing problem for one transformation' (cited as MultipleMixing2026, Theorem 1.1), which I did not read. The abstract says: 'We solve the probability-preserving form of Banach's simple Lebesgue-spectrum problem in smooth dynamics.'
banachs-problem.delivers: Existence of an ergodic, probability-preserving, discrete-time (Z-action) system with simple Lebesgue spectrum on its mean-zero L² space. The example is a smooth (C^∞) volume-preserving diffeomorphism of T³ with standard volume. Simple means multiplicity one, and Lebesgue means the spectral type is Haar measure on the circle; both are obtained from one cyclic orbit. The manuscript states its own scope. The abstract restricts the claim to 'the probability-preserving form', and §1 says that formulation is 'distinct from the historical real-line question recorded by Ulam and attributed to Banach'. So the claim is not offered for the infinite-measure line version. The manuscript defines the probability-preserving form in §1 as the Koopman operator on the orthogonal complement of the constants. It does not restate the list's bullet word for word, so this is a reading of that bullet, and the family matches the reading that the problem_asks note names for finite measure and Z-actions. The generator f is only required to lie in L² (real, centered, norm one), so the observable is not smooth. The smoothness claim is for T alone.
banachs-problem.remains: If the claim is correct, the probability-preserving, discrete-time reading is answered by existence, and parts (1)–(3) of problem_asks are met under that reading. Left open by this family: the infinite-measure (Ulam, real-line) reading, which the manuscript explicitly sets aside; continuous time (flows and R^d actions), which §1 discusses only through other results (Prikhod'ko, Fayad–Forni–Kanigowski, Abdedou–Fayad–Kessi) without settling the simple-Lebesgue question for flows; and any class of examples other than C^∞ volume-preserving diffeomorphisms of T³ (other manifolds, other regularity classes, analytic maps).

machine_checked.scope: Banach's simple Lebesgue-spectrum problem asks for a probability-preserving transformation with simple Lebesgue spectrum on its mean-zero $L^2$ space. The formalization constructs a smooth volume-preserving diffeomorphism of the three-torus with this property. It gives a real-valued cyclic vector whose integer iterates form an orthonormal basis of the entire mean-zero space, and an isometric identification under which the Koopman operator becomes multiplication by the coordinate function on the circle. The transformation is also ergodic.

banachs-problem.doubts: The text flags no step as sketched, hedged or deferred. A search for 'sketch', 'omit', 'routine' and 'left to' found nothing of the kind. The argument is long and compressed, and each stage is a sequence of choices of the form 'arbitrarily small after the earlier finite data are fixed'. The key inputs are the passage lemma (§2), the signal lemma (§3), and the prediction proposition and finite phase-test lemma (§4). I read their statements and only selected passages, so my account of them rests mainly on their statements. The abstract's 'solve' is qualified to the probability-preserving form in the abstract itself, but the title has no such qualification. The mixing corollary's order-≥3 mixing depends on the separate MultipleMixing2026 preprint. Its zero-entropy step uses Rokhlin's finite-multiplicity theorem, and its vanishing-exponent step uses Pesin's formula as stated by Mañé. These are cited rather than proved here, and they are not needed for the spectral claim itself. I found no inconsistency between the abstract and Theorem 1.1.
banachs-problem.direction: proves existence: a positive answer, constructing an example in the probability-preserving discrete-time form
banachs-problem.object: The diffeomorphism T and the generator f are not explicit. They are the limit of an inductive construction (Proposition 'one stage' in §5, then the smooth limit in the proof of Theorem 1.1), and no formula is given. The intermediate maps are explicit twists, but the limit map is specified only as a limit.

rokhlins.what_happened: One manuscript, 'Rokhlin's multiple-mixing problem for one transformation' (dated 23 September 2026; the only manuscript in this family). Its main theorem (introduction, thm:main) says: if T is an invertible measure-preserving transformation with measurable inverse on an arbitrary probability space (no standardness or countable-generation assumption) and T is mixing, meaning mu(A cap T^{-n}B) -> mu(A)mu(B) as |n| -> infinity, then for every k >= 3 and all measurable A_1,...,A_k, mu(A_1 cap T^{-n_1}A_2 cap ... cap T^{-(n_1+...+n_{k-1})}A_k) -> product of mu(A_i) as min(n_1,...,n_{k-1}) -> infinity through positive integers. The manuscript counts order by the number of sets (order k = k sets, which it says is multiplicity k-1 in Rokhlin's and Ryzhikov's convention). The proof is by contradiction on a least failing order k. Section 2 extracts a zero-entropy mixing finite-alphabet shift with centred one-site functions that witness a nonvanishing k-fold correlation along diverging layouts. Sections 3-6 build a saturated ordered array object, an operator description of exact lines, measurable labels grouped into finite blocks, and a one-dimensional cancellation result (Proposition orbit-cancellation) that makes the Cesaro averages of the block coefficients vanish. Section 7 integrates these to contradict a constant positive block integral. Section 8 (Corollary, endomorphisms and flows) extends the conclusion to (1) non-invertible measurable endomorphisms on arbitrary probability spaces, for forward times only, and (2) real-time flows whose Koopman operators are strongly continuous on L^1.
rokhlins.delivers: Answers the bullet's question affirmatively for a single invertible measure-preserving transformation (a Z-action, the classical setting) on any probability space: every strongly (2-fold) mixing system is strongly 3-mixing, and in fact mixing of every order k >= 3. Order 3 in the manuscript is three sets, which matches the bullet's A_0, A_1, A_2 reading; the all-k statement also covers the four-set (A_0,...,A_3) reading. Restrictions: (a) convergence is along layouts whose successive gaps tend to infinity, i.e. min(n_1, n_2) -> infinity for three sets with n_1 = t_2 - t_1 and n_2 = t_3 - t_2, with t_1 = 0 by invariance. This is the gap form the introduction uses to define mixing of order k. The manuscript does not state a condition that each shift diverges separately, so the bullet's phrase 'shifts m_1, m_2 -> infinity' is ambiguous here and the manuscript's statement is the gap form. (b) The hypothesis is two-sided mixing, which for invertible T is the bullet's strong mixing. (c) The manuscript says Theorem thm:main 'answers Rokhlin's multiple-mixing problem affirmatively for one transformation', and its abstract says the same. Its framing (whether ordinary mixing alone implies the next order) matches the bullet in substance. The endomorphism and flow corollaries go beyond the bullet: they cover non-invertible maps, and flows (R-actions) only under an extra L^1 strong-continuity hypothesis.
rokhlins.remains: If the claim is correct, nothing remains of the bullet's question for single invertible transformations. Outside it: (i) multi-generator actions (Z^d or other groups). The introduction says the one-generator distinction is essential and cites Ledrappier's zero-entropy mixing Z^2 example, which is not threefold mixing. (ii) For flows, the continuity hypothesis is assumed, not proved, and the text treats it as automatic only for jointly measurable flows on standard probability spaces (cited). (iii) For endomorphisms, only forward times are covered.

machine_checked.scope: Rokhlin's multiple-mixing problem asks whether ordinary mixing of one invertible probability-preserving transformation implies mixing of every finite order. The formalization proves this implication. For each $k\ge3$ and every $k$ measurable sets, the measure of their translated intersection tends to the product of their measures as all successive time gaps tend to infinity.

rokhlins.doubts: The text flags no step as sketched or conjectural, and the main claim is not hedged. Points a reader should check: (1) Several steps are closed by 'the same argument', 'similarly', or 'the analogous assertion holds with rows and columns exchanged' (for example the common-exact-lines proposition and the incident-operator claim in Section 4, and the first-factor replacement in Section 2), so part of the verification is left to the reader. (2) The proof of Proposition orbit-cancellation (Section 6) is a short case assembly that relies on lemmas stated just before it, and the dissociated case depends on an entropy lemma whose hypothesis H_n = o(n) is checked only afterwards, via a progression-word estimate. (3) The no-standardness claim in the introduction depends on the Section 2 reduction to a finite-alphabet factor. Section 2 opens by saying it places the failure 'in a standard probability space', and the conventions say standardness is obtained only after passing to that factor. (4) The array construction is deliberately asymmetric: row independence is explicitly not asserted (Section 3), and the argument handles the other axis by permuting groups. (5) The main theorem is long (about 3,100 lines of TeX over eight sections). The abstract matches the theorem's statement.; conditional on: None for the main theorem beyond its stated hypotheses (invertible, measure-preserving, mixing). The proof uses standard background results (conditional-expectation convergence, the entropy chain rule, the spectral theorem for compact positive operators) and refers outward at a few steps. The saturation construction in Section 3 follows the 'method of sated extensions' of Austin, cited to a preprint version (its proof of Theorem 3.11 and Lemma 3.12) and not reproduced in full. The exponential-moment estimate for dissociated characters is cited to Green (2002, Section 2.2, Proposition 17), and the manuscript gives the projective-character version itself. The endomorphism corollary uses the natural extension of a standard factor (Rokhlin 1960, Section 9). The flow corollary assumes strong continuity of the Koopman operators on L^1; the text says this holds for jointly measurable flows on standard spaces, citing Rokhlin 1960, Section 1.7. No other manuscript in this family is used.
rokhlins.direction: proves the conjecture (affirmative: mixing implies mixing of every order k >= 3 for one invertible transformation)

rokhlins.what_happened: None of the four manuscripts claims or proves that strong mixing implies strong 3-mixing. The link is a dependency on a companion. 'Pointwise Multiple Ergodic Averages for Mixing Transformations' (MEA) and 'Pointwise convergence of fourfold ergodic averages for mixing transformations' (fourfold) both take as an input Theorem 1.1 of the companion 'Rokhlin's multiple-mixing problem for one transformation' (MixingCompanion, dated September 23, 2026; not in this family, not read). As the family restates it (MEA, build/sections/inputs.tex; fourfold, build/sections/02-structure.tex, eq. all-orders-input): for an invertible mixing probability-preserving T, any fixed s≥2, bounded g_1,...,g_s and integer times t_1,...,t_s, the integral of the product of g_j(T^{t_j}x) tends to the product of the integrals as min over i≠j of |t_i−t_j| tends to infinity. MEA's introduction calls this 'the assertion of Rokhlin's multiple-mixing problem'. MEA uses it for all orders in its arbitrary-length selected-law argument (build/sections/channels.tex, correlation decay); the fourfold paper does the same (build/sections/05-channels.tex). What each manuscript itself proves: (1) MEA: for every n≥2 and bounded f_1,...,f_n, the averages (1/N) times the sum over k=1..N of the product of f_j(T^{jk}x) converge a.e. to the product of the integrals, along all positive integers N, for invertible bimeasurable mixing T on an arbitrary probability space, with no mixing rate. (2) Fourfold: the same for the times n,2n,3n,4n and four bounded functions. (3) 'Triple ergodic averages with distinct integer slopes': for three bounded functions at any three pairwise distinct nonzero integer slopes, positive or negative, the averages converge a.e. to the product of the integrals, under mixing. (4) 'Pointwise convergence of triple ergodic averages for mixing transformations': the times n,2n,3n, a.e. on an arbitrary probability space with measurable inverse. Manuscripts (3) and (4) identify their limits using only two-function mixing (build/sections/transfer.tex, 'Identifying the limit by mixing', in (3); the Cesàro lemma in build/paper/sections/ergodic.tex in (4), an induction on pairwise correlations). Neither cites MixingCompanion.
rokhlins.delivers: Nothing that settles Rokhlin's question. The family makes no 3-mixing claim of its own. Its bearing is conditional: MEA and the fourfold paper rely on the companion's all-orders statement, and no other manuscript in the family does. The companion's restated form covers the k = 3 case only in the min-gap sense: μ(A0 ∩ T^{-t2}A1 ∩ T^{-t3}A2) → μ(A0)μ(A1)μ(A2) as min(|t2|, |t3|, |t2−t3|) → ∞. The list's wording is different. It asks for convergence as the shifts m1 and m2 tend to infinity, with no condition on m1 − m2. The restated form does not cover shift pairs with m1 − m2 bounded, so as written it is weaker than the list's wording. The restated form is the usual k-fold mixing definition and covers all s, so it goes beyond the three-set case the list asks about.
rokhlins.remains: Nothing of the problem is settled by this family itself. If the companion's Theorem 1.1 holds in the restated form, the min-gap version of the k = 3 case follows from it. That is the companion's claim, not this family's, and I did not assess it. The list's literal form (m1, m2 → ∞ with no gap condition) is not addressed by the restated companion form. The family's own results are pointwise a.e. convergence statements, not 3-mixing statements.
rokhlins.doubts: (a) The theorem statements carry no conditional hypothesis, but the proofs rest on companion results not reproduced here. MEA says 'These companion proofs are not reproduced here.' The fourfold paper says 'The local analytic theorems themselves are cited with their hypotheses and locations.' Manuscript (3) says 'the technical part is a proof by reference to those manuscripts, whereas the ergodic deduction is presented in full', and describes its new estimates as 'extensions of the proofs in H, V, not new proofs of their coefficient-independent projection and row estimates.' (b) Manuscript (4) uses H's uniform local bound at one exponent q in (2,3) and justifies that choice by the parameter order in H's proof. (c) MEA's introduction calls FourfoldCompanion Theorem 1.1 'the fourfold mixing theorem', but in the fourfold manuscript that theorem is a pointwise convergence statement for four functions. (d) The restated companion form and the list's 3-mixing wording differ (see delivers).; conditional on: MEA and the fourfold paper: MixingCompanion Theorem 1.1 in the restated all-orders form above, used for the selected-law and correlation-decay steps; not proved in this family. MEA also takes FourfoldCompanion Prop. 2.2 and Lemma 2.3 (relative structure and relative norm convergence) and SlopesCompanion Prop. 3.5, Lemma 3.6 and Lemma 3.9 (triple oscillation and profile approximation), and cites Austin's sated extensions. The fourfold paper also takes its analytic local estimates from TripleCompanion (manuscript (4) here) and HilbertCompanion ('An L^3 bound for the trilinear Hilbert transform', outside this family). Manuscript (3) takes its local estimates from H (the trilinear Hilbert paper, outside this family) and V (manuscript (4) here). Manuscript (4) takes its local estimate from H.
rokhlins.direction: no direct claim on the question; pointwise convergence of multiple averages, conditional on an affirmative companion result

birkhoff-conjecture.what_happened: Two OpenAI manuscripts, both dated 24 September 2026, which depend on each other. (1) 'Rigidity of Smooth Billiards with a Continuous Caustic Collar' (the companion, cited as NB in the other paper) proves: if a bounded, strictly convex planar domain Ω with C∞ boundary of positive curvature has a continuous physical caustic collar, meaning a homeomorphism H0 from S¹×[0,1) onto a relatively open neighbourhood A of ∂Ω in the closed table, with H0 on the zero leaf equal to ∂Ω and every positive leaf a C∞ smooth closed convex caustic, then Ω is an ellipse (circles included; the conclusion is Ω = {x : (x−c)ᵀQ(x−c) < 1} with Q symmetric positive definite). No differentiability across leaves is assumed. The proof goes through analytic boundary regularity (§2), a joint parametrization (§3), continuation and shape-lift arguments and growth-order exclusions (§4 to §7), a critical-case reduction (§8 to §9), and a sign-test contradiction for the remaining finite critical wall (§10 to §11). (2) 'Continuous Phase Foliations Create Analytic Caustic Collars' (the Phase paper) proves the same conclusion for the same class of tables under a different hypothesis: if a T-invariant open annulus U in the billiard phase cylinder contains (ℝ/Lℤ)×(0,η) for some η>0, and there is a homeomorphism H from S¹×(0,1) onto U whose leaves are essential simple closed curves each individually invariant under the billiard map, then Ω is an ellipse. Its route is to show the boundary is real analytic, to construct a jointly real-analytic family of smooth strictly convex caustics Γ_λ (0 ≤ λ ≤ λ0) whose positive leaves fill a relatively open collar of ∂Ω, and then to conclude by applying the companion's Theorem 1.2 (physical-collar rigidity). So the Phase paper replaces the companion's caustic hypothesis with a continuous invariant-curve hypothesis on a grazing annulus, and its own proof ends at the caustic collar.
birkhoff-conjecture.delivers: For the list's question (strictly convex and integrable implies ellipse), the family gives a positive answer for a near-boundary integrability notion only. If Ω is bounded, has C∞ boundary of positive curvature, and either (companion) a full neighbourhood of its boundary is continuously foliated by smooth closed convex caustics, or (Phase paper) a full grazing annulus is continuously foliated by individually invariant essential billiard-invariant curves, then Ω is an ellipse. The companion's abstract says it 'resolves the near-boundary Birkhoff conjecture in the stated smooth class'; the Phase paper says it resolves the near-boundary version 'positively in the continuous phase-foliation formulation'. Neither says it settles the Birkhoff conjecture as the list words it. Against the list's wording, the manuscripts add boundedness, C∞ smoothness and positive curvature, and they take integrability only near the boundary. The companion's hypothesis is the list's 'caustic-integrable' variant restricted to a neighbourhood of the boundary; the Phase paper's is the invariant-curve form of that variant, also near the boundary. The conclusion matches the list: ellipse, circles included. The converse is not claimed.
birkhoff-conjecture.remains: Still open if the claims are correct: (a) the general planar statement for smooth strictly convex integrable tables under the other notions of integrability, namely total integrability by non-contractible invariant curves on the whole phase cylinder (Bialy's theorem is cited, not reproved here), a first integral with nonvanishing gradient, polynomial integrability, and integrability away from the boundary; (b) tables whose boundary is only C^k or C², or that have points of vanishing curvature (the papers assume positive curvature throughout, and the Phase paper cites Mather for why grazing caustics fail when curvature vanishes); (c) unbounded domains; (d) any statement about the converse direction, which the list does not ask for. Also outside the family: higher dimensions and other billiard models, which the list does not ask about.
birkhoff-conjecture.doubts: (1) The companion's critical-case reduction is explicitly conditional. Its 'Conditional angle-budget reduction' assumes that no prohibited sequence exists, and the model section says that until the exclusion proof is completed, the angle-budget and polynomial bounds conditional on it will not be used. The exclusion proof (§9) is a single paragraph that assembles earlier named results: the limiting moment law, steep and bounded contact alternatives, normal epochs, uniform witnesses, and a mesh contradiction. The finite-critical-wall case of the main proof rests on this exclusion. (2) The Phase paper's joint section says it 'follows the Newton construction of [NB, Section 3]' and cites the buffered-division and recursion lemmas from the companion instead of proving them. Its analytic section imports two estimates from the companion without proof. Its only route to the ellipse conclusion is the companion's Theorem 1.2, so the Phase paper's own proof ends at a caustic collar. borsuks-problem.what_happened: One manuscript, 'A nine-dimensional counterexample to Borsuk's covering assertion' (credited to OpenAI, dated 23 September 2026), claims that X = {uuᵀ : u ∈ ℝ⁴, |u| = 1}, the set of rank-one orthogonal projectors on ℝ⁴ inside the nine-dimensional trace-one affine space of real symmetric 4×4 matrices with the Frobenius metric, has diameter √2 and cannot be covered by ten subsets of diameter strictly less than √2. Its main theorem states this and writes it as b(X) > 10, where b(Y) is the least number of pieces of strictly smaller diameter needed to cover Y. The same manuscript's corollary extends this to every dimension d ≥ 9: for each such d there is a compact subset of ℝᵈ of diameter √2 that cannot be covered by d+1 subsets of strictly smaller diameter. It is built from a translate of X in ℝ⁹ together with s = d−9 further points, which lie at mutual distance √2 from each other and from every point of the translate (vectors with Gram matrix I_s + (1/4)·11ᵀ). The proof of the main theorem is topological and combinatorial. A cover by pieces of diameter below √2 yields a smooth partition of unity on ℝP³ whose positive supports are disjoint for orthogonal lines. Extending the resulting map to symmetric matrices gives an odd map from the 9-sphere to the 9-sphere. Its mod-two degree forces every maximal support to have four labels, with their sum a simplicial cycle. Degree and double-cover counts then force a six-label triangle system on the complement of each tetrahedral support, and a combinatorial analysis of these systems across adjacent tetrahedra gives a contradiction, so no admissible map ℝP³ → Δ⁹ exists.
borsuks-problem.delivers: For the bullet's lower-bound part: the manuscript exhibits a compact set in ℝ⁹ of diameter √2 that cannot be covered by ten pieces of strictly smaller diameter, so the minimum number of pieces for that set is at least 11, i.e. f(9) ≥ 11. By the corollary, for every d ≥ 9 some compact set in ℝᵈ needs at least d+2 pieces, giving f(d) ≥ d+2 for all d ≥ 9. This disproves the conjecture that d+1 pieces always suffice in each of those dimensions. Restrictions: the bounds are lower bounds only, and they apply to d ≥ 9. The manuscript says nothing about dimensions 8 and below and does not claim the conjecture fails there. The examples have diameter √2 rather than 1; the piece count is unchanged by scaling. The manuscript states the covering form, which matches the list's wording. It also remarks that covers and partitions give the same count, because overlaps can be removed without increasing diameters. That remark bears on the cover-versus-partition question the frozen statement leaves open. The manuscript does not claim to settle the problem. It says the theorem 'does not determine the smallest dimension in which it fails or the exact value of b(X)'.
borsuks-problem.remains: If the claim is correct, still open: the exact value of f(n) in every dimension, and the exact value of b(X) (only b(X) > 10 is proved). Also open: the smallest dimension in which the covering assertion fails, including whether it fails in any dimension from 2 to 8, which the manuscript does not address. Every upper bound on f(n) is open; the manuscript gives none. The growth of f(n) as n increases is open too: the manuscript's only new bound is the linear lower bound n+2.

machine_checked.scope: Borsuk's conjecture predicts that every bounded subset of $\mathbb R^d$ can be covered by $d+1$ sets of strictly smaller diameter. The formalized counterexample is the compact set of rank-one orthogonal projectors onto lines in $\mathbb R^4$, with the Frobenius metric. It lies in the nine-dimensional affine space of trace-one symmetric matrices, has diameter $\sqrt2$, and cannot be covered by ten arbitrary sets of smaller diameter.

borsuks-problem.doubts: (1) The non-coverability proof is a long hand argument spanning the geometry, topology, six-label and ten-label sections. The text reports no computer check. (2) Several combinatorial steps are compressed into a sentence and are not flagged as sketched: the 'realizes every possible choice of omissions' step in the partner-block lemma; the claim in the two-tetrahedra lemma that the transported systems 'agree everywhere' from agreement on five labels; and, in the six-label lemma, the statement that a perpendicular line 'could use none of the six labels', where the contradiction also uses that a line's coordinates sum to one, which the text leaves implicit. (3) The claim that the result improves the dimension bound from 63 rests on a cited public note (Grinsztajn 2026), which the manuscript neither proves nor uses in its argument.
borsuks-problem.direction: disproves the conjecture f(n) = n+1 for every n ≥ 9 (lower bound f(n) ≥ n+2)
borsuks-problem.object: The set X = {uuᵀ : u ∈ ℝ⁴ unit}, the image of ℝP³ under u ↦ uuᵀ, is explicit. The manuscript gives an explicit isometry from its trace-one matrix space to ℝ⁹ in a remark on Euclidean coordinates. Its non-coverability is proved by a contradiction argument, not by an explicit certificate. For d ≥ 10 the added points are given by the explicit Gram matrix I_s + (1/4)·11ᵀ, which determines them up to an orthogonal change of basis.

hadwiger-conjecture-graph-theory.what_happened: Three manuscripts in the family bear on this. (1) 'A counterexample to Hadwiger's conjecture' (folder A-counterexample-to-Hadwigers-conjecture-September-23-2026) proves Theorem 1.1: for arbitrarily large m there are m-vertex finite simple graphs G with independence number alpha(G) <= 2 and cm(G) < m/100, where cm(G) is the largest connected matching (disjoint edges, every two of which are joined by an edge between their endpoint sets). Its Proposition 'matching-minor' proves that every finite graph has h(G) <= (m + 4 cm(G) + 2)/3, and since every colour class has at most two vertices, chi(G) >= m/2. For the constructed graphs this gives h(G) < 26m/75 + 2/3 < m/2 <= chi_f(G) <= chi(G) (Corollary 1.2), so chi(G) > h(G) and chi_f(G) > h(G). (2) 'A counterexample to the Colin de Verdiere chromatic conjecture' (folder A-counterexample-to-the-Colin-de-Verdiere-chromatic-conjecture-September-23-2026) builds, by a separate route, clique blow-ups H[s] of sampled base graphs H with alpha <= 2, and proves mu(G) + 1 < |V(G)|/2 <= chi(G). Its fractional-colouring corollary chains chi_f >= |V|/2 > kappa + 1 >= mu + 1 >= h, and the manuscript itself says these graphs also violate Hadwiger's inequality. The step mu + 1 >= h is the classical minor-monotonicity inequality, cited to van der Holst, Lovasz and Schrijver rather than proved there. (3) 'A linear list-coloring bound in terms of the Hadwiger number' (folder A-linear-list-coloring-bound-in-terms-of-the-Hadwiger-number-September-23-2026) proves list-chi(G) <= C h(G) for an absolute integer C, hence chi(G) <= C h(G) by a common list. This is a linear-coefficient statement; it is not chi <= h and does not assert it.
hadwiger-conjecture-graph-theory.delivers: If correct, it disproves the conjecture as the list states it: the list asks for chi(G) <= h(G) for every loopless graph, and the manuscript states the conjecture for finite nonempty simple graphs. Its counterexamples are simple and hence loopless, so the disproof transfers to the list's wording. The colouring form (2) also fails: for a counterexample G with h = h(G), take t = h + 1; G has no K_t minor and chi(G) >= t, so G is not (t-1)-colourable. The failure is not confined to small t: the examples are arbitrarily large, with h(G) below 26m/75 + 2/3 (about 0.35m) and chi(G) >= m/2. The same graphs also disprove the Reed-Seymour fractional weakening (fractional chi <= h), which the list does not ask about. Restrictions: the examples have independence number at most two; there are no restrictions on the scope of the disproof itself, since one counterexample suffices for a universal statement. The manuscript does not say the result settles the problem in so many words, but its abstract says 'We disprove Hadwiger's conjecture'.
hadwiger-conjecture-graph-theory.remains: If the claim holds, neither problem_asks (1) nor (2) remains open, since both the universal inequality and its colouring form are false. Variants the list excludes (linear, asymptotic, odd, or restricted-class forms) are not decided by these manuscripts, except that the list manuscript proves a linear-coefficient bound chi <= C h with an absolute C, which is a different statement from the one asked.

machine_checked.scope:
Hadwiger's conjecture predicts $\chi(G)\le h(G)$ for every finite graph, where $h(G)$ is the largest clique-minor order. The formalization constructs arbitrarily large finite simple counterexamples with independence number at most two. For a graph on $m$ vertices it proves
$h(G)<26m/75+2/3<m/2\le\chi(G)$.
This disproves the ordinary chromatic form. The paper's fractional-chromatic strengthening and the Colin de Verdière consequence are outside this selected statement.

The Linear List Hadwiger conjecture asks for a universal linear bound on list chromatic number in terms of clique-minor size. The formalization proves that there is one integer $C\ge1$ such that every finite nonempty simple graph $G$ satisfies $\chi_{\mathrm{list}}(G)\le C h(G)$, where $h(G)$ is the largest order of a clique minor. The constant is independent of the graph.

hadwiger-conjecture-graph-theory.doubts: I found no sketch flags, hedges, or deferral phrases bearing on the main argument in the three manuscripts (a search for sketch, omitted, routine, analogous, and similar wording found only local remarks). Scope of my reading: the probabilistic core (Theorem 'raw-supersaturation') is spread across roughly a dozen sections. I read its statement, the graph-deduction proposition, the matching-count proposition (its proof and arithmetic, including 26/75 and 2/3), and the completion argument. The completion argument invokes earlier propositions (status preparation, positive overlap, rare overlap) for its overlap inputs, and I did not check those inputs, so the step-level correctness of the core is not assessed here.
hadwiger-conjecture-graph-theory.direction: disproves the conjecture (chromatic and colouring forms), and also its fractional weakening
hadwiger-conjecture-graph-theory.object: No explicit object. The graphs are random samples: the Hadwiger manuscript builds them by sampling positions from a finite probability space, with holes fixed by an algebraic tensor/frame relation, and shows the sample has the required properties with probability 1 - exp(-Omega(m)) (Proposition 'raw-to-graph'). Existence is therefore probabilistic, not explicit. The Colin manuscript's graphs are clique blow-ups of such sampled base graphs and have the same status.

hadwiger-nelson-problem.what_happened: One manuscript, “The Euclidean plane is not five-colorable” (dated September 23, 2026), claims that every colouring of the Euclidean plane with five colours has a monochromatic unit-distance pair, with no regularity assumption on the colour classes. Its main theorem (thm:main) states that the plane has no proper five-colouring even when arbitrary colour classes are allowed, and so 6 ≤ χ(ℝ²) ≤ 7. The upper bound 7 is the classical hexagonal colouring (Hadwiger 1961), which the paper reproduces; the new content is the lower bound 6. The argument has two parts. (1) Transfer (thm:transfer, with Proposition palettes-forward and a density-point converse): for every positive integer k, a proper k-colouring of the plane exists if and only if a “weak measurable” k-colouring exists. A weak measurable colouring is a Lebesgue-measurable colouring in which same-coloured unit pairs have zero measure in the product of plane Lebesgue measure and normalised arc length on the circle. The forward direction averages a proper colouring over the algebraic plane, projects onto the continuous factor by conditional expectation, and uses a rigidity theorem (thm:rigidity: every K-invariant probability on the character group with zero mass on the ordinary continuous characters is Haar). The converse uses density points and de Bruijn–Erdős compactness. (2) Theorem weak-five (no weak measurable five-colouring): the paper builds angular palettes at each centre with at most two labels (prop:palette-size), shows that the centres whose transition graph contains a cycle form a locally finite set (thm:cyclic-local-finiteness), extracts a label cycle of length 3, 4 or 5 with compact connected exclusion sets (prop:interface-cycle), and excludes each cycle length by an angular argument (prop:angular-five, prop:angular-four, prop:angular-three). The three-cycle case uses a rational placement certificate for seven points forming a Moser-spindle-type configuration (lem:angular-certificate). A corollary (cor:positive-badness) also states, as a consequence, that a finite unit-distance graph is not five-colourable, with an existential positive constant for the monochromatic-pair frequency.
hadwiger-nelson-problem.delivers: For the list's problem, the claim establishes the lower bound χ(ℝ²) ≥ 6: there is no proper five-colouring of the plane, with arbitrary colour classes, in ZFC. Together with the known seven-colouring it gives 6 ≤ χ(ℝ²) ≤ 7, which moves the lower bound from the known 5 to 6. This is the list's part (1). For part (2), the claim gives only an existential finite statement: by de Bruijn–Erdős compactness there is a finite unit-distance graph that is not five-colourable, so its chromatic number is at least 6. The paper does not display this graph, and gives no size or explicit construction. The paper's statement of the problem matches the list's: the plane, distance exactly one, no regularity on the colour classes. The paper does not claim to settle the problem. Its introduction says the alternatives six and seven remain unresolved. Part (3) of the list's problem statement, covering other distances, dimensions other than two, and fractional or density versions, is not addressed.
hadwiger-nelson-problem.remains: If the claim is correct, χ(ℝ²) is either 6 or 7, and which one holds is open. The paper's footnote mentions a May 14, 2026 manuscript of Reed that claims χ(ℝ²) = 7. The paper says that manuscript's displayed theorem assumes the key density bound as a hypothesis, so it does not establish 7; this is context, not part of this family's claim. Also open: whether six colours suffice (a 6-colouring of the plane would be needed for the lower bound to be sharp), an explicit finite unit-distance graph with chromatic number at least 6 (the paper's graph is existential and of unknown size), and the list's variants with other distances, other dimensions, or fractional and density versions.

machine_checked.scope: The Hadwiger–Nelson problem asks for the fewest colors needed to color the plane so that points at distance one have different colors. The formalized results prove that five colors do not suffice and that seven colors do suffice. The lower bound applies to arbitrary colorings, with no measurability or continuity assumption; the upper bound includes every boundary point of the coloring regions.

hadwiger-nelson-problem.doubts: (1) Length and compression: the argument spans about 4,600 lines of LaTeX across eight section files, and the abstract and introduction give only an outline. The interface-cycle construction (prop:interface-cycle) is summarised in an overview paragraph (“A planar cover obstruction forces a nontrivial loop…”), and the caption of its exclusion figure calls the shape “schematic”. I read that proposition's statement and the start of its section only. (2) The seven-point certificate (lem:angular-certificate) is verified by tables of decimal coordinate boxes, polynomial bounds and residual numerators, and the text calls this a rational verification. I read that verification but did not recheck its arithmetic. (3) I did not read the relative-singularity and multiple-averages lemmas in rigidity.tex, nor the middle parts of palettes.tex, transitions.tex, interfaces.tex and angular.tex. My account of them rests on the introduction's outline and the statements I did read. (4) The bounds in cor:positive-badness part (ii) are imported from Bourgeat et al. by citation, and the constant δ = 1/m is non-constructive. I found no inconsistency between the abstract and thm:main.; conditional on: The main theorem assumes nothing beyond ZFC. It cites standard results: the abelian spectral theorem and Bochner's theorem, the Følner criterion for amenable groups, Fourier uniqueness, and de Bruijn–Erdős compactness. Corollary cor:positive-badness part (i) depends on Gwyn and Stavrianos 2020 (Lemma 2.10 and Theorem 2.11), and part (ii) depends on Bourgeat, Heinrich, Melotti and Robert 2015 (Theorems 1–2) for its needle-frequency bounds. The paper cites Sokolov–Voronov 2025 and Voronov 2025 as precedents for its interface and strip arguments, not as steps it relies on.
hadwiger-nelson-problem.direction: proves a lower bound: χ(ℝ²) ≥ 6, improving the known lower bound 5
hadwiger-nelson-problem.object: None for the lower bound. Non-five-colourability is proved by contradiction. The finite unit-distance graph in cor:positive-badness is obtained by compactness and is not displayed. The seven-colouring in the proof of thm:main (hexagonal, from Hadwiger 1961) is explicit, but it is the known upper bound, not a new object.

erdos-conjecture-on-arithmetic-progressi.what_happened: The manuscript 'Quasipolynomial Bounds for Arithmetic Progressions' (OpenAI, dated September 23, 2026) states as its first claim that it proves Erdős's conjecture: every set of positive integers with divergent reciprocal sum contains arithmetic progressions of every finite length. Its Corollary 'Divergent reciprocal sums' says that every A ⊆ ℕ with Σ_{a∈A} 1/a = ∞ contains nonconstant arithmetic progressions of every finite length. The corollary is derived from the main Theorem: for each fixed k ≥ 3 there are constants Cₖ, cₖ, εₖ > 0 such that, for every N ≥ 2, rₖ(N) ≤ Cₖ·N·exp(−cₖ(log N)^εₖ), where rₖ(N) is the largest subset of {1,…,N} with no nonconstant k-term progression (common difference d > 0). The proof sums the density bound over dyadic blocks [2^m, 2^(m+1)), using that a progression-free A meets each block in at most rₖ(2^m) elements, and shows the reciprocal sum is finite. Lengths one and two follow from A being infinite. The same manuscript also proves a weighted version: Σ (log(2+a))^B / a = ∞ for any fixed B ≥ 0 forces progressions of every length (Corollary 'Logarithmic weights and every length'), and it recovers Green and Tao's theorem on dense subsets of the primes.
erdos-conjecture-on-arithmetic-progressi.delivers: Claims the list's question in full as stated: for every set of positive integers with divergent reciprocal sum, and for every finite length, there is a nonconstant arithmetic progression of that length, with positive common difference. The abstract says outright 'We prove Erdős's conjecture', and the manuscript's statement matches the list's hypothesis (Σ 1/a = ∞ over the set) and conclusion (arbitrarily long progressions, read as every finite length). No density, class or dimension restriction is attached to the corollary. Sets such as the primes are instances of the universal claim. The density bound behind it is quantitative but the corollary needs only its summability consequence.
erdos-conjecture-on-arithmetic-progressi.remains: Nothing in the list's statement, if the claim is correct. The quantitative density question is not closed: the bound is stretched-exponential in log N with an unspecified exponent εₖ and is stated as not optimized, and the manuscript makes no claim about the exact size of rₖ(N).

machine_checked.scope:
Erdős's reciprocal-sum conjecture asks whether every set of positive integers with divergent reciprocal sum contains arithmetic progressions of every finite length. The formalization proves this statement: for every requested length, such a set contains a progression with positive common difference.

The selected theorem is the reciprocal-sum consequence. The paper's quantitative upper bound for the largest progression-free subset of $\{1,\ldots,N\}$ is outside this statement.

erdos-conjecture-on-arithmetic-progressi.doubts: (1) No constant is given a value. Cₖ, cₖ, εₖ and Aₖ are asserted to exist for each k, and the text says the exponent is not optimized. (2) The central new estimate, that the width loss at weight h is bounded by a polynomial independent of the current width Q_h, is argued in Section 8 through a four-step parameter schedule and two propositions. The polynomials Fⱼ, Gⱼ, Pⱼ and P'ᵢ are asserted to exist rather than written out, and several steps defer to other sections ('as in Section …'). The key justification reads 'Every step in the descending schedule uses a bounded composition of polynomial logarithmic bounds'. (3) In the root-compression lemma the radii are chosen 'with equality up to fixed factors'. (4) The corollary says 'nonconstant' progressions of every finite length, but a one-term progression cannot be nonconstant. The text handles lengths one and two by infinitude, so the statement is in effect for k ≥ 2. (5) I checked the statements of the appendix results and the places where the main text cites them, not their proofs; the foundations appendices run to about 10,000 lines.; conditional on: The main density bound is proved in the manuscript from external inputs it cites rather than proves. The two principal ones, named in the introduction, are the quasipolynomial inverse theorem for the Gowers U^(s+1)[N] norm of Leng, Sah and Sawhney (arXiv:2402.17994, Theorem 1.2; the appendices also cite its Lemma B.5 and Theorem 5.4 with Corollary 5.5), and the radius-sensitive almost-periodicity theorem of Schoen and Sisask (arXiv:1408.2568, Theorem 5.4), restated in the manuscript as its Lemma 'Almost-periodicity with a width bound'. Other cited inputs include Leng's efficient equidistribution theorem (Theorem 4), Green–Tao results on polynomial orbits (Proposition 7.2 and Lemma 7.4), Conlon–Fox–Zhao densification, and Bergelson–Leibman. The manuscript says it proves the box and product-of-cyclic-groups extensions of the Leng–Sah–Sawhney interval theorem itself. The corollary depends on the main theorem of this same manuscript. It does not depend on the companion van der Waerden manuscript, which is cited only for a coloring remark.

determine-growth-rate-of-r-k-n-see-szeme.what_happened: The manuscript 'Quasipolynomial Bounds for Arithmetic Progressions' (OpenAI, September 23, 2026) proves an upper bound on rₖ(N), the largest progression-free subset of {1,…,N}, for every fixed k ≥ 3: rₖ(N) ≤ Cₖ·N·exp(−cₖ(log N)^εₖ), with positive constants depending only on k. This is a stretched-exponential saving in log N. The title's 'quasipolynomial' refers to the equivalent density threshold log N ≥ Aₖ(2+log(1/α))^Aₖ for a set of density α to contain a k-term progression, which the manuscript states as an equivalent form of its main theorem. The manuscript proves no new lower bound on rₖ(N). Its only lower bound is Behrend's construction for k = 3, quoted as prior work: r₃(N) ≥ N·exp(−C√(log N)). A companion coloring corollary, Wᵣ(k) ≤ exp(Aₖ(2+log r)^Aₖ), follows from the same bound, and the lower bound that makes it two-sided is from the companion paper, not this one.
determine-growth-rate-of-r-k-n-see-szeme.delivers: The upper half of the growth-rate question, for each fixed k ≥ 3: rₖ(N)/N ≤ Cₖ·exp(−cₖ(log N)^εₖ) → 0, which is a stronger decay than Szemerédi's o(N). For k ≥ 5 it improves the Leng–Sah–Sawhney saving exp(−(log log N)^cₖ), and for k = 4 it improves Green and Tao's N/(log N)^c. For k = 3 the text claims no improvement of the three-term exponent, so the existing bounds (Kelley–Meka, Bloom–Sisask, Raghavan) are not claimed to be beaten. The manuscript does not claim the growth rate of rₖ(N) is determined, and it does not claim the exact growth rate.
determine-growth-rate-of-r-k-n-see-szeme.remains: (a) Upper bound: supplied for each k ≥ 3, but with the exponent εₖ unspecified. (b) Lower bound of the form N·gₖ(N) for k ≥ 3: not supplied by this manuscript; the only one stated is the cited Behrend bound for k = 3, and none is stated for k ≥ 4. (c) That the two bounds match, so that the growth rate is determined: not claimed. If the upper bound is correct, the question of the exact growth rate, and of the matching lower bound, remains open.

sidorenkos-conjecture.what_happened: The manuscript 'A counterexample to Sidorenko's conjecture' (OpenAI, dated September 23, 2026) is the only manuscript in this family. It claims one bipartite graph H on 35 vertices and 66 edges, and a finite simple graph G with at least one edge, such that t(H,G) < p(G)⁶⁶. Here t(H,G) is the homomorphism density (non-injective maps counted, normalised by |V(G)|^|V(H)|) and p(G) = 2|E(G)|/|V(G)|² is the edge density. H is the incidence graph of 22 triples on 13 points, listed explicitly in Table 'tab:complex' (sections/complex.tex); it is connected, with parts of size 13 and 22, degrees 4, 5 and 6 on the point side and 3 on the face side. The argument has three steps. (1) A finite symmetric [0,1]-valued kernel U with mean μ > 0 and t(H,U) < μ⁶⁶ is built from a rectangular kernel over random symmetric matrices over F_q, symmetrised by a crossed product and diluted (Proposition 'negative-kernel', sections/kernel.tex). (2) That step is conditional on the rank-layer limit, Lemma 'Rank-layer limit', which the manuscript proves in its own Sections 3 to 6. (3) A finite simple host G on n vertices is sampled from U, with n > (595 + 66μ⁶⁶)/Δ and Δ = μ⁶⁶ − t(H,U) (Lemma 'finite-host'). The same manuscript also refutes the graphon form: the {0,1} adjacency kernel W₀ of G on the uniform measure on V(G) has t(K₂,W₀) = p(G) and t(H,W₀) = t(H,G) < p(G)⁶⁶ (proof of Corollary 'Failure of the forcing conjecture', sections/consequences.tex). The manuscript also claims, for this same H, a failure of the Conlon–Fox–Sudakov forcing conjecture and amplification and injective-copy results. Those are not matched problems here and are not described further.
sidorenkos-conjecture.delivers: Disproves Sidorenko's conjecture as the list states it. The conjecture quantifies over every bipartite graph H, so a single bipartite H with t(H,W) < t(K₂,W)^{e(H)} for some graphon W refutes the universal claim. The counterexample is for this one graph, which is connected, bipartite and has 35 vertices and 66 edges. It is given in the finite-graph form (a finite simple host G with at least one edge). The graphon form in the list is also refuted, by the step graphon W₀ of G, since t(K₂,W₀) = p(G) and t(H,W₀) = t(H,G). The manuscript's own statement (its displayed inequality, with p(G) = 2|E|/|V|² for finite simple G, and 'bipartite with at least one edge') matches the list's statement up to the finite-graph versus graphon wording, which W₀ bridges. The manuscript says 'We disprove this conjecture', so it claims a full negative answer to the universal statement, not a partial or sharpened one. The manuscript also notes that H has no vertex adjacent to the whole opposite part, is not weakly norming (its point-side degrees are not regular), and fails the degree-count hypotheses of the positive results it cites. So it does not contradict those positive theorems, which concern other graphs.
sidorenkos-conjecture.remains: If the claim is correct, the universal statement as frozen is false and nothing of it remains open. Not addressed: which bipartite graphs do satisfy the inequality, beyond the positive classes already known; whether H is minimal in size or edge count; and whether any local or restricted version holds for H (the manuscript says the local kernel results of Lovász do not apply to its kernel). The host G is given only by existence, not explicitly.

machine_checked.scope: Sidorenko's conjecture predicts that every bipartite graph $H$ has homomorphism density at least the host graph's edge density raised to $|E(H)|$. The formalization disproves this for the paper's fixed bipartite graph with $35$ vertices and $66$ edges: it constructs a nonempty finite simple host graph with $t(H,G)<t(K_2,G)^{66}$. The separate forcing-conjecture consequence in the paper is outside this statement.

sidorenkos-conjecture.doubts: (1) The rank-layer lemma carries the whole result. Its proof spans about 2,400 lines (Sections 3 to 6). I read its statement, the assembly at the end of tail.tex, and the passages flagged here, not the full proof. (2) The singular-contribution proposition (tail.tex, 'Vanishing singular contribution') bounds the local maximising tuples only by necessary dimension inequalities. The text says these 'need not be realizable simultaneously', so the bound is an upper bound by design. (3) The numerical remainder 1641 and the requirement D > 1641 (tail.tex, 'Costs for the remaining profiles' and the singular-contribution proof) are asserted. The text says D > 1641 'is needed here only for the nondirect residual case and is not asserted to be a threshold for the whole proof'. I did not check the derivation of 1641. (4) The choice of D, ε and q is non-quantitative throughout, so the existence of G is not quantified. (5) In the rank-layer proof, the comparison that drops the prescribed signs off the transverse set is dismissed in one sentence: 'dropping the prescribed signs only enlarges the integrand after the comparable normalizations'. (6) The finite-host proof calls the probability that a map is a homomorphism a 'homomorphism indicator between zero and one'. The quantity is a probability; the collision bound is unaffected. (7) The abstract, the displayed theorem and the corollary statements agree on 35 vertices, 66 edges and a strict inequality for a finite simple graph with at least one edge.; conditional on: No external unproven hypothesis is stated for the Sidorenko disproof. Internally, the finite kernel (Proposition 'negative-kernel') and the host lemma are proved conditional on Lemma 'Rank-layer limit' (kernel.tex). The manuscript proves that lemma itself in Sections 3 to 6 (transverse, orbits, planted, tail), so the dependence is internal rather than on another paper. The sampling step follows the standard graphon sampling construction of Lovász and Szegedy (Section 2.6, Lemma 2.4) and gives its own collision bound. Standard inputs used without re-proof are the quadratic Gauss-sum rank bound (Gowers–Wolf, Lemma 3.3), the association-scheme counts of symmetric matrices by rank and sign (Huo–Wan; Schmidt), the Lagrangian counting formulas (Taylor), and the colour-refinement facts (Weisfeiler–Leman; McKay).

sidorenkos-conjecture.object: H is explicit: the incidence graph of 22 triples on 13 points, all triples written out in Table 'tab:complex' (sections/complex.tex). The host G is not explicit. It is produced by a probabilistic sampling argument from a finite kernel, after choosing a large fixed even dimension D, a small ε > 0 and a large odd prime q, each chosen only as 'sufficiently large' or 'sufficiently small'. The manuscript does not write G down and does not give its order beyond the existential bound n > (595 + 66μ⁶⁶)/Δ, where Δ depends on the constructed kernel.

rysers-conjecture.what_happened: Two manuscripts, both titled as counterexamples to Ryser's covering conjecture, claim the conjecture is false at infinitely many ranks. (1) 'Balanced counterexamples to Ryser's conjecture at prime orders' (dated 27 September 2026): for every sufficiently large prime q it constructs a finite intersecting (q+1)-partite (q+1)-uniform hypergraph H with covering number τ(H) = q+1, with exactly q+1 nonisolated vertices in each part. Since ν(H) = 1, this gives τ(H) = r > (r−1)ν(H) at r = q+1. The construction starts from the affine plane over F_q, with one vertex part per direction and one vertex per line. In each direction it merges two lines into one block and splits two other lines into two blocks each, so the count is (q−4)+1+4 = q+1. Each split line keeps four designated points, split into opposite pairs. The split lines are chosen by a probabilistic argument (random constituent lines, candidate four-point tuples, an independent-transversal selection, and a local-lemma completion). Covers of size at most q are excluded by a deletion estimate that gives an almost-cover, followed by the Szőnyi–Weiner prime-plane stability theorem to force a large pencil; this is the only step where primality of q is used. The paper also derives a corollary: a complete graph with a (q+1)-edge-coloring whose vertices need exactly q+1 monochromatic trees to cover, and the same minimum for connected monochromatic subgraphs. (2) 'A counterexample to Ryser's covering conjecture' (dated 23 September 2026): for every prime s ≥ s₀ with s ≡ 2 (mod 3), and every odd n ≥ n₀(s), with q = s^n, it constructs an intersecting (q+1)-partite (q+1)-uniform hypergraph H with τ(H) = q+1, so r = s^n+1. The paper does not assert equal part sizes. The construction takes the prime plane F_s², removes one line of each nonzero finite slope to get a set Y, and applies the bijection f(x,y) = (x³,y) (bijective because s ≡ 2 mod 3). A gadget lemma then says any cover of f(Y) by a lines and b points with a + b/2 ≤ s must be a full parallel class. Copies of Y are embedded in F_{s^n} with exceptional edges that change labels in one or two directions, using independent random candidate translates and an independent-transversal selection. The ambient cover argument uses an incidence bound proved in the paper along the sum–product strategy of Bourgain–Katz–Tao, valid when every proper subfield of F_q has order at most q^{1/3}; for odd n every proper subfield has order at most s^{n/3} = q^{1/3}. The paper also derives an r-edge-coloring corollary with r = s^n+1 that needs r monochromatic trees (or connected monochromatic subgraphs, or maximal components) to cover, which refutes Gyárfás's monochromatic tree-cover conjecture at these ranks, along with the Miličević bounded-diameter strengthening and the α = 1 case of a DeBiasio–Kamel–McCourt–Sheats conjecture, as the companion states.
rysers-conjecture.delivers: Refutes Ryser's conjecture in the form the problem states: for every r ≥ 2 and every r-partite r-uniform hypergraph H, τ(H) ≤ (r−1)ν(H). Both manuscripts state exactly this inequality as their eq:ryser, so the r-partite reading matches. Each counterexample is intersecting, so ν(H) = 1 and τ(H) = r exceeds (r−1)ν(H) at that rank. Ranks covered: (1) balanced paper: r = q+1 for every prime q ≥ q₀, with q₀ existential. (2) companion paper: r = s^n+1 for every prime s ≡ 2 (mod 3) with s ≥ s₀ and every odd n ≥ n₀(s), with s₀ and n₀(s) existential. Both families of ranks are infinite, so the universal claim (for every r) is refuted, and so is the inequality at each covered r. The matching-number part of the problem is refuted only at ν = 1, which is enough for the refutation. The balanced paper also gives equal part sizes |V₁| = … = |V_{q+1}| = q+1 with τ(H) = q+1; this is a stronger property than the problem requires. The companion does not assert balance and says so.
rysers-conjecture.remains: If the claims are correct, the conjecture as stated fails and nothing of the universal form survives. What these manuscripts leave open: (a) the inequality at every rank r not of the form q+1 (q prime ≥ q₀) or s^n+1 (in the companion's range), including the small ranks where the manuscripts cite positive results (the intersecting case through rank four attributed to Gyárfás, rank five to Tuza, and linear hypergraphs through rank nine); (b) the inequality for hypergraphs with ν ≥ 2, which the manuscripts do not treat directly; (c) the exact set of covered ranks, since the thresholds q₀, s₀ and n₀(s) are not quantified; (d) any sharp form of the bound in terms of r.

machine_checked.scope:
Ryser's covering conjecture predicts that an intersecting $r$-partite hypergraph has a vertex cover of size at most $r-1$. The formalization proves that every sufficiently large prime $q$ has a finite intersecting $(q+1)$-partite, $(q+1)$-uniform hypergraph with covering number $q+1$ and exactly $q+1$ nonisolated vertices in each part. Thus the conjecture fails even with equal part sizes. The prime threshold is existential.

Ryser's covering conjecture predicts $	au\le(r-1)
u$ for an $r$-partite hypergraph, where $	au$ and $
u$ are its covering and matching numbers. The formalized constructions give finite intersecting $r$-partite $r$-uniform hypergraphs with $
u=1$ and $	au=r$, contradicting the bound. The ranks have the form $r=p^n+1$: one fixed prime $p\equiv2\pmod3$ works for all sufficiently large prime degrees $n$, and a second result covers every sufficiently large such prime $p$ and every sufficiently large odd $n$, with the degree threshold allowed to depend on $p$. Infinitely many ranks occur. Equal part sizes and numerical thresholds are not asserted.

rysers-conjecture.doubts: Neither manuscript gives a numerical threshold; both say so. The balanced paper says its threshold 'is not numerical' and rests on finitely many 'with probability o(1)' estimates, combined by subtracting failure probabilities from a positive lower bound. Its deletion theorem covers any probability law that is at most e^{Kq} times uniform. The text says a qualitative estimate for uniform deletion would not suffice under this change of measure, and the introduction attributes the needed saving to a profile-counting bound of order exp(−Ω(q log q)); that step is carried out in deletion.tex. Several arguments are closed by 'as before' or 'the same process as before' (candidates.tex, selection.tex). The companion's gadget lemma and pool lemma hold only with high probability as s or n tend to infinity, and their constants δ = exp(−4K(s−1)) and ρ = δ/10 depend on s, so its thresholds depend on s through these constants. No inconsistency between the abstracts and the main theorems of either paper was found. I did not check the long probabilistic estimates line by line; this entry reports what the text claims and how it is organized.; conditional on: Balanced paper: no unproven hypothesis. It uses the Szőnyi–Weiner prime-plane stability theorem (Szőnyi–Weiner 2012, Theorem 4; also Héger–Nagy, Result 3.6) as an external black box, in the form the paper restates with explicit constants. It also uses the Lovász local lemma and an Azuma-type bound; the latter is proved in its appendix. Companion paper: no unproven hypothesis in the statements. It takes three elementary estimates (affine second-moment identity, bounded-drift concentration, and the independent-trial exposure bound) from the appendix of the balanced paper, which it cites as Lemmas A.1–A.3; I checked the appendix statements and proofs of A.1 and A.2. It follows the Bourgain–Katz–Tao sum–product strategy for its incidence theorem and proves the incidence theorem itself, and it proves its own Freedman-type martingale bound.
rysers-conjecture.direction: disproves the conjecture at infinitely many ranks (intersecting counterexamples)
rysers-conjecture.object: Yes, but not explicit. For each large prime q, an intersecting (q+1)-partite (q+1)-uniform hypergraph H with τ(H) = q+1 and parts of size q+1 (balanced paper). For each s ≡ 2 (mod 3) and odd n in the companion's range, an intersecting (s^n+1)-partite (s^n+1)-uniform hypergraph H with τ(H) = s^n+1 (companion paper). Each H is defined from a configuration whose existence is shown by a probabilistic argument with positive or high probability, with no numerical threshold, so no closed-form construction is given.

turans-brick-factory-problem.what_happened: The manuscript 'The crossing number of complete bipartite graphs' (build/paper.tex, dated 23 September 2026) claims Theorem 1: for all positive integers m and n, cr(Kₘ,ₙ) = dₘ dₙ, where dᵣ = ⌊r/2⌋⌊(r−1)/2⌋. This is exactly the Zarankiewicz number Z(m,n) of the list. Upper bound: the classical axis drawing (one vertex class on a vertical axis, the other on a horizontal axis, straight edges, positions chosen generically to avoid triple concurrences) has dₘ dₙ crossings; the count is written out. Lower bound: for odd n = 2s+1 with m ≥ 3, take a minimum drawing with no crossings between edges sharing an endpoint. Its signed-intersection matrix J satisfies zᵀJy = 0 for every pair of cycles (Lemma 'Cycle pairing'). A polynomial rank detector Φ built from Lagrange weights makes the off-diagonal blocks have rank at most the crossing count between two stars. A subspace-intersection inequality, Σᵢ,ⱼ dim(Uᵢ∩Vⱼ) ≤ ⌊m²/4⌋N, which the text proves, then gives a sum over ordered pairs i ≠ k of ranks of at least 2dₘ dₙ. Each crossing is counted twice, so c(D) ≥ dₘ dₙ. For even n, deleting each second-class vertex in turn gives (n−2)c(D) ≥ n dₘ dₙ₋₁ = (n−2)dₘ dₙ. The cases m ≤ 2 or n ≤ 2 are zero by nonnegativity. The other manuscript in the family, 'The crossing number of complete graphs', concerns Kₙ only and is not used for this match.
turans-brick-factory-problem.delivers: For every pair of positive integers m, n, the claim gives cr(Kₘ,ₙ) = Z(m,n), so no drawing of Kₘ,ₙ in the manuscript's class has fewer crossings than Z(m,n). This is the 'no' answer to the list's question. It covers all pairs (m,n), as the list's part (i) requires, and it includes the lower bound the list identifies as open. The class is restricted. A drawing has distinct vertex points and each edge is a simple continuous arc avoiding the vertices. Edge interiors meet in finitely many proper crossings (locally two arcs crossing transversally), with no tangencies, overlaps, triple points or common subarcs. Crossings are counted as points, so repeated crossings of one edge pair each count. Within that class there is no restriction on vertex positions or edge routes. The abstract says the result resolves Turán's brickyard problem. The manuscript does not restate the list's yes/no question, but its theorem is the two-sided equality over all (m,n) that answers it.
turans-brick-factory-problem.remains: If the claim holds, nothing is left open for Kₘ,ₙ within the manuscript's class. Outside that class the manuscript says nothing. Drawings with tangential contacts, triple points, infinitely many intersection points, or other crossing conventions (counting crossing pairs, or only odd crossings, which the introduction distinguishes) are not addressed.

machine_checked.scope:
The formalized result proves Hill's proposed formula for the crossing number of the complete graph: for every $n\ge3$, $\mathrm{cr}(K_n)=\frac14\lfloor n/2\rfloor\lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor\lfloor(n-2)/2\rfloor\lfloor(n-3)/2\rfloor$. It proves the lower bound and constructs a matching two-page drawing. Crossings are spatial points, so repeated crossings of one edge pair count separately.

Zarankiewicz's crossing-number conjecture predicts $\mathrm{cr}(K_{m,n})=\lfloor m/2\rfloor\lfloor(m-1)/2\rfloor\lfloor n/2\rfloor\lfloor(n-1)/2\rfloor$. The formalized result proves this equality for every positive $m,n$ and constructs a drawing attaining it. Crossings are counted as spatial points for continuous simple edge paths, including repeated crossings between the same pair of edges.

turans-brick-factory-problem.doubts: The lower bound rests on the cycle-pairing identity. Its proof handles edges shared by the two cycles through a prose description of shifted tracks in crossing and bend disks, supported by figures. The claims that a common small shift creates no new intersections and that seam contributions cancel are asserted in words, not checked in formulas. The manuscript flags no step as sketched and states no hedge. The abstract and Theorem 1 agree.
turans-brick-factory-problem.direction: proves the Zarankiewicz formula for all Kₘ,ₙ, answering Turán's question 'no' (no drawing beats Z(m,n))
turans-brick-factory-problem.object: No counterexample is constructed, since none exists under the claim. The only explicit drawing is the classical axis drawing, which gives the upper bound dₘ dₙ. Its vertex positions are chosen by a genericity argument, not written out.

how-many-unit-distances.what_happened: The manuscript 'A power saving for planar unit distances' (dated September 23, 2026) claims Theorem 1: there are absolute constants 0 < C < infinity and 1 <= beta < 4/3 such that u(n) <= C n^beta for every nonnegative integer n, where u(n) is the maximum, over n-point sets in the Euclidean plane, of the number of unordered pairs at distance exactly 1. The proof is by contradiction. Assuming no fixed power saving exists, it takes configurations with t^(4-o(1)) ordered unit pairs at n = t^3, turns them into a point-unit-circle incidence graph, and derives a contradiction from a bounded-versus-unbounded height scale, arithmetic budgets, and an algebraic-independence obstruction on rectangles of unit-distance ratios. The introduction also cites, without proving, a separate OpenAI construction (Theorem 1.1 of openaiUnitLower2026) giving at least n^(1+eps) unit distances along an unbounded sequence of n, and Sawin's construction giving u(n) >= n^1.014114 along an unbounded sequence; the manuscript does not claim either. The other manuscript in this family, 'The weak pinned planar distance theorem', does not bear on this problem.
how-many-unit-distances.delivers: An upper bound valid for every n: u(n) = O(n^beta) for some fixed beta < 4/3, i.e. a power saving over the Spencer-Szemeredi-Trotter bound O(n^(4/3)). It is a bound on every configuration and gives no construction. It is stated for the Euclidean plane and unordered pairs at distance exactly 1, matching the list's wording. It does not settle the problem as the list words it. The list asks for the exact value of u(n) and for matching lower and upper bounds on its order of growth. This manuscript provides only the upper side, with a non-explicit exponent below 4/3, and no lower bound of its own. It does state that the Erdos conjecture u(n) = n^(1+o(1)) was disproved, but that disproof is the cited separate construction, not this manuscript.
how-many-unit-distances.remains: The exact value of u(n) for each n. The order of growth: this manuscript does not identify the exponent of u(n), so the gap between the cited lower exponents (1+eps from the separate OpenAI construction, 1.014114 from Sawin, both cited and not proved here) and the unspecified upper exponent beta < 4/3 is left open. The paper neither computes beta nor shows beta = 1 is attained or excluded.

machine_checked.scope:
The formalized result shows that large repeated distance fibers are rare in arbitrary finite planar point sets. For each fixed $s>0$, the largest possible fraction of ordered distinct pairs $(x,y)$ whose distance from the pin $x$ occurs at least $n^s$ times tends to zero as the set size $n$ grows. Consequently, for every $\varepsilon>0$, the fraction of pins determining fewer than $n^{1-\varepsilon}$ distances tends uniformly to zero. The separate unit-distance power-saving theorem is not included.

The planar unit-distance problem asks how many pairs at distance one can occur among $n$ points. The formalization proves that there are absolute constants $C>0$ and $1\le\beta<4/3$ such that every finite planar point set of size $n$ determines at most $Cn^\beta$ unordered unit-distance pairs. The same constants work for every $n$, giving a fixed power improvement over the classical exponent $4/3$.

how-many-unit-distances.doubts: The argument is by contradiction, and the introduction says it establishes 'the existence of a fixed positive gap without estimating its size'. So beta and C are not computed; the abstract's 'for some absolute beta < 4/3' is literal. The introduction's survey lists no earlier improvement of the exponent 4/3 (its earlier results are a constant-factor improvement, a structural description, and a conditional logarithmic improvement), so this is the first power saving the family reports. The text flags no step as sketched and contains no explicit hedge. The introduction's outline is informal, and the decisive steps (the prediction lemma, the height bounds, popular-unit-circle deletion, and the sign-change argument over a finite radical field in Section 7) are long and use nonstandard constructions.
how-many-unit-distances.direction: improves the upper bound: power saving, u(n) = O(n^beta) with beta < 4/3
