values-of-the-ramsey-numbers-particularl.what_happened: Two OpenAI manuscripts in the openai/math release claim the sharp logarithmic exponent of off-diagonal classical Ramsey numbers r(s,t) (the two-colour numbers R(s,t) in the problem's notation; r(s,t) is the least n such that every graph on n vertices has a K_s or an independent t-set). (1) 'The Sharp Logarithmic Exponent of r(5,t)' (paper.tex, dated 24 September 2026) claims, for an absolute constant C, that for every eps>0 and all sufficiently large t, t^4/(log t)^(3+eps) <= r(5,t) <= C t^4/(log t)^3, hence lim (4 log t - log r(5,t))/log log t = 3, i.e. r(5,t) = t^4/(log t)^(3+o(1)). The lower bound comes from a K_5-free graph on floor(q^4 log q) vertices with independence number below q(log q)^(1+eta), for prime q near t/(log t)^(1+eta) (Bertrand's postulate). The graph's vertices are positions in a random stream of ordered point-hyperplane flags (a in PG(4,q), b a hyperplane containing a), with an edge for i<j when a_i lies on b_j but a_j does not lie on b_i; the existence of a stream with no long consistent subsequence is shown by an entropy/compression contradiction. The upper bound is an elementary sampling argument (uniform independent sets, triangle-free independence bound, random sampling and deletion), giving r(5,t) <= C t^4/(log t)^3. (2) 'Sharp Logarithmic Exponents for Fixed Off-Diagonal Ramsey Numbers' (main.tex, dated 24 September 2026) claims, for each fixed s >= 6 and constant C_s, that for every eps>0 and all sufficiently large t, t^(s-1)/(log t)^(s-2+eps) <= r(s,t) <= C_s t^(s-1)/(log t)^(s-2), hence lim ((s-1) log t - log r(s,t))/log log t = s-2. It runs the same method in PG(d,q) with d = s-1 >= 5, producing K_(d+1)-free graphs on floor(q^d log q) vertices with independence number below q(log q)^(1+eta) (Theorem intro:prime-construction, proved via the entropy contradiction in end:section), and derives the upper bound by induction on s (Proposition end:upper-bound, stated for every s >= 2). Together the two manuscripts cover every fixed s >= 5.
values-of-the-ramsey-numbers-particularl.delivers: Asymptotic information only, for the family r(s,t) with s fixed (s >= 5) and t -> infinity: the logarithmic exponent of r(s,t) is s-2 over t^(s-1), i.e. r(s,t) = t^(s-1)/(log t)^(s-2+o(1)). This is a statement about the order of magnitude of one row of the two-colour table, in the off-diagonal regime. It does not determine the value of any R(r,s), and it gives no numerical bound on any specific value: the constants are unspecified (absolute C and C_s), and the lower bound carries (log t)^eps slack that absorbs constants. Neither manuscript mentions the diagonal number R(5,5) or any diagonal value, and the asymptotic regime (s fixed, t large) does not reach R(5,5). The manuscripts do not claim to determine the values of the Ramsey numbers. Paper 2 explicitly says its theorem 'does not assert that r(s,t) is bounded below by a positive constant times t^(s-1)/(log t)^(s-2)'. Neither manuscript restates the list's problem; both state an asymptotic exponent for r(s,t), which is a different question from determining the values. These results are progress only in the bound sense the matching pass recorded.
values-of-the-ramsey-numbers-particularl.remains: If the claims are correct, still open for this problem: (a) the exact value of R(5,5), and the values of R(r,s) generally; the problem's own statement gives 43 <= R(5,5) <= 46, which neither manuscript changes; (b) for R(s,t) with s fixed, the constant-factor asymptotic: paper 1 says it 'leaves open a constant-factor asymptotic for t^4/(log t)^3', and paper 2 leaves open whether r(s,t) is bounded below by c_s t^(s-1)/(log t)^(s-2); (c) any explicit (non-probabilistic) lower-bound construction, since the lower-bound graphs are shown to exist by a contradiction argument; (d) all regimes other than s fixed with t -> infinity, including the diagonal case and the multicolour, hypergraph and graph-Ramsey readings of the bare phrase 'the Ramsey numbers'.

machine_checked.scope:
The formalization determines the sharp logarithmic exponent of the off-diagonal Ramsey number $r(5,t)$. It proves
$r(5,t)=t^4/(\log t)^{3+o(1)}$ as $t\to\infty$.
For every $\varepsilon>0$, the lower bound $t^4/(\log t)^{3+\varepsilon}$ holds eventually, while the upper bound is $Ct^4/(\log t)^3$ for an absolute $C>0$. The corresponding logarithmic exponent converges to three along all natural values of $t$.

The formalization determines the sharp logarithmic exponent of the off-diagonal Ramsey number for every fixed integer $s\ge6$. It proves
$r(s,t)=t^{s-1}/(\log t)^{s-2+o(1)}$ as $t\to\infty$.
More explicitly, for each $\varepsilon>0$ the lower bound $t^{s-1}/(\log t)^{s-2+\varepsilon}$ holds eventually, while the upper bound is $C_s t^{s-1}/(\log t)^{s-2}$. The logarithmic exponent limit is taken along all natural values of $t$.

values-of-the-ramsey-numbers-particularl.doubts: Paper 1: the lower bound rests on the stream theorem (compression-tree.tex, thm:stream) and the sparse-pair description theorem (predictor-statement.tex, thm:predictor). The proof of the compression stage (prop:compression-stage) is a short paragraph that assembles lemmas from other files (lem:marking, lem:decoupling, lem:high-ranks, lem:flat-levels, lem:pivot-retention, lem:pivot-compression), and the text does not label any step as sketched or conditional. The lower bound is only as strong as that chain. The theorem's constants are absolute, and the limit statement is equivalent to the stated two-sided bound. Paper 2: the text cites the companion paper for the s = 5 framework that it adapts to d >= 5, and also says the present paper supplies all the required arguments locally; the text does not say precisely which companion results are carried over versus re-proved. The uniformity of constants across the T+1 compression stages is argued by a recursive prescription (06-conclusion, the paragraph beginning 'The constants and thresholds can be fixed without knowing the actual conditional laws') rather than by explicit computation. Both manuscripts hold their statements for sufficiently large q or t with thresholds not made explicit.; conditional on: No unproven hypothesis is assumed; both results are claimed unconditional. Paper 2's rich-subspace bound is said to be a consequence of Nie and Wang's finite-degree closure inequality (Theorems 4.1 and 5.6), though a self-contained evaluation-rank proof is given. Paper 2's theorem is not derived from paper 1's theorem; it depends on paper 1 only through the framework it cites.

values-of-the-ramsey-numbers-particularl.what_happened: One manuscript, 'The hypercube Ramsey number has linear order' (OpenAI, dated 23 September 2026). Its main theorem (Theorem 1.1 in build/sections/01-introduction.tex, repeated in the abstract) claims that there is an absolute constant C > 0 with R(Qₙ) ≤ C·2ⁿ for every integer n ≥ 0. Here Qₙ is the n-dimensional cube graph, and R(H) is the least M such that every red-blue colouring of the edges of K_M contains a monochromatic copy of H, not required to be induced. The abstract says this resolves the Burr–Erdős hypercube Ramsey conjecture positively. The introduction also gives the lower bound R(Qₙ) ≥ 3·2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1, from an explicit two-block colouring, so R(Qₙ) is of order 2ⁿ. Two corollaries are stated: for a spanning subgraph F of Qd, R(F^□k) ≤ C·|V(F)|ᵏ with the same C for all k; and for a subgraph H of Qd with 2ᵈ ≤ A·|V(H)|, R(H) ≤ C·A·|V(H)|. The method is a proof by contradiction along sequences, with a discrepancy and patch-tiling argument over eighteen sections, ending in a Hall-matching step.
values-of-the-ramsey-numbers-particularl.delivers: Only under a graph-Ramsey reading of 'the Ramsey numbers' (the scope note allows Ramsey numbers of graphs H). On that reading, the claim fixes the order of growth of the two-colour cube Ramsey numbers: linear in the number of cube vertices, with an unspecified constant. The manuscript does not say it settles this problem, and its statement is not the list's: it concerns cube graphs, not classical numbers R(r,s). On the classical reading (R(r,s) for pairs r, s, and in particular R(5,5)), the manuscript gives no value or bound for any R(r,s), does not discuss R(k,k), and uses 'diagonal' only to mean that the cube grows in both colours. It delivers nothing for that reading.
values-of-the-ramsey-numbers-particularl.remains: On the graph-Ramsey reading: the constant C is not identified, and the paper says it does not determine whether R(Qₙ)/2ⁿ converges or what its limit would be. On the classical reading, everything in problem_asks remains open: R(r,s) for all pairs r, s, and the exact value of R(5,5), which problem_asks records as known only to satisfy 43 ≤ R(5,5) ≤ 46. The manuscript does not touch R(5,5).
values-of-the-ramsey-numbers-particularl.doubts: The text flags no step as unproven, and the abstract and Theorem 1.1 agree. Points in the text that bear on how far to read it at face value: (i) the argument is non-constructive and gives no numerical C; (ii) the proof is long, roughly 10,000 lines of TeX across eighteen sections and an appendix table of regimes, and it works with constants chosen in a stated order and 'for large n' conventions throughout; (iii) build/sections/02-reduction-and-notation.tex (lines 59–60) says: 'We leave integer roundoffs in scales and layer counts implicit when the accompanying asymptotic inequalities have slack'; (iv) the late-prefix transfer lemma (build/sections/18-late-dynamics-and-its-transfer-problem.tex, Lemma late-prefix-transfer), which the text itself names as the step still needing a transfer, is given after a short roadmap and then as compressed estimates.
values-of-the-ramsey-numbers-particularl.direction: proves the Burr–Erdős hypercube conjecture positively (linear order, unspecified constant); no bearing on classical R(r,s) or R(5,5)
values-of-the-ramsey-numbers-particularl.object: No explicit upper-bound object. The upper bound is proved by contradiction and gives no colouring of K_{C·2ⁿ} and no numerical C. The explicit object is the two-block lower-bound colouring for n ≥ 1: vertex blocks of sizes 2ⁿ − 1 and 2ⁿ⁻¹ − 1, edges inside a block red, edges between the blocks blue. A red Qₙ does not fit in a block, and a blue Qₙ would need 2ⁿ⁻¹ vertices in each block. The text attributes this construction to Conlon, Fox, Lee and Sudakov.

values-of-the-ramsey-numbers-particularl.what_happened: One manuscript, 'Cycle–clique Ramsey numbers' (OpenAI, dated September 25, 2026), claims the exact value R(Cₘ,Kₙ) = (m−1)(n−1)+1 for every pair m ≥ n ≥ 3 other than (m,n)=(3,3), where it gives R(C₃,K₃)=6. R(H,J) is the least N such that every red/blue colouring of the edges of K_N contains a red H or a blue J; Cₘ is a cycle on m vertices and Kₙ a clique on n vertices, and copies need not be induced. The lower bound is an explicit colouring: n−1 disjoint red copies of K_{m−1} with all edges between different copies blue. The upper bound is claimed as a proof of the Erdős–Faudree–Rousseau–Schelp cycle–clique conjecture, by contradiction from a minimal counterexample G with no cycle on k+1 = m vertices and independence number at most a = n−1. Expansion of independent sets (|N[I]| ≥ k|I|+1) and a large-clique lemma give a maximum clique of order t with max{3,⌊k/2⌋} ≤ t ≤ k. The paper then handles k = 3, 4 and t ≥ 9 by hand, and for 5 ≤ k ≤ 17 with 3 ≤ t ≤ 8 (42 parameter pairs, 3,099 pattern instances) it runs a finite enumeration of path-system patterns, which it reports gives a contradiction in every case. The abstract says the paper establishes the conjecture. The R(C₃,K₃)=6 lower bound uses a red 5-cycle with blue complementary 5-cycle on K₅.
values-of-the-ramsey-numbers-particularl.delivers: Exact values of the two-colour graph Ramsey numbers R(Cₘ,Kₙ) for all m ≥ n ≥ 3, i.e. one two-parameter family of cycle-versus-clique numbers, and with it the Erdős–Faudree–Rousseau–Schelp conjecture in the Keevash–Long–Skokan formulation, which the paper says it establishes in full. The paper does not state the Ramsey problem in the bullet's words and does not claim to settle it. Reading A (classical two-colour numbers R(r,s), complete graphs in both colours): nothing new is determined. The only overlap is R(C₃,K₃)=6, which is the classical value R(3,3)=6 since C₃=K₃; R(5,5) and its bounds 43 ≤ R(5,5) ≤ 46 are not touched, since R(C₅,K₅)=17 by the formula is a different number. Reading B (graph-Ramsey numbers in general): the paper adds exact values for every cycle-versus-clique pair with m ≥ n ≥ 3, and nothing for other pairs of graphs. So the family bears on the bullet only under Reading B, and then only on the cycle–clique subfamily.
values-of-the-ramsey-numbers-particularl.remains: Reading A: essentially all of it, including the determination of R(r,s) for the complete-graph pairs and the exact value of R(5,5). Reading B: Ramsey numbers for graph pairs other than cycle versus clique, such as R(Kᵣ,Kₛ) with r,s ≥ 4, which the paper does not address, and multicolour, hypergraph and graph-Ramsey numbers outside this family. Within cycle versus clique nothing remains, if the claim is correct.

machine_checked.scope: The cycle–clique Ramsey conjecture predicts the exact number of vertices forcing either a cycle $C_m$ or a clique $K_n$ in complementary colors. The formalization proves $R(C_m,K_n)=(m-1)(n-1)+1$ for all integers $m\ge n\ge3$ except $(m,n)=(3,3)$, where it proves $R(C_3,K_3)=6$. This is the complete parameter range of the paper's main theorem.

values-of-the-ramsey-numbers-particularl.doubts: (1) The finite part is a computer calculation: 3,049 patterns with output 1 and 50 with output 2 (3,099 in all, over 42 parameter pairs). Section 9 states the inference rules and the pattern-enumeration argument, but the text reproduces only the compact program (Appendix, Section 10); the second implementation and the full deduction traces are supplied as separate files. The paper says the traces are 'not offered as proof objects for an additional independent minimal validator', so checking this part means re-running code, not reading a written proof. (2) The t ≥ 9 exclusion (Section 8) and the clique bound (Section 3) are long hand arguments that rely on many lemmas across Sections 3–8; the introduction describes one step as 'a short numerical classification'. No step in the sections I read is flagged as sketched or conditional. (3) The abstract calls the result the full conjecture; the introduction says the conjectured range was already known for n = 4–7 and partly for n = 8, and that this paper completes the range. I found no inconsistency between the abstract and Theorem 1.1.; conditional on: No unproved hypothesis is assumed, and the paper uses no other manuscript. The finite part for 5 ≤ k ≤ 17 and 3 ≤ t ≤ 8 rests on the paper's own computer enumeration (the two programs in verification/code, which the paper says give the same results), not on a written-out hand proof.

values-of-the-ramsey-numbers-particularl.object: The lower-bound colouring is explicit: n−1 disjoint red K_{m−1} with all cross edges blue. For R(C₃,K₃) ≥ 6 the colouring of K₅ by a red 5-cycle and a blue complementary 5-cycle is explicit. second-neighborhood-problem.what_happened: One manuscript, 'A proof of Seymour's second-neighborhood conjecture' (OpenAI, dated 23 September 2026), claims Theorem 1.1: every nonempty finite oriented graph has a vertex v with |N₁⁺(v)| ≤ |N₂⁺(v)|, where N₂⁺(v) is the set of vertices at exact directed distance two from v (excluding v and its out-neighbours, each counted once). The proof is by contradiction. Proposition 2.1 reduces a minimal counterexample (fewest vertices, then fewest arcs) to a graph G with positive indegrees in which every nonempty proper vertex set U satisfies |U| + |F²(U)| < 2|F(U)|, where F is the one-step out-image; Lemma 2.2 (subset deficit, adapted from Seacrest's Lemma 4) and Lemma 2.3 (transitive-tournament blow-up) give this. Section 3 (Lemma 3.1, a pruning bound for two families of ordered pairs, proved by a rank/matching argument) and Proposition 4.1 then rule out any such G. The same manuscript also derives, in Section 5 (Corollary 5.1) via Seacrest's 2015 equivalences, vertex-weighted forms (for every nonnegative vertex weighting some v has η(N₁⁺(v)) ≤ η(N₂⁺(v)); and a total-mass-one weighting under which every v satisfies this) and an arc-weighted form, and in Section 6 (Corollary 6.1) directed-cycle consequences: a digraph with no directed triangle has some v with d⁺(v) ≤ |Z(v)| and n−1 ≥ 2d⁺(v)+d⁻(v); minimum in- and outdegree at least n/3 forces a directed triangle; and a regular digraph with d⁺ = d⁻ = r and directed girth 4 has n ≥ 3r+1.
second-neighborhood-problem.delivers: Claims to settle the problem as the list states it. The list asks whether every oriented graph (no loops, no parallel arcs, no digons) has a vertex with at least as many vertices at distance two as at distance one. Theorem 1.1 gives exactly that, for every nonempty finite oriented graph, with no connectivity, degree or order hypothesis; a sink satisfies it trivially. The manuscript measures out-distance; reversing all arcs gives the in-distance reading, so both readings are covered. Tournaments, the special case known as Dean's conjecture, are covered by the general statement. The manuscript's wording matches the list's: its abstract says it 'resolves Seymour's second neighborhood conjecture positively', and Section 1 calls Theorem 1.1 that resolution.
second-neighborhood-problem.remains: Nothing, if the claim is correct: the problem asks only for the existence of such a vertex in every oriented graph, which Theorem 1.1 states. The weighted forms and directed-cycle consequences (Sections 5 and 6) go beyond what the problem asks.

machine_checked.scope: Seymour's second-neighborhood conjecture asserts that every nonempty finite oriented graph has a vertex with at least as many second out-neighbors as first out-neighbors. The formalized result proves this assertion, where the second neighborhood consists of vertices at directed distance exactly two. The initial vertex and first neighbors are excluded from that count, and sinks are included.

second-neighborhood-problem.doubts: The argument is a long contradiction proof across Sections 2 to 4. Its most compressed step is the choice of coefficients in Lemma 3.1: the text relies on the cited Edmonds correspondence and a brief argument that the required minors can be nonzero at one real assignment (a product of nonzero polynomials). It does not flag this as sketched, but it is the least expanded part. The manuscript reports no computer verification. Its weighted and arc-weighted consequences depend on Seacrest's equivalences, which it cites and does not reprove.; conditional on: None for Theorem 1.1 beyond published results it cites: Edmonds (1967) for the generic-rank/matching correspondence used in Lemma 3.1, and König's theorem (re-derived in the text). Corollary 5.1 (weighted and arc-weighted forms) rests on Seacrest (2015), Proposition 2 and Theorem 1, cited rather than proved in the manuscript; that dependence does not affect the problem's own statement.

barnettes-conjecture.what_happened: The manuscript 'Paired states and Hamiltonian cycles in cubic bipartite planar graphs' (OpenAI, dated 24 September 2026; the only manuscript in this family) claims a proof of Barnette's conjecture: every finite simple cubic, bipartite, planar, 3-vertex-connected graph has a Hamiltonian cycle (Theorem 1.1 in the Introduction; the abstract says 'We prove Barnette's conjecture'). The method passes to the sphere dual, a triangulation whose faces are colored black and white. It proves a partition of the triangulation's vertices into two sets, each inducing a tree (every edge between its vertices included), with the endpoints of any chosen facial edge in one set and the third vertex of that face in the other (Theorem 2.2, the partition theorem). The complement of the induced edges in the original graph is then a single spanning cycle, which is the Hamiltonian cycle. The partition is obtained from a finite weighted exponential sum over pairs of 'states' (incidence matchings between black faces and non-root vertices). Cancellation of terms whose second state gives a cyclic graph, together with a positive-circulation argument showing the sum is nonzero, forces some pair whose second state gives a forest. Plane-tree duality and a disk-counting identity then yield the two induced trees. Separating triangles are handled by induction, splitting along the triangle and gluing the partitions. The paper also states, as corollaries, single-edge avoidance (a Hamiltonian cycle avoiding any prescribed edge) and that every three-edge path in a Pfaffian cubic 3-connected bipartite graph lies in a Hamiltonian cycle; both are derived from the main theorem and the cited Gorsky-Steiner-Wiederrecht equivalence.
barnettes-conjecture.delivers: If correct, the claim proves the full statement of the list's problem for the whole class: every finite simple cubic bipartite 3-vertex-connected planar graph is Hamiltonian. No face-size, order, or other restriction is imposed beyond the class itself. The paper's statement matches the list's: it uses the same hypotheses (cubic, bipartite, planar, 3-vertex-connected, finite simple) and asks the same question (existence of a Hamiltonian cycle). The one convention the paper states is that 3-vertex-connected requires at least four vertices and that deleting at most two vertices leaves the graph connected; this excludes no bipartite cubic planar 3-connected graph. The result is existence only: the paper says the argument places no bound on order or face length and does not assert a polynomial-time construction of the cycle. The problem asks only for existence, so this is not a gap for it.
barnettes-conjecture.remains: Nothing of the bullet's question remains open if the claim is correct. The paper does not address a polynomial-time or explicit construction of the cycle, which the list's bullet does not ask for.

machine_checked.scope: Barnette's conjecture states that every finite simple cubic bipartite planar graph that is 3-vertex-connected has a Hamiltonian cycle. The formalization proves this statement for every such graph. The selected result is the existence of a cycle visiting every vertex exactly once.

barnettes-conjecture.doubts: The paper does not flag any step as sketched and does not hedge the main claim, whose abstract states the result without qualification. Several steps that carry weight are compressed into a few sentences with no displayed verification: (i) the lemma producing positive spoke circulations, whose proof prescribes face circulations and sums along dual paths in one paragraph; (ii) the isotopy argument that the detoured spoke curve is simple and counterclockwise, which is asserted in a few sentences; (iii) the grouping step that the pairs with a given undirected edge set are exactly the independent orientation choices on its cycles; (iv) the leading-coefficient argument that contributions from different groups cannot cancel; and (v) the gluing across separating triangles, where the claim that the two induced trees meet in a connected subtree is stated in one sentence. The paper's Pfaffian corollary is labelled a consequence of the cited equivalence, so its strength depends on that external result.; conditional on: The main theorem's proof does not assume any hypothesis beyond the paper's own lemmas. It uses standard facts without proof: Euler's formula, the max-flow/min-cut principle (Ford-Fulkerson 1956), and a two-orientations regrouping of cycle covers that the paper cites to Kenyon 2014 (Section 3.2.1, Lemma 1) and does not reprove; that regrouping is used in the nonvanishing step. The Pfaffian three-edge-path corollary, which is not the main theorem, depends on Gorsky, Steiner and Wiederrecht 2023 (Theorem 4.16 for the equivalence, Theorem 4.6 for planar graphs being Pfaffian), cited and not proved. The single-edge-avoidance corollary is proved directly from the construction; its equivalence with Barnette's conjecture (Kelmans, via Hertel 2005 and Gorsky-Steiner-Wiederrecht 2023) is cited as context only.

finding-matching-upper-and-lower-bounds-.what_happened: One manuscript in the family: “A power saving for planar halving lines” (OpenAI, dated September 25, 2026). Its Theorem 1 (thm:halving-power) says there are absolute constants ε>0, C and n0 such that every even n ≥ n0 and every n-point set in R² with no three collinear has h(P) ≤ C n^{4/3−ε} unordered halving pairs; since distinct pairs give distinct lines, this bounds halving lines too. This improves the classical O(n^{4/3}) halving-line bound that the introduction attributes to Dey (1998). The core is Theorem 2 (thm:all-ranks): for a generic N-point planar configuration and any rank k, the number of switches S_k(P) in a rank-k sweep is at most C N^{4/3−ε}, uniformly in k. The middle-rank case gives Theorem 1. Corollary 3 (cor:k-sensitive) is the k-set statement: for every n-point Q ⊂ R² with no three collinear and every 1 ≤ k ≤ n/2, the number of k-sets is at most C₀ n (k+1)^{1/3−ε₀}, with absolute ε₀ > 0 (the proof takes ε₀ = min{ε, 1/6}). The same bound is given for the complexity of a level in an arrangement of n non-vertical lines with no parallel pair and no three concurrent. Dey's bound for k-sets is O(n(k+1)^{1/3}) (stated in the manuscript's introduction), so the new result improves the exponent of (k+1) from 1/3 to 1/3−ε₀. At k near n/2 it gives about n^{4/3−ε₀}, the same order as the new halving bound. The proof is a finite reduction to exchange graphs and crossing counts, followed by a proof by contradiction that produces a uniform little-o improvement of a packing estimate. That improvement is taken from a limiting spatial measure of dimension 32/17, and a fixed-scale induction turns it into the power saving. The manuscript gives no lower-bound result of its own. It recalls the existing lower bounds for halving lines, Ω(n log n) from Erdős, Lovász, Simmons and Straus and n·exp(Ω(√log n)) from Tóth and Nivasch, and says they remain far below any fixed power n^{1+δ}.
finding-matching-upper-and-lower-bounds-.delivers: For the upper-bound half of the problem, the claim establishes: (i) for planar halving lines, a bound of O(n^{4/3−ε}) for even n ≥ n0 with no three collinear, for an absolute but unspecified ε > 0; (ii) for planar k-sets, a bound of O(n(k+1)^{1/3−ε₀}) for all 1 ≤ k ≤ n/2 and no three collinear, for an absolute but unspecified ε₀ > 0; (iii) the same level-complexity bound for arrangements of complete straight lines (not pseudolines, not segments), which the manuscript says gives no corresponding saving for pseudolines or line segments. The constants and exponents are nonquantitative: no numerical value of ε, ε₀, C, C₀ or n0 is given. The results are planar only. Nothing in the manuscript is stated for dimensions above two. The claim is an upper bound only. It gives no lower bound for k-sets or for halving lines, and it does not show that the upper and lower bounds have the same order. The abstract and the theorems describe a power saving over O(n^{4/3}); the manuscripts do not claim to settle the problem, and their framing does not say the problem is solved.
finding-matching-upper-and-lower-bounds-.remains: If the claim is correct, the following remain open. (a) Halving lines: the gap between the new upper bound n^{4/3−ε} and the known lower bounds of order n·exp(Ω(√log n)) (and the older Ω(n log n)) is not closed, and the manuscript itself says the lower bounds stay far below any fixed power n^{1+δ}. (b) K-sets: the manuscripts give no lower bound at all for the maximum number of k-sets as a function of n and k, so the matching-bounds question for part (a) of problem_asks is open in full. The k-dependence exponent 1/3−ε₀ is not claimed to be tight. (c) The value of the exponent is not determined, so even the upper bound is not explicit. (d) Dimensions above two, and pseudoline or segment settings, are not addressed.

machine_checked.scope: A halving pair in an even planar point set is a pair whose line leaves equally many remaining points on each side. The formalization proves that some absolute $\varepsilon>0$ and $C$ bound the number of halving pairs by $Cn^{4/3-\varepsilon}$ for every sufficiently large even $n$ and every $n$-point set with no three collinear. It also proves a bound of the same form for all level-switch counts under the additional generic-position assumptions in the statement. The constants are existential.

finding-matching-upper-and-lower-bounds-.doubts: (1) The power saving depends on Theorem activity-packing, a little-o improvement of a packing estimate. Its proof is by contradiction (rank-limits.tex opens with 'suppose, for a contradiction'; boundary.tex closes it) and runs through rank coordinates, differentiability, a zoom lemma, a spatial measure, and a strip count. That chain is long and several links are stated in prose. The introduction says the conditional-measure and Lipschitz-differentiability statements are 'specified at their applications'. (2) The introduction calls the limit order 'crucial': limits are taken first at a fixed small rank scale and then far along the sequence of configurations. boundary.tex also says that restriction to G is done only after weak convergence, and that the limits along countably many windows come from diagonal subsequences. (3) finite.tex, eq. (finite-localized-crossing), keeps an additive 13824 S³ term, and the text says this term 'may only be discarded after an appropriate limiting normalization'. (4) Some proofs are only partly written out. The spatial proposition's proof begins with 'We first select a positive set' and relies on a metric input stated only as eq. (spatial-metric-input), with its own quantifiers. The zoom lemma is called elementary but its proof is long. (5) The k-set corollary's level-to-cell step is given in outline ('the cited shallow-cutting reduction now gives'). (6) The abstract, the introduction and Theorem 1 agree with each other. I found no inconsistency between the statements and the main theorems. The text says the constants are nonquantitative, which limits how far the bound can be checked numerically.; conditional on: No unproven hypothesis is assumed by the theorems. Some steps rely on cited external results that the manuscript does not reprove: the shallow-cutting lemma of Matoušek as stated by Agarwal, Aronov, Chan and Sharir (used for the level and k-set corollary, in recurrence.tex, where the cut-to-level step is stated as following from the cited reduction); and standard background cited in the introduction (Simon 2014 for differentiation of finite measures; Chabrillac and Crouzeix 1987 for monotone-function differentiability, which the text also proves in outline). The imbalanced crossing argument is attributed to Pach, Solymosi and Tardos, and the classical crossing lemma to Ajtai et al. and Leighton; the manuscript says it reproves the reduction and constants it needs. improving-lower-and-upper-bounds-for-the.what_happened: One manuscript in this family: 'A power improvement in the Heilbronn triangle lower bound' (OpenAI, dated 25 September 2026). It claims the main theorem of the Introduction: there are absolute constants η, c₁ > 0 and an integer n₀ ≥ 3 such that Δ(n) ≥ c₁·n^(−2+η) for every integer n ≥ n₀, where Δ(n) is the largest, over n-point sets P in the unit square, of the smallest triangle area determined by P. The abstract states the same as: for every sufficiently large n one can place n points in the unit square with every determined triangle of area at least c₁·n^(−2+η). The manuscript gives the exponent explicitly as η = 2/(45435k+16) for an integer k ≥ 2 (Section 8, equation alt:exponent); k = 2 gives η = 1/45443, about 2.2×10⁻⁵. The construction works over prime-indexed sizes n_r ≈ r^α with α = 45435k+16, using a field-norm determinant obstruction over F_{r^41}, integral columns lifted from residues modulo h = B^k and a second prime q, a random sample of 2n_r such columns, and deletion of one index from each violating pair or triple (Sections 3–8). Interpolation to every large n uses a Bertrand-type prime-interval lemma (Appendix). The manuscript also states that this disproves the almost-n^(−2) upper-bound formulation: for every ε > 0 it asks for C_ε with Δ(n) ≤ C_ε·n^(−2+ε), and taking ε = η/2 contradicts the lower bound. The prior lower bound it improves is Komlós–Pintz–Szemerédi's Δ(n) ≫ (log n)/n², which the Introduction recalls. The manuscript does not claim any new upper bound on Δ(n); it cites Komlós–Pintz–Szemerédi (n^(−8/7+ε)) and Cohen–Pohoata–Zakharov (n^(−7/6+ε)) only as background.
improving-lower-and-upper-bounds-for-the.delivers: A lower-bound improvement only, for the unit square, which is the container in the list's working reading. Its definition of Δ(n) (maximum over P ⊂ [0,1]² with |P| = n of the minimum over unordered distinct triples of Area(pqr); collinear triples give 0) matches that reading. If correct, it establishes Δ(n) ≥ c₁·n^(−2+η) for all n ≥ n₀ with η = 2/(45435k+16), k ≥ 2 an integer. Only η is explicit; c₁ and n₀ are existence claims, and the constants A_k, D_k, C_k are introduced as 'fixed constants' without computation. This converts the earlier log factor into a power gain n^η, and it refutes the almost-n^(−2) upper-bound formulation, which the list's problem does not itself ask about. The statement of the problem as the list gives it asks for improved lower and upper bounds on the order of Δ(n). The manuscript settles only the lower-bound half, and only as a power gain with a very small exponent. It does not claim to settle the problem.
improving-lower-and-upper-bounds-for-the.remains: If the claim is correct: (1) the upper-bound half of the list's question is untouched; the best upper bounds the manuscript cites remain n^(−7/6+ε) (Cohen–Pohoata–Zakharov) and the true order of Δ(n) is not determined; the gap between n^(−2+η) and n^(−7/6+ε) is unchanged in kind. (2) The exponent η ≈ 2×10⁻⁵ is not optimised, and the text says no attempt was made to optimise the construction parameters. (3) The constants c₁ and n₀ are not quantified. (4) Only the unit square is treated; the variant containers the list names as analogues (unit disc, convex regions of unit area, equilateral or right triangles, the cube and higher dimensions, k-gons) are not addressed. (5) Exact small-n values are not addressed.

machine_checked.scope: Heilbronn's triangle problem asks how large the smallest triangle determined by $n$ points in the unit square can be. The formalization constructs an unbounded sequence of sizes $n$ and point sets for which every triangle has area at least $n^{-2+\eta}$, for one fixed $\eta>0$. It consequently refutes the proposed upper bound of order $n^{-2+\varepsilon}$ for every $\varepsilon>0$. The linked construction is for an unbounded sequence of sizes; the paper's statement for every sufficiently large $n$ is broader.

improving-lower-and-upper-bounds-for-the.doubts: No step is flagged as sketched or conjectural, and the abstract and the main theorem agree. Points in the text that bear on how far the statement is quantified: (i) only the exponent η is explicit, while n₀ and c₁ are asserted to exist through the constants A_k, D_k and C_k, which the text does not compute; (ii) the zero-determinant case is handled by an auxiliary construction which the text says is proved in a later section (Section 7); (iii) the Introduction records that two other preprints (Ellmann 2025, Agama 2026) claim stronger power lower bounds but have flagged unproved steps; the manuscript does not rely on those preprints, and the remark concerns those claims rather than this one.
improving-lower-and-upper-bounds-for-the.direction: improves the lower bound by a power (log factor replaced by n^η); disproves the almost-n^(−2) upper-bound formulation
improving-lower-and-upper-bounds-for-the.object: Not explicit. The n points are chosen by existence: a random sample of 2n_r integral columns projected to [0,1)² (built from random field labels, digit matrices, auxiliary residues and lifts) has expected number of violating pairs and triples EZ = o(n_r), so some outcome has Z < n_r; deleting one index per violation and keeping any n of the remaining points gives the set. Algebraic structure (the field-norm polynomial and the Chinese remainder theorem over h and q) is explicit, but the final point set is picked from a probability space rather than given by a formula.

serres-positivity-conjecture.what_happened: Manuscript 'Positivity of Serre's Intersection Multiplicity' (build/paper.tex, dated September 23, 2026). Its Theorem 1.1 (thm:main) claims: for a commutative Noetherian regular local ring (R, m) of dimension d, and nonzero finitely generated R-modules M, N with length(M tensor N) < infinity and dim M + dim N = d, the Serre multiplicity chi^R(M,N) = sum_i (-1)^i length Tor_i^R(M,N) is strictly positive. The abstract and introduction say this proves Serre's positivity conjecture with no restriction on characteristic or ramification, and without requiring either module to lift to an unramified base. Taking M = R/P and N = R/Q gives the list's statement. The proof (sections lengths, descent, asymptotic, positivity) reduces to complete domain pairs D = R/P, E = R/Q of dimensions h, l > 0 with h + l = d, over a complete base with algebraically closed residue field of characteristic p > 0; the equicharacteristic case is attributed to Serre. It then builds normalized-length algebras C_D and C_E over regular normalization bases, equates ordinary and normalized Euler sums over Galois conjugates (supported rational descent, Theorem ds:descent; asymptotic norm comparison, Theorem as:norm), and shows each term is positive using a uniform lower bound on minimal generator counts. Separately, Corollary cor:tangent-cone (introduction, 'Consequences') states chi^A(A/P,A/Q) >= e(A/P) e(A/Q) for primes P, Q of a regular local A with A/(P+Q) of finite length, complementary dimensions and dim T <= 1, with equality iff dim T = 0. The same section derives from Theorem 1.1, via Kurano--Roberts, the containment P cap Q^(r) contained in m^(r+1) for r >= 1, for ramified R with sqrt(P+Q) = m and ht P + ht Q = dim R.
serres-positivity-conjecture.delivers: If correct, establishes the list's statement for every commutative regular local ring: for primes P, Q with dim R/P + dim R/Q = dim R, chi(R/P,R/Q) > 0, with no restriction on characteristic, ramification or lifting. The manuscript says it proves the conjecture. Its statement matches the list's in two respects that differ: (a) it adds the hypothesis length(R/(P+Q)) < infinity, i.e. P+Q is m-primary, which chi needs in order to be defined and which the list's wording leaves implicit; (b) it proves Serre's module form, which is more general than the prime-quotient form the list asks about. Otherwise the statement matches: nonzero, finitely generated, commutative Noetherian regular local ring, with strict positivity as the conclusion. No dimension range, bound or counterexample is involved.
serres-positivity-conjecture.remains: If the claim holds, nothing in the bullet or in problem_asks (1)-(4) remains open. Outside the claim: prime pairs with R/(P+Q) of infinite length, for which chi is undefined and the list's inequality has no content. The corollary and the symbolic-power consequence in the introduction are additional statements, not parts of the list's problem.
serres-positivity-conjecture.doubts: The text flags no step as sketched, but it compresses or cites several key steps. (1) The mixed-characteristic input (Theorem len:input, mixed case) is one short paragraph. It says 'the stated hypotheses there are exactly' those of CLMST and Bhatt-Scholze, then applies their results to C_D without checking those hypotheses in the text. (2) Several structural lemmas are argued in a few sentences: residue-field extension (len:residue-extension), normalization (len:normalization), the tower and its length (len:tower), and the orbit argument in the descent proof. In len:normalization the positive-characteristic case, including generic separability of A in D, is attributed to Cohen-Gabber, with no separate argument for the separability clause. (3) Statement and proof differ in Theorem ds:descent: it states that the K_0 map is surjective, but its proof concludes that it is an isomorphism ('in fact as an isomorphism'). The text does not reconcile the two. (4) Corollary cor:tangent-cone assumes dim T <= 1, which the proof uses only implicitly, to assert that S is finite. It applies lemmas from Skalit's SkalitUnramified, whose title is 'in the unramified case', to a general regular A, and does not say why the unramified hypothesis is unnecessary. (5) The symbolic-power consequence is introduced with 'now gives' via Kurano-Roberts Thm. 3.2, without restating that theorem's hypotheses. (6) Footnote 1 records a public post dated December 9, 2025 by Editan, credited also to Copilot and Gemini, asserting the same prime-quotient form. The authors record it as a same-scope claim, 'not as an established theorem', and give no further account of it.; conditional on: No hypothesis beyond the theorem's own. The argument does rely on published results it cites rather than proves: the Roberts and Gillet-Soule vanishing theorem (pos:vanishing, used in the reduction); Serre's theorem for the equicharacteristic case; Cohen-Gabber normalization in characteristic p (cited via Kurano-Shimomoto); in mixed characteristic, the perfectoid length results of Cai-Lee-Ma-Schwede-Tucker (Cor. 4.0.4, Props. 4.0.10 and 4.0.14, on Bhatt-Scholze Prop. 8.5) and Faltings' normalized-length formalism; in characteristic p, Roberts' Frobenius homology theorem (as stated in Ma, Thm. 2.4) and Monsky's Hilbert-Kunz existence theorem; and Land-Tamme truncating descent with Goodwillie, Thomason-Trobaugh and BGT for the K-theory inputs. The only OpenAI manuscript cited is OpenAILech2026 (Lech's multiplicity conjecture), cited in lengths.tex for related normalized-length constructions; the text does not say the proof depends on it. The corollary depends on Skalit's SkalitUnramified lemmas, and the symbolic-power consequence on Kurano-Roberts Thm. 3.2; both are cited, not reproved.
serres-positivity-conjecture.direction: proves the conjecture (strict positivity for all regular local rings, mixed characteristic and ramified case included)

homological-conjectures-in-commutative-a.what_happened: The manuscript 'A Complete Local Domain without a Small Cohen–Macaulay Module' (OpenAI, dated 23 September 2026) claims a three-dimensional complete Noetherian normal local domain R containing ℂ, with residue field ℂ, that has no nonzero finitely generated module of depth 3 (equal to dim R), i.e. no small (maximal) Cohen–Macaulay module. This is the domain form of the small Cohen–Macaulay module conjecture, which is item (14) of the list's named homological conjectures. The ring is R(X,H), the completion at its homogeneous maximal ideal of T(X,H) = ⊕ H⁰(X, jH), for a smooth projective complex surface X with an ample globally generated H. The specific pair used has n = 7: X is an abelian (ℤ/7)⁵ Kummer cover of the blow-up of ℙ² at four points, branched along the six lines joining them and the four exceptional curves, with H² = 1715. Non-existence is derived from a numerical obstruction (Theorem 1.2 in the manuscript): if R(X,H) admits a small Cohen–Macaulay module then K_X² − 2c₂(X) ≤ 6H², which the chosen surface violates (13377 > 10290). The manuscript also claims a corollary that the uncompleted localisation T_𝔫 is a three-dimensional local domain essentially of finite type over ℂ with no nonzero finitely generated maximal Cohen–Macaulay module.
homological-conjectures-in-commutative-a.delivers: If the claim holds, it refutes the small Cohen–Macaulay module conjecture in the list's form. The list asks for a nonzero finitely generated module on which some (equivalently every) system of parameters is regular, for every complete local ring. The ring here is a complete local ring with no such module, so the counterexample refutes the list's form. The manuscript itself states only the domain form ('every complete Noetherian local domain has one'), which is a special case of the list's statement, so the two statements do not match word for word; the implication to the list's form is not stated in the text. Restrictions: the counterexample is a normal domain of dimension three in equal characteristic zero (it contains ℂ with residue field ℂ). The non-existence is only for finitely generated modules; the manuscript says big Cohen–Macaulay modules exist and are not affected. The proof uses only the n = 7 member of the surface family. The corollary gives a counterexample in the class of three-dimensional local domains essentially of finite type over ℂ.
homological-conjectures-in-commutative-a.remains: If the claim is correct, item (14) is settled negatively and nothing in it remains open. Items (1)–(13) of the list's named conjectures (Zero Divisor, Bass's question, Intersection, New Intersection, Improved New Intersection, Direct Summand, Canonical Element, balanced big Cohen–Macaulay existence, Cohen–Macaulayness of direct summands of regular rings, Tor vanishing, Strong Direct Summand, weakly functorial big Cohen–Macaulay algebras, and Serre's multiplicity conjecture) are not addressed by this manuscript, which cites several of them as already known. The Peskine–Szpiro, Huneke–Şega–Vraciu, Huneke–Wiegand, and Auslander–Reiten/Nakayama/Tachikawa conjectures are not discussed in the text.

machine_checked.scope:
The small Cohen–Macaulay module conjecture asks whether every complete local domain has a nonzero finitely generated maximal Cohen–Macaulay module. The linked formalization verifies only the ring-theoretic candidate: there exists a three-dimensional complete Noetherian integrally closed local domain over $\mathbb C$ whose residue field is $\mathbb C$.

It does not prove that this ring lacks a nonzero finitely generated maximal Cohen–Macaulay module, or the paper's counterexample essentially of finite type.

homological-conjectures-in-commutative-a.doubts: Lemma 3.1 (the slope-balancing modification) is adapted from Chen–Sun's analytic setting, which the manuscript says differs in its hypotheses; the authors 'recall briefly' the Harder–Narasimhan filtration and give the termination argument in a few sentences. Several structural steps are argued in outline: the depth-inequality step that CM modules of full support localise to CM modules, the depth bound for coherent duals on regular schemes, the regularity of the models V and W, and the étale local normal form of the cover in Lemma cover-smooth, which is argued with 'after an étale base change' steps. The surface section cites Anghel2026 §7.2 as the source of the construction, but says all required numerical and positivity checks are carried out directly in the manuscript.
homological-conjectures-in-commutative-a.direction: disproves the conjecture (domain form, and so the list's form)
homological-conjectures-in-commutative-a.object: R = completion of T(X,H) at its homogeneous maximal ideal, where X is a specific surface: the abelian (ℤ/7)⁵ Kummer cover of the blow-up of ℙ² at four points, branched along six joining lines and four exceptional curves, and H = 3J − E with H² = 1715. The ring is explicitly defined by this construction, but the manuscript does not write out its generators or relations, and the non-existence of a small Cohen–Macaulay module is proved by contradiction from the Chern-number obstruction, not by an explicit check on modules.

is-every-group-surjunctive.what_happened: Two manuscripts claim a negative answer, each by exhibiting a group with an injective, non-surjective cellular automaton over a finite field. (1) 'A Counterexample to Kaplansky's Direct-Finiteness Conjecture in Characteristic Two': for a finite field K of characteristic two, a finitely presented group G containing an element of odd prime order, and sums a, b in K[G] with ab=1 and ba≠1 (Theorem 1.1). The coefficients of b give a local rule with memory supp(b). The map Tᵦ: K^G→K^G on all configurations is injective, because a is a left inverse, and not surjective, because a point indicator δₕ with (ba−1)ₕ≠0 has no preimage. Its corollary on non-surjunctivity states that G is not surjunctive. Its F∞ corollary also gives an overgroup U with the same failure, conditional on an external embedding theorem. (2) 'A Counterexample to Kaplansky's Direct-Finiteness Conjecture in Odd Characteristic': for p the least prime divisor of (m!)²+1 with m = binom(1200,600), an odd prime, a field K of order p⁴, a finitely generated group G with torsion, and sums a, b in K[G] with ab=1 and ba≠1. Its Section 06 applies the same transfer to these sums, giving an injective, non-surjective cellular automaton on K^G, and states that this negatively answers Gottschalk's surjunctivity conjecture. 'A Torsion-Free Group Algebra That Is Not Directly Finite' and 'A Counterexample to the Group-Ring Determinant Conjecture' do not treat cellular automata.
is-every-group-surjunctive.delivers: If the claims hold, they answer the list's question negatively. The question asks whether every group is surjunctive, for every finite alphabet, with every injective cellular automaton surjective. One group, one finite alphabet and one injective non-surjective automaton refute that, and each of (1) and (2) supplies one. Restrictions: each gives a single group. In (1) the alphabet is a finite field of characteristic two whose order the text does not state, and the group is finitely presented with odd-order torsion. In (2) the alphabet has order p⁴ for the one prime p above, and the group is finitely generated with torsion. The manuscripts' statement matches the list's: they define surjunctive as every injective cellular automaton over every finite alphabet being surjective, and they state Gottschalk's conjecture as 'every group is surjunctive'.
is-every-group-surjunctive.remains: Nothing in the list's question, if the claims hold. The question is a universal yes/no over all groups and names no subclass, and the manuscripts make no claim about the surjunctivity of other specific groups.

machine_checked.scope:
Kaplansky's direct-finiteness conjecture asserts that $ab=1$ implies $ba=1$ for $a,b\in K[G]$, for every field $K$ and group $G$. The formalized results construct a finite field of characteristic two and a group algebra violating this implication. One statement records the counterexample for a finitely generated group; the more detailed construction gives a finitely presented group with an element of odd prime order.

The detailed construction also gives a precise recipe for choosing the data and proves that the required search terminates. The further conclusion that the group is nonsofic is outside these statements.

A nonsingular integer matrix has absolute determinant at least $1$. The group-ring Determinant Conjecture extends this bound to matrices over $\mathbb Z[G]$ for every discrete group $G$. If $T_A$ is the operator induced by such a matrix $A$ on finite direct sums of $\ell^2(G)$, and $\mu_A$ is the spectral measure of $T_A^*T_A$ with respect to the group trace, the conjecture asserts

$\displaystyle \int_{(0,\infty)}\log t\,d\mu_A(t)\ge0,$

with the zero spectral atom omitted. For an invertible square matrix, this is equivalent to its Fuglede–Kadison determinant being at least $1$.

The formalized result contradicts that bound. It gives a finitely generated group $G$ and an $n\times n$ matrix over $\mathbb Z[G]$, with $n\ge1$, that is invertible over $\mathbb Q[G]$. Its bounded left-regular operator is invertible and has determinant strictly between $0$ and $1$.

The formalization uses the trace of $\log(T^*T)$ to define the determinant for the invertible operator $T$. The paper's additional spectral-measure integral conclusion is not included.

Kaplansky's direct-finiteness conjecture asserts that $ab=1$ implies $ba=1$ in every group algebra over a field. Let $p$ be the smallest prime divisor of $\bigl(\binom{1200}{600}!\bigr)^2+1$; this prime is odd. The formalized result constructs a field $K$ of order $p^4$, a finitely generated group $G$ with torsion, and elements $a,b$ violating this implication. The associated cellular automaton on all configurations $K^G$ is injective but not surjective.

The formalization also contains fixed-field transfer results, separate from the statement linked below.

is-every-group-surjunctive.doubts: (1) The authors say the prescription 'has not been executed', and that no practical execution of the finite search is asserted. The witnesses are established by termination proofs and algebraic certificates rather than by a computed instance. (2) The text says the construction 'is not claimed to have been evaluated as a practical computation' and concerns only the one prime p. It does not evaluate p.; conditional on: (1) Termination of the finite search for the incidence data uses Linnik's theorem, via a uniform bound cited from Xylouris, and the paper's own hypergraph existence theorem. The non-surjunctivity of its overgroup U depends on an external companion embedding theorem; the claim for G itself does not. (2) No unproven hypothesis is stated. The construction draws on published constructions for some ingredients (Haviv; Golovnev and Haviv; Dykema and Juschenko), but the text says it proves the matrix and group steps itself.
is-every-group-surjunctive.object: The cellular automaton Tᵦ on all configurations K^G, with local rule given by the coefficients of b and memory set supp(b), together with the group G and its sums a, b. None is written out. In (1) the sums come from a terminating finite prescription that the text says has not been executed. In (2) G and K are built from finite formulas and a specified prime, with no computed instance.

is-every-discrete-countable-group-sofic.what_happened: Four manuscripts claim a nonsofic group, all by the same route: Elek and Szabó's theorem that group algebras over fields are stably finite for sofic groups would make the group algebra directly finite, contradicting the scalar defect. (1) 'A Torsion-Free Group Algebra That Is Not Directly Finite': its finitely presented torsion-free group G over F₂ is said, in the introduction, to be not sofic, by Elek–Szabó Corollary 4.7. (2) 'A Counterexample to Kaplansky's Direct-Finiteness Conjecture in Characteristic Two': its finitely presented group G with odd-order torsion is nonsofic (abstract and introduction). Its F∞ corollary also calls an overgroup U nonsofic, by the same route applied to U. (3) 'A Counterexample to the Group-Ring Determinant Conjecture': its finitely generated group G_D = (⊕ over H₂ of C₃) ⋊ H₂, with H₂ taken from the characteristic-two paper's scalar pair, is said to be not sofic. The argument applies Elek–Szabó's determinant bound for sofic groups to the positive integral matrix A*A. The paper calls this an external consequence, not used to build A. (4) 'A Counterexample to Kaplansky's Direct-Finiteness Conjecture in Odd Characteristic': its finitely generated group G with torsion is said, in the introduction only and not the abstract, to be nonsofic by Elek–Szabó's theorem.
is-every-discrete-countable-group-sofic.delivers: If the claims hold, each refutes the universal statement, since one discrete countable nonsofic group suffices, and each manuscript gives one. Restrictions: (1) torsion-free, finitely presented, over F₂, with a finite two-dimensional classifying complex. (2) finitely presented, characteristic two, with odd-order torsion; the text asserts finite presentation in a section I did not check. (3) finitely generated, with the determinant-bound obstruction. (4) finitely generated, with torsion, over a field of order p⁴. On the statement: (2) uses Elek–Szabó's finite-map definition. For every finite E in the group and every ε in (0,1), there is a finite Ω and a map σ from the group to the self-maps of Ω that is approximately multiplicative on E, nearly the identity at 1, and moves almost every point for g in E∖{1}. This matches the list's approximate-multiplicativity and almost-free conditions. The list speaks of maps into permutations, whereas this uses all self-maps of Ω, and the text does not argue that the two versions agree.
is-every-discrete-countable-group-sofic.remains: Nothing for the universal yes/no question, if the claims hold. The list names no subclass, and the manuscripts claim no positive result about soficity of any other group.

machine_checked.scope:
Kaplansky's direct-finiteness conjecture asserts that $ab=1$ implies $ba=1$ for $a,b\in K[G]$, for every field $K$ and group $G$. The formalized results construct a finite field of characteristic two and a group algebra violating this implication. One statement records the counterexample for a finitely generated group; the more detailed construction gives a finitely presented group with an element of odd prime order.

The detailed construction also gives a precise recipe for choosing the data and proves that the required search terminates. The further conclusion that the group is nonsofic is outside these statements.

A nonsingular integer matrix has absolute determinant at least $1$. The group-ring Determinant Conjecture extends this bound to matrices over $\mathbb Z[G]$ for every discrete group $G$. If $T_A$ is the operator induced by such a matrix $A$ on finite direct sums of $\ell^2(G)$, and $\mu_A$ is the spectral measure of $T_A^*T_A$ with respect to the group trace, the conjecture asserts

$\displaystyle \int_{(0,\infty)}\log t\,d\mu_A(t)\ge0,$

with the zero spectral atom omitted. For an invertible square matrix, this is equivalent to its Fuglede–Kadison determinant being at least $1$.

The formalized result contradicts that bound. It gives a finitely generated group $G$ and an $n\times n$ matrix over $\mathbb Z[G]$, with $n\ge1$, that is invertible over $\mathbb Q[G]$. Its bounded left-regular operator is invertible and has determinant strictly between $0$ and $1$.

The formalization uses the trace of $\log(T^*T)$ to define the determinant for the invertible operator $T$. The paper's additional spectral-measure integral conclusion is not included.

Kaplansky's direct-finiteness conjecture asserts that $ab=1$ implies $ba=1$ in every group algebra over a field. Let $p$ be the smallest prime divisor of $\bigl(\binom{1200}{600}!\bigr)^2+1$; this prime is odd. The formalized result constructs a field $K$ of order $p^4$, a finitely generated group $G$ with torsion, and elements $a,b$ violating this implication. The associated cellular automaton on all configurations $K^G$ is injective but not surjective.

The formalization also contains fixed-field transfer results, separate from the statement linked below.

is-every-discrete-countable-group-sofic.doubts: (2) Its nonsoficity is only as firm as its scalar pair, which the text says has not been executed as a computation. (3) The text itself calls the sofic conclusion 'an external consequence, not an ingredient in constructing A'. (4) The nonsoficity claim appears only in the introduction, and the abstract omits it.; conditional on: All four rely on a cited published theorem that the manuscripts do not prove: Elek–Szabó (2004, Corollary 4.7) for (1), (2) and (4), and Elek–Szabó (2005, Theorem 5, the determinant bound for sofic groups) for (3). (2)'s overgroup U also depends on an external companion embedding theorem. (3) takes its existence input from the characteristic-two paper's scalar pair, a separate manuscript in this family.
is-every-discrete-countable-group-sofic.object: In each case the nonsofic group itself: (1) a finitely presented torsion-free group built from cones on finite labeled graphs drawn from a random model; (2) a finitely presented group G with odd-order torsion, and its overgroup U of type F∞; (3) G_D; (4) a finitely generated group with torsion. None is written out. Each is given by a finite prescription or a probabilistic existence argument, and the characteristic-two prescription is stated to be unexecuted.

finite-lattice-representation-problem.what_happened: Two OpenAI manuscripts, both dated 24 September 2026, claim a negative answer to whether every finite lattice is isomorphic to Con(A) for some finite algebra A. (1) 'Finite congruence lattices: characterization and undecidability' claims: (a) a graph criterion (Theorem f:criterion): a finite nonempty lattice L is Con of a finite algebra iff there is a finite complete graph (A,d), with d(p,q) in L, d(p,p)=0, satisfying a triangle inequality, a reflection condition (whenever a is not below b there are p,q with d(p,q) <= a and d(p,q) not <= b) and a connectivity condition; representability is therefore semidecidable (Corollary f:cor-witness-bound). (b) No Turing machine decides, from the order table of a finite lattice, whether it is Con of a finite algebra (Theorem n:undecidable). The text says the negative answer to the problem follows because the constant 'yes' algorithm would otherwise be a decider (Theorem m:main(ii) discussion). (c) There is a nonrepresentable finite lattice L0 of minimum cardinality, specified by a finite order-table description that refers to an unevaluated Busy Beaver constant, with 7 < |L0| <= M_* (Theorem q:minimum; the ceiling M_* comes from Theorem q:size-ceiling). Every finite lattice with at most seven elements is representable (Theorem f:small-lattices). (d) Recognising full subgroup intervals [H,G] of finite groups is undecidable (Corollary n:interval-undecidable). (2) 'A negative solution to the finite lattice representation problem' claims (Theorem main:congruences) that there is a finite nonempty lattice L with L not isomorphic to Con(A) for every finite nonempty algebra A of every finite signature. Its route is Theorem main:group: a finite lattice that is not isomorphic to any full subgroup interval [D,G] of a finite group. The congruence statement then follows from the cited Palfy-Pudlak 1980 equivalence. The obstructing lattice is the decorated lattice of Proposition lat:decorated-lattice, whose chain parameter is chosen from an absolute constant in Theorem cls:chain-rigidity.
finite-lattice-representation-problem.delivers: Taken as correct, both manuscripts establish that not every finite lattice is the congruence lattice of a finite algebra, so the yes/no question in the list is answered negatively. The result covers finite algebras of any finite signature, with nullary operations allowed, and places no bound on algebra or lattice size, which matches the list's wording. Paper (1) also gives the decision-theoretic answers: representability is semidecidable but not decidable from order tables, and it gives a minimum-cardinality counterexample with 8 <= |L0| <= M_*. These decision and minimality claims go beyond the list's question. Paper (2) gives only an existence statement for one nonrepresentable lattice, with no size bound. The text says its subgroup-interval obstruction is not identified pointwise with the congruence obstruction, so the transfer to Con is global rather than lattice-by-lattice. Neither manuscript states the problem in a form different from the list's.
finite-lattice-representation-problem.remains: If the claims hold, the list's question is fully answered. Still unidentified in the text: a numerically evaluated or small nonrepresentable lattice. Paper (1) gives only 8 <= |L0| <= M_*, with no numerical value for |L0|, and it describes M_* only as an ordinary computable integer in the parts I read. Paper (2) gives no size bound for its lattice. The absolute constants (S in Lemma n:circuit-template of paper (1), B in Theorem cls:chain-rigidity of paper (2)) are shown to exist but not identified.

machine_checked.scope: The finite lattice representation problem asks which finite lattices occur as the full congruence lattice of a finite algebra. The formalization proves the paper's colored-graph characterization: a finite nonempty lattice is representable exactly when it admits the specified finite nonempty graph witness, whose edge colors encode the required congruence relations. This selected theorem is the equivalence with the graph criterion; the paper's undecidability and subgroup-interval conclusions are outside it.

finite-lattice-representation-problem.doubts: Paper (1): (a) The undecidability proof fixes an absolute integer S whose existence is shown but whose value is not identified. The text says it does 'not assert an algorithm for extracting a sharp, or even a specified, sufficient stock', so the reduction is non-effective in that constant. (b) The proof of Theorem f:negative-family is a summary: it lists parameter-choice orders and cites results in several other sections (patterns, classical, alternating, bounded, weights), and ends with 'It proves the required finite large-family nonrepresentation statement'. The substance is in those other sections, which I did not check. (c) Theorem w:lp is stated as a uniform degree bound derived from the 'uniform constructible-family formulation' of Larsen-Pink Theorem 0.5. The same passage says the alternative argument in the quantitative section 'will also establish the implication needed over the indicated algebraic closures', which signals that the uniform form is used beyond the cited statement. (d) The minimum-cardinality result is descriptive, not numerical; the text says it 'does not supply a numerically evaluated value of that cardinality'. Paper (2): (a) The obstructing lattice is not specified. Its construction uses 'a sufficiently large finite chain parameter' whose existence follows from an absolute bound proved by contradiction (Theorem cls:chain-rigidity). The text says that 'an explicit numerical value of that parameter is unnecessary for the existence conclusion'. (b) The text itself says the obstruction is not identified with the congruence lattice of Theorem main:congruences, so that theorem rests on the cited equivalence rather than a single lattice. (c) The text states that 'none of these results alone bounds the lengths of the tested chains', so the uniform bound on chain length is the authors' own argument, and the proof is spread over many sections. (d) In the rigidity section the text says 'We omit restrictions on p and on the weight of V that only remove cases', so the reader must accept that the omitted restrictions only remove cases.; conditional on: Paper (1): the undecidability proof (Theorem n:undecidable) depends on the weighted success and realization theorems of the same paper (Theorems t:weighted-realization and t:weighted-product-success, Proposition t:weighted-algebra, Theorem n:template-bound). Those depend on the sufficiently-general subgroup theorem of Larsen-Pink, in a uniform form stated in the paper (Theorem w:lp), on classification-of-finite-simple-groups inputs, and on the Davis-Putnam-Robinson-Matiyasevich theorem for the final contradiction. The proof also uses an absolute integer S from Lemma n:circuit-template, shown to exist but not identified. The nonrepresentability of the affine family (Theorem f:negative-family) and the size claims (Theorems q:size-ceiling and q:minimum) rest on the paper's own structural pruning and bounded-path argument (Theorem w:path-bound and related results). The claim |L0| > 7 uses DeMeo's small-lattice classification (DeMeo 2012, Theorem 6.1.1) for every lattice of at most seven elements except L7, which the paper represents directly. The graph criterion itself depends on no unproved input. Paper (2): the transfer from Theorem main:group to Theorem main:congruences depends on the Palfy-Pudlak equivalence, which is cited, not proved. The obstruction (Theorem main:group, via Proposition ext:reduction and Theorem glue:contradiction) depends on Theorem cls:chain-rigidity and the literature inputs listed in Proposition cls:literature and the introduction: the classification of finite simple groups, Aschbacher's maximal-subgroup theorem, Kleidman-Liebeck, Larsen-Pink fixed-type envelopes, Landazuri-Seitz, Steinberg, Luebeck's small-degree classification, Seitz's irreducible-triples classification with Cavallin-Testerman corrections, and Burness-Liebeck-Shalev Proposition 8.1.
finite-lattice-representation-problem.object: Paper (1): L0, a nonrepresentable finite lattice of minimum cardinality, given by bounded, unambiguous formulas for its full order table that refer to the unevaluated Busy Beaver constant. It is explicit as a finite description but not numerically computed, and no diagram is given. Paper (1) also has a family of nonrepresentable affine-chart lattices (Theorem f:negative-family), shown to exist for suitable parameter choices. Paper (2): no explicit lattice. The obstruction is the decorated lattice of Proposition lat:decorated-lattice, whose chain-length parameter is only shown to exist, and the text says no explicit numerical value is needed or given.
