finding-a-function-to-model-n-step-self-.what_happened: Main claim, in 'Mass and covering exponents for fixed-length honeycomb walks'. Let W_n be the n-edge self-avoiding walks on the honeycomb lattice from a fixed vertex o, with uniform law P_n and free endpoint. For every δ>0 and k>0 there are C_{δ,k} and n_0(δ,k) such that for all n ≥ n_0, outside an event of P_n-probability at most C_{δ,k} n^{-k}: (i) the diameter D satisfies n^{3/4-δ} ≤ D ≤ n^{3/4+δ}; (ii) for every visited vertex z and every real s in [1,n], the number of visited vertices in the closed ball of radius s about z lies between n^{-δ} min{n, s^{4/3}} and n^{δ} min{n, s^{4/3}}; (iii) the least number N(s) of radius-s balls covering the visited set lies between n^{-δ}(1+n s^{-4/3}) and n^{δ}(1+n s^{-4/3}). Corollaries: the projection onto each lattice-normal direction has span at least n^{3/4-δ}; log N(s)/log(D/s) tends to 4/3 in probability for s up to n^{3/4-ε}; the radius of gyration R_g and the p-th moments of D and R_g are n^{3p/4+o(1)}. The proof works with the critical activity ρ=(2+√2)^{-1/2} (Duminil-Copin and Smirnov), uses the normalization c_n ρ^n ≥ 1, and passes from full-box estimates to fixed length by absolute exceptional masses; its analytic inputs come from three companion manuscripts (see conditional_on). Related manuscripts in the family: 'Renewal and changes of law for critical honeycomb walks' claims that uniform strict bridges with n visited vertices (even n) have terminal distance and diameter n^{3/4+o(1)} in probability, and that for uniform full-plane n-step walks from a fixed center, endpoint distance and maximum radius are n^{3/4+o(1)} in probability along a set of lengths of natural density one, with moments n^{3p/4+o(1)}; its every-length diameter upper bound is taken from the Mass paper. 'Radial transfer estimates and polygon length laws for honeycomb walks' claims polygon diameter tails r^{-2+o(1)} (unrooted) and r^{-2/3+o(1)} (length-weighted), a truncated second length moment r^{2/3+o(1)}, and that polygons conditioned on length at least n have diameter n^{3/4+o(1)} in probability. 'Critical strip-crossing mass on the honeycomb lattice' claims total strip-crossing weight ≍ N^{-1/4} and a first displacement moment ≍ N^{3/4}. 'Uniform marked-polygon estimates and sharp finite bridge moments' claims bridge mass ≍ h^{-1/4}, first-length mass at most C h^{13/12}, and mass at least c h^{-1/4} on bridges of length at least c h^{4/3}. 'Cylinder loop weights and planar nesting' claims the cylinder partition exponent at every fixed positive loop fugacity, with exponent 1/6 at fugacity two, and planar and middle-strip nesting exponents 1/12. 'Marked polygon correlations and one-arc bounds' claims that the length-square mass of simple polygons of diameter at most H, modulo translations, is at most H^{2/3+o(1)}, plus a two-mark cylinder estimate and a one-arc bound. 'Signed cylinder propagation and marked polygons on the honeycomb lattice' claims the same 1/6 and 1/12 exponents, hexagon chord partition R^{3/4+o(1)} and normalized mean length R^{4/3+o(1)}, and the same H^{2/3+o(1)} length-square bound. 'Disk transfer representations and confined bridge mass' claims strip bridge mean length R^{4/3+o(1)} (also after confinement to a multiple of the strip width), bridge mass ≍ R^{-1/4}, and half-plane arch kernel ≍ m^{-5/4}. 'Polynomial vacuum representations and bridge mass for honeycomb walks' claims strip bridge mean length h^{4/3+o(1)} under the all-length critical measure, and central visit probability R^{-2/3+o(1)} with mean length R^{4/3+o(1)} for free-boundary hexagon chords. 'Cylinder amplitudes and logarithmic bridge-length windows on the honeycomb lattice' claims that bridges with lengths between h^{4/3}(log h)^{-1/8} and 2h^{4/3}(log h)^{1/2} have mass at least h^{3/4}(log h)^{-C}, summed through height 2h(log h)^{1/64}. 'Critical honeycomb chords with prescribed boundary endpoints' claims that critical walks between prescribed ports of a regular hexagon of scale R have length R^{4/3+o(1)} in probability, with a half-plane mean of the same order. 'Cap-selected amplitudes and triangle chords for honeycomb walks' claims triangle-chord partition sum ≍ R^{3/4} with mean length R^{4/3+o(1)}, and a cylinder amplitude N^{1/6+o(1)}. The Strip, Cylinder loop weights, Marked polygon and Uniform marked-polygon claims are checked against the statements the Mass and Renewal papers quote from them; the remaining manuscripts are summarized from their abstracts only.
finding-a-function-to-model-n-step-self-.delivers: Taken as correct, the Mass paper gives, for the uniform law on n-edge honeycomb walks from a fixed vertex, two-sided exponent-level bounds on three spatial statistics (diameter n^{3/4}, local mass s^{4/3} capped at n, covering number n s^{-4/3}), valid at every sufficiently large n with polynomially small failure probability and n^{±δ} slack for each δ>0. This describes how large a fixed-length walk is and how it fills space as a function of n, but only up to exponent-level factors: it gives no formula, no explicit constant, and no approximation with a stated error for any of the three quantities. Its scope is the honeycomb lattice only, and the exponents 3/4 and 4/3 are the predicted values, here established up to n^{±δ}. The paper does not say it settles the Wikipedia question, which asks for a function modelling the walks; its nearest claim is the 3/4 size exponent, a scaling law for the trace rather than a count, generating function or algorithm. The Renewal paper gives the corresponding endpoint and maximum-radius law for uniform full-plane n-step walks only along a set of lengths of natural density one; its strict-bridge result (even n) is for a different ensemble. The Radial paper's law concerns polygons conditioned on length, not walks of fixed length.
finding-a-function-to-model-n-step-self-.remains: If the claims are correct, still open: (1) the count c_n = |W_n| and its asymptotics, including the connective constant's role in the count and any polynomial correction; the paper uses c_n only through c_n ρ^n ≥ 1 and submultiplicativity, and takes the connective constant from Duminil-Copin and Smirnov. (2) Explicit functions or constants: every statement carries C_{δ,k}, n_0(δ,k) and n^{±δ} or n^{o(1)} slack, so the exponents are not established as exact limits. (3) Endpoint displacement |γ_n - o| at fixed length: the Mass paper states it does not prove a fixed-length lower bound on this, and a diameter lower bound does not imply far-apart endpoints; the Renewal paper gives endpoint distance only on a density-one set of lengths. (4) Scaling limits: the Mass paper includes no convergence to a continuum curve and no continuum Hausdorff dimension; it does not identify an SLE limit. (5) Other lattices, dimensions, or universality across lattices, which the paper excludes. (6) Any interpretation of 'model' beyond exponent-level scaling of diameter, local mass and covering number.

machine_checked.scope:
The linked formalization establishes finiteness of the critical bridge measures used in the paper. For every strip height $h\ge1$, the total weight and first length moment of self-avoiding honeycomb bridges from a fixed initial port to a free terminal port are finite. The corresponding sums are also finite when the bridge is confined to the corridor of horizontal width $h(\log h)^2$, including the normalized first-moment sums.

These are supporting summability statements. The paper's $h^{4/3+o(1)}$ mean-length law and its central-visit and hexagonal-chord exponents are outside them.

The linked formalization proves existence of the infinite-length free energy for the critical honeycomb self-avoiding-walk partition function. For every starting vertex, force direction, and real force parameter, the logarithm of the length-$n$ partition function divided by $n$ converges to its stated free-energy limit.

This selected result supplies the limiting free energy. It does not state the paper's small-force exponent, near-critical correlation scale, or the $3/4$ spatial and moment laws.

For critical self-avoiding walks on the honeycomb lattice, the formalization proves that the total weight of paths crossing a strip of height $N$ is comparable to $N^{-1/4}$, while the first horizontal-displacement moment of return paths is comparable to $N^{3/4}$. It also proves finiteness of the strip sums, the exact arch–bridge balance identity, comparison of successive moment increments with bridge mass, and monotonicity of bridge mass. The comparison constants are uniform in the strip height.

For the prescribed-boundary-endpoint companion, let $B_h$ be the total critical weight of strict bridges crossing a strip of integral height $h$, from one fixed bottom port to all compatible top ports, with $B_0=1$. The formalization proves
$c(1+h)^{-1/4}\le B_h\le C(1+h)^{-1/4}$
for all $h\ge0$ and fixed positive constants $c,C$. This includes finiteness of the path sum. The prescribed-endpoint length law, arch and strip mean laws, and remaining moment and renewal conclusions are outside this supporting statement.

finding-a-function-to-model-n-step-self-.doubts: The sections I read (introduction, inputs, completion) carry no sketch or hedge markers. I did not read the middle sections (sewing, probes, slow paths, roughly 3,000 lines), so I cannot report their internal status. Points the text itself bears on: (1) every claim is an n^{±δ} or n^{o(1)} statement with non-explicit constants C_{δ,k} and n_0(δ,k). (2) The proof's analytic content is delegated to the three companion manuscripts, so the strength of the Mass result equals that of those inputs as cited. (3) The Mass paper proves the diameter lower bound n^{3/4-δ} at every large n, while the Renewal paper states its endpoint-distance and maximum-radius laws for uniform full-plane walks only on a density-one set of lengths. The two papers do not cross-reference each other on this point (Renewal cites Mass for its diameter upper bound and several lemmas, and Mass does not cite Renewal), so the different length qualifications are not reconciled in the text. (4) The family contains overlapping claims: the H^{2/3+o(1)} length-square mass bound appears in both the Marked polygon and Signed manuscripts, and the 1/6 and 1/12 exponents appear in both the Cylinder loop weights and Signed manuscripts, so these are not independent confirmations of each other.; conditional on: Yes. The Mass paper's proof uses three companion manuscripts in this family, cited but not proved in it: (a) 'Critical strip-crossing mass on the honeycomb lattice' (its Theorem 1.1 and Lemma 2.1 as quoted in the Mass paper): the boundary flux identity, B_h ≍ (1+h)^{-1/4} and m_h ≍ h^{3/4}; the normalization lemma's proof argues by contradiction from the bridge lower bound B_h ≍ h^{-1/4}. (b) 'Cylinder loop weights and planar nesting' (Lemma 11.4, Theorems 11.2 and 8.1, Corollaries 8.2 and 11.3, Proposition 11.5): the length-nest normalization, the raw first-length mass at most h^{13/12+o(1)}, and the all-count cylinder tail bound used for polygon families. (c) 'Marked polygon correlations and one-arc bounds' (Theorem 1.1 and Theorem 8.3): the polygon length-square mass bound H^{2/3+o(1)} and the uniform one-arc bound. External inputs: Duminil-Copin and Smirnov (2012) for the value of ρ, and Kesten's renewal method as presented by Madras and Slade for bridge factorization. The Renewal paper's finite bridge inputs come from its companion 'Uniform marked-polygon estimates and sharp finite bridge moments' (Theorem 1.1), and its every-length diameter upper bound (its uniform-law diameter clause) and several geometric lemmas come from the Mass paper's Theorem 1.1 and Lemma 4.1.
finding-a-function-to-model-n-step-self-.direction: proves the predicted 3/4 size exponent and the 4/3 mass and covering exponents for uniform fixed-length honeycomb walks (scaling exponents, up to n^{±δ}; not a count or formula)

shelahs-eventual-categoricity-conjecture.what_happened: The manuscript 'Eventual categoricity for abstract elementary classes' claims a ZFC proof of its Theorem 'Uniform eventual categoricity'. For every infinite cardinal λ there is a cardinal μ(λ) ≥ λ such that, for every AEC K with LS(K) ≤ λ, if K is categorical in some κ ≥ μ(λ) then K is categorical in every κ' ≥ μ(λ). The threshold depends only on λ, not on K. Categoricity includes the existence of a model. The manuscript first proves a qualitative version (an AEC categorical in unboundedly many cardinals is categorical on a tail) and says the uniform version follows from it by a set-coding reduction over the set of codes of AECs with LS number at most λ. The companion manuscript 'A CH obstruction to a prescribed categoricity threshold' is cited in the introduction only as context. It bears on this problem only indirectly. Under CH it builds an AEC with LS ℵ₀ that is categorical in every μ ≥ Λ but has two nonisomorphic models at h(ℵ₀) = ℶ_{ω₂}, so the explicit threshold h(LS(K)) fails for that class. It does not contradict an existential threshold.
shelahs-eventual-categoricity-conjecture.delivers: Gives the list's statement in ZFC, with no amalgamation, joint embedding, tameness, no-maximal-models, large-cardinal or GCH-type hypothesis, and with the same threshold in premise and conclusion. Compared with the list: (a) the manuscript quantifies over infinite λ only. Its LS number is always infinite by definition (ℓ ≥ |τ|+ℵ₀ is infinite), so the finite cases of 'every cardinal λ' are vacuous under its conventions. (b) It asserts categoricity at or above μ(λ), which implies the list's version with 'above μ(λ)'. The manuscript says this resolves Shelah's conjecture positively. The threshold is existential and is not given numerically. My inference from reading both manuscripts, which neither states: under CH, μ(ℵ₀) must exceed ℶ_{ω₂}, because the CH companion's AEC with LS ℵ₀ is categorical in Λ but not at ℶ_{ω₂}. The two claims are consistent.
shelahs-eventual-categoricity-conjecture.remains: Nothing in the list's statement. The manuscript gives no explicit or numerical μ(λ). It treats the explicit-threshold question (Shelah, Conjecture N.4.3(1)(b)) as separate, and the list's statement does not ask for it.

machine_checked.scope:
Under the continuum hypothesis, the formalized result refutes the proposed transfer of categoricity down to the Hanf threshold. It gives an abstract elementary class in a countable relational language, with Löwenheim–Skolem number $\aleph_0$, that has two nonisomorphic models at $\beth_{\omega_2}=h(\aleph_0)$ but is categorical in every cardinal at least $\beth_{(2^{\aleph_1})^+}$.

No amalgamation, joint embedding, tameness, or absence-of-maximal-models assumption is imposed. The later canonical-point obstruction and the separate eventual-categoricity theorem are not included.

shelahs-eventual-categoricity-conjecture.doubts: (1) The paper has 14 sections. I read the introduction, the proof overview, the final cardinal-transfer section and the closing reduction, but not sections 02 to 13. The uniform form depends on the set-coding reduction (Proposition found:uniform-reduction) and on a forward-referenced existence of a categorical pointed level (Proposition geom:pointed-levels). I did not check either. (2) The introduction says Boney and Vasey found a gap in the unrestricted syntactic characterization in Shelah's Chapter IV, and that their valid variants need exponentiation or cofinality assumptions that do not cover all starting cardinals. The manuscript says it proves the needed reversal of strong maps directly (Theorem found:reversal). I did not verify this. (3) The introduction contrasts this result with earlier positive results (Boney 2014, Grossberg–VanDieren, Shelah–Vasey) that needed amalgamation, tameness, strongly compact cardinals or WGCH. The claim is therefore strong relative to that literature, and I did not verify its proof.
shelahs-eventual-categoricity-conjecture.direction: proves the conjecture (existential uniform threshold, ZFC)

origin.family_title: Shelah's eventual categoricity and the prescribed-threshold obstruction

shelahs-categoricity-conjecture.what_happened: The manuscript 'Eventual categoricity for abstract elementary classes' says in its introduction that its uniform theorem applies to sentences of L_{ω1,ω} in countable languages. For such a sentence φ, one chooses a countable fragment containing φ and orders models by elementarity for that fragment. The text says this gives an AEC with LS number ℵ₀ (citing Boney–Vasey 2017 survey, Example 2.0.2), with the same models and isomorphisms. So one threshold μ(ℵ₀) serves all such sentences: if φ is categorical in some κ ≥ μ(ℵ₀), it is categorical in every κ' ≥ μ(ℵ₀). The same introduction says the prescribed ℶ_{ω1} threshold of the classical infinitary formulation 'remains a separate question' (Boney–Vasey 2015, Conjecture 1.1). The companion manuscript 'A CH obstruction to a prescribed categoricity threshold' concerns general AECs, not L_{ω1,ω} sentences. Its threshold is h(ℵ₀) = ℶ_{(2^ℵ₀)⁺}, which under CH is ℶ_{ω₂}, not ℶ_{ω1}. Its counterexample is not claimed to be L_{ω1,ω}-definable. It is the closer of the two to the bullet's wording, since it calls its target 'the prescribed-threshold form of Shelah's categoricity conjecture', but it does not address the bullet's threshold.
shelahs-categoricity-conjecture.delivers: An existential-threshold version for countable-vocabulary L_{ω1,ω} sentences: categoricity in some cardinal at or above μ(ℵ₀) implies categoricity in every cardinal at or above μ(ℵ₀), where μ(ℵ₀) is an unspecified cardinal. Against the bullet's parts: (1) scope is covered only for countable vocabularies, which the manuscript states explicitly; (2) the premise is read as 'categorical in some κ at or above the threshold', the usual Shelah reading, which the manuscript uses; (4) the conclusion covers all cardinals at or above the threshold. Part (3) is not covered: the threshold is not the Hanf number, and the manuscript does not say it is. The manuscript does not claim to settle the classical form.
shelahs-categoricity-conjecture.remains: The bullet's threshold, the Hanf number of L_{ω1,ω}. The manuscript supplies only the unspecified μ(ℵ₀) and names the ℶ_{ω1} version as open. Uncountable vocabularies are not covered. Read literally with the Hanf number as threshold, the bullet is left open by this family.

machine_checked.scope:
Under the continuum hypothesis, the formalized result refutes the proposed transfer of categoricity down to the Hanf threshold. It gives an abstract elementary class in a countable relational language, with Löwenheim–Skolem number $\aleph_0$, that has two nonisomorphic models at $\beth_{\omega_2}=h(\aleph_0)$ but is categorical in every cardinal at least $\beth_{(2^{\aleph_1})^+}$.

No amalgamation, joint embedding, tameness, or absence-of-maximal-models assumption is imposed. The later canonical-point obstruction and the separate eventual-categoricity theorem are not included.

shelahs-categoricity-conjecture.doubts: The reduction is one paragraph. The text asserts that the models and isomorphisms are unchanged and that the same μ(ℵ₀) works for all sentences. It does not check the AEC axioms (union, coherence, LS) for the fragment ordering, nor that the AEC's models are the sentence's models. I did not check the cited survey example.; conditional on: The AEC step is cited, not proved: that the fragment-ordered class is an AEC with LS number ℵ₀ (Boney–Vasey 2017 survey, Example 2.0.2). The corollary also depends on the uniform theorem of the 'Eventual categoricity for abstract elementary classes' manuscript.
shelahs-categoricity-conjecture.direction: proves a special case: existential threshold (not the Hanf number) for countable-vocabulary L_{ω1,ω} sentences

is-every-finitely-presented-periodic-gro.what_happened: Two manuscripts in the family. (1) 'An infinite finitely presented periodic group' (the companion; build/paper.tex, dated 23 September 2026) constructs a graded, finitely presented unital F₂-algebra R = F₂ ⊕ I, infinite-dimensional, in which every square matrix over I is nilpotent (Theorem thm:algebra). For n ≥ 5 it gives an ordinary finite group presentation of the Steinberg group St_n(R) (Theorem finite-presentation). For n = 12 it claims St₁₂(R) is infinite (its elementary image E₁₂(R) is infinite), that E₁₂(R) is periodic by matrix nilpotence, and that the kernel J₁₂(R) is torsion (Theorem kernel-torsion), so every element of St₁₂(R) has finite order. Its main theorem is that St₁₂(R) is an infinite periodic group with an ordinary finite presentation. (2) 'An infinite finitely presented residually finite 2-group' (build/main.tex, dated 5 October 2026) takes Γ = St₁₂(R) from the companion as given and proves Γ is residually finite, using the finite quotients St₁₂(R/R_≥d). It then passes to G = ker(Γ → St₁₂(F₂)), which has finite index in Γ, and claims G is infinite, ordinarily finitely presented (Reidemeister–Schreier), residually finite, and that every element of G has finite 2-power order, with unbounded orders. Its Theorem thm:main states the existence of an infinite residually finite group with an ordinary finite presentation in which every element has finite 2-power order.
is-every-finitely-presented-periodic-gro.delivers: Gives a negative answer to the yes/no question: there is an infinite finitely presented periodic group. St₁₂(R) from the companion is one, and G from the residual paper is another, which is also residually finite with all element orders 2-powers. 'Periodic' is used in the list's sense: each element has some finite order, with no common exponent. The companion says the order of an element 'may depend on that element', and the residual paper says the orders are unbounded. The presentations are ordinary, with finitely many generators and relators and no variety identities. The companion's introduction states the question in the list's terms ('whether a periodic group with such a presentation must be finite'), and its abstract says the construction answers 'the finitely presented Burnside question negatively'. So the companion's statement of the problem matches the list's. The list places no restriction on characteristic, and the construction uses F₂ only as the ground ring of the algebra R.
is-every-finitely-presented-periodic-gro.remains: Nothing of the yes/no question as stated. Not addressed by either manuscript: finitely presented periodic groups of bounded exponent (the constructed groups have unbounded orders, so they give no information there), and the free Burnside groups B(m,n).

machine_checked.scope: The finitely presented Burnside question asks whether a finitely presented group in which every element has finite order must be finite. The formalization gives a negative answer by constructing an infinite finitely presented periodic group, including a witness realized as a Steinberg group over an algebra of characteristic two. Periodicity means that each element has some finite order; no common exponent is asserted. The paper's separate nil-algebra and radical-algebra conclusions are outside these selected statements.

is-every-finitely-presented-periodic-gro.doubts: (a) The residual paper proves none of Γ's infiniteness, presentation or periodicity itself; its new content (residual finiteness, G, 2-power orders) rests on the companion inputs listed above. (b) The residual paper cites companion results by number (Theorem 3.7, Theorem 4.1, Lemma 5.1, Proposition 5.4, Lemma 5.5). The companion labels I read match these by content; I did not confirm the numbering. (c) In proving Proposition finite-quotients, the residual paper says St₁₂(B_d) is perfect without citing the companion lemma that proves it (Lemma fp:perfectness). This is a standard fact but is unproven in the residual text. (d) The companion's periodicity depends on matrices over I being nilpotent, which is proved in cancellation.tex and finite-rules.tex (about 1,650 lines together). Its introduction describes the cancellation mechanism only in prose. I read the statements and portions of those proofs, not all of them.; conditional on: The residual paper's residual finiteness and 2-power orders depend on inputs it quotes from the companion: the algebra R and its matrix-nilpotence (companion Theorem 3.7, Proposition ring-input), the word hierarchy used to derive phases (Proposition hierarchy-input), the finite-rank facts for stability (companion Lemma 5.1, Proposition 5.4, Lemma 5.5), and the ordinary finite presentation of Γ (companion Theorem 4.1, and Krstić–McCool Theorem 3). The companion's own claim of an infinite finitely presented periodic group has no unproven hypothesis; it uses the Krstić–McCool method and proves what it uses.
is-every-finitely-presented-periodic-gro.direction: negative answer: exhibits an infinite finitely presented periodic group
is-every-finitely-presented-periodic-gro.object: St₁₂(R) (companion), for a finitely presented F₂-algebra R, and its finite-index subgroup G (residual paper). Both are given by finite presentations: generators g_ij(w) for |w| ≤ 2 over a finite alphabet, with listed commutation, product and algebra-relator families (companion Theorem finite-presentation). The algebra's finite rule table comes from the companion's hierarchy in finite-rules.tex, which I sampled but did not check line by line. The object is explicit as a finite presentation, not an existence-by-counting argument.

eilenberg-ganea-conjecture.what_happened: One manuscript, 'A finitely generated counterexample to the Eilenberg-Ganea conjecture' (OpenAI, dated September 23, 2026). Its Theorem thm:main asserts a finitely generated residually finite group G with integral cohomological dimension cd_Z(G) = 2 and geometric dimension gd(G) = 3, and that G has no two-dimensional classifying space, whatever the number of its cells. Construction: start from the presentation complex K of <x,y | x²=y⁵, x²=(xy⁻¹)³>, which is integrally acyclic (the exponent-sum matrix has determinant 1). Lemma geometric-seed flag-triangulates K into a finite two-dimensional flag complex L with vanishing reduced integral homology and a nontrivial homomorphism alpha from pi_1(L) to SU(2), given by an explicit pair of unit quaternions. G is the height kernel ker(lambda) in the right-angled Artin group A_L, where lambda sends each standard generator to 1 (a Bestvina-Brady group). Proposition model: G is countable, finitely generated and residually finite; G acts freely on an integrally acyclic two-dimensional level complex X with one vertex orbit and finitely many cell orbits; the cellular chains of X give an exact sequence 0 -> Λ^(D) -> Λ^(S) -> Λ -> Z -> 0 with Λ = Z[G], so cd_Z(G) ≤ 2; cd_Z(G) ≥ 2 by restriction to a Z² subgroup; and the contractible three-dimensional cubical space E, on which G acts freely, gives a three-dimensional K(G,1) = E/G, so gd(G) ≤ 3. The lower bound excluding a two-dimensional K(G,1) is by contradiction. Theorem presentation: for a residually finite group Γ with a finite list D of words trivial in Γ whose chains form a free basis of the cycle module, and any two-dimensional K(Γ,1), there is η > 0 such that every SU(2)-labelling of the generator edges within distance η of 1, with trivial product around every translate of every word in D, has trivial product around every closed edge path. Proposition small-labels: for every ε > 0 there are labels on the edges of X within ε of 1, with trivial product around every triangle, and nontrivial product around some closed edge path; these are pulled back from alpha along direction maps from X to L. Taking ε < η gives a contradiction, so gd(G) = 3.
eilenberg-ganea-conjecture.delivers: Disproves the Eilenberg-Ganea statement as the list words it, on the integral reading. The list states that a group with cohomological dimension 2 has a two-dimensional K(G,1); the manuscript states the conjecture with integral cohomological dimension (introduction) and refutes it with one group, which is enough for a universal claim. The list names no coefficient ring, and the manuscript uses only integral coefficients. The witness is countable, finitely generated, residually finite, of type FP_infinity, and has a finite free resolution of length two over Z[G]. The manuscript says it is not finitely presented, because L has nontrivial fundamental group and the Bestvina-Brady criterion applies. So the counterexample does not cover finitely presented groups. The paper's statement of the problem matches the list's on the integral reading. The introduction says the result answers the question negatively.
eilenberg-ganea-conjecture.remains: If the claim is correct, nothing remains of the integral form of the bullet. Not addressed: the same question with other coefficient rings, which the list does not specify and the manuscript does not use; the question restricted to finitely presented groups, since the witness is not finitely presented; and cohomological dimensions other than 2, which the manuscript does not treat.

machine_checked.scope: The Eilenberg–Ganea conjecture predicts that a group of integral cohomological dimension two has a two-dimensional classifying space. The formalization constructs a finitely generated residually finite group of cohomological dimension two that has a three-dimensional classifying space but no two-dimensional one. Thus its geometric dimension is three, contradicting the conjecture.

eilenberg-ganea-conjecture.doubts: Lemma localized-degree (sections/degree.tex) is written in condensed form. The equivariant perturbation and transversality step is settled in a few sentences, including 'By compactness, sufficiently small perturbations introduce no zeros elsewhere'. The displayed argument establishes the degree only modulo an odd prime p larger than b. The Remark then states the exact value b·sign(det B) by repeating the argument for arbitrarily large primes, which the displayed proof does not spell out. The text flags no step as sketched or hedged.; conditional on: No unproven hypothesis beyond standard foundations: ZFC (choice, and Tychonoff's theorem for arbitrary products, which the comparison theorem needs for presentations of arbitrary cardinality), standard CW and covering-space theory, and finite-dimensional degree theory (Milnor). The height-kernel framework of Bestvina-Brady and Dicks-Leary is cited, but the properties used in the proof are proved in the manuscript. The Bestvina-Brady finite-presentability criterion is cited only for the remark that G is not finitely presented. Gerstenhaber-Rothaus and Froyshov are cited for the degree formula; the manuscript proves the localized statement it uses (Lemma localized-degree). No other OpenAI manuscript is used. Leary-Petrosyan (LP2026) appears only as background in the introduction.
eilenberg-ganea-conjecture.direction: disproves the conjecture (integral cd 2, geometric dimension 3)
eilenberg-ganea-conjecture.object: G = ker(lambda) in the right-angled Artin group A_L, a height kernel of an explicit finite flag complex L obtained from the presentation complex of <x,y | x²=y⁵, x²=(xy⁻¹)³> by an explicit subdivision and cone construction. The group, its level complex X and the three-dimensional classifying space E/G are explicit. The non-existence of a two-dimensional classifying space is proved by contradiction, using compactness of arbitrary products and choice, and gives no explicit object.

can-integer-factorization-be-done-in-pol.what_happened: The manuscript 'Exact quantum factoring over a fixed finite gate set' (OpenAI, dated 25 September 2026; the only manuscript in this family) claims a polynomial-time uniform family of quantum circuits that, for every integer N ≥ 2, outputs the complete prime factorization of N (primes in nondecreasing order with multiplicity) with probability exactly one (Theorem 1 in the introduction; abstract). Gate count and qubit count are bounded by a fixed polynomial in n = max{128, ⌊log₂N⌋+1}. The gate set is NOT, CNOT, Toffoli, Hadamard, S = diag(1,i), their inverses and their singly controlled versions. The construction has four parts. (a) An order trial (Proposition 'order-trial') replaces the Fourier phases of Shor's order sampling by a piecewise-linear phase register and adds classical correction modes. It returns either no candidate or a multiple of the order r of a mod m, and the probability that it returns exactly r is φ(r)λ(r), with λ(d) = 2^(−⌈log₂d⌉−10). (b) A recursive process (Proposition 'process') factors N and, recursively, p−1 for each odd prime factor p. Primes are checked by a deterministic polynomial-time test (Lemma 'primality', an AKS-type variant proved in the appendix). Composites are split by gcd(a^(r/2)−1, m) using orders found by the trial. It uses K = n⁵ repetitions per transition and L = n¹⁰ transition slots. (c) Deferred filters applied after the data have been generated (Lemma 'completion', Proposition 'known-probability') make the success probability of the whole preparation exactly p* = (1−2⁻ⁿ)^(n¹⁰) > 1/2. (d) A further dyadic correction gives a preparation whose success flag has probability exactly 1/4 (Lemma 'quarter'). One exact reflection step at that known probability, which the proof of the theorem carries out itself, then yields the factorization with certainty. The manuscript states that it 'makes no claim of a classical deterministic or randomized polynomial-time factoring algorithm'.
can-integer-factorization-be-done-in-pol.delivers: In the quantum circuit model with classical basis inputs, the claim gives the exact, zero-error, worst-case version of the quantum case: a uniform, polynomial-size family of quantum circuits over one fixed finite gate set that outputs the full factorization with probability one, with no repetition, no bounded-error guarantee and no supplied advice. It strengthens Shor's bounded-error polynomial-time quantum factoring, which the introduction cites. Restrictions: the bounds are polynomial in n with no explicit degree stated, and the body's parameters are large (L = n¹⁰ slots, K = n⁵ repetitions per transition, phase grid Q = B¹⁶ with B = 2ⁿ). The introduction says these are not intended as practical resource improvements. The result is about quantum circuits only. The manuscript's statement of the problem ('the nondecreasing list of primes whose product is N, including multiplicities') matches the list's 'outputs its prime factorization'. The manuscript does not restate the list's classical question and does not claim to settle it.
can-integer-factorization-be-done-in-pol.remains: If the claim holds, the classical question is untouched: whether a classical deterministic or randomized algorithm can factor N in time polynomial in log N, and the classical decision version. Also left open within the quantum model: the degree of the polynomial bounds and any practical resource count.

machine_checked.scope: The formalization constructs a polynomial-time uniform quantum circuit family that outputs the complete prime factorization of every integer $N\ge2$ with probability exactly one. The circuits use one fixed finite set of bounded-arity gates, and both the gate count and number of qubits have polynomial worst-case bounds in the bit length of $N$. The probability-one conclusion is exact, rather than an asymptotic or bounded-error guarantee.

can-integer-factorization-be-done-in-pol.doubts: (1) The identification of the implemented acceptance event, with deferred filters computed from the generated data, with the analytic event used in the probability calculation (Proposition 'known-probability') is argued in prose. The quantum-implementation step is deferred to Lemma 'records', whose proof is a short sketch ('Induction over the procedure shows that their squared norms ... equal those in the measured procedure'). The introduction calls the deferred-test identification 'the crucial argument'. (2) The primality test (Lemma 'primality') is presented as a variant of AKS. Its correctness proof adapts AKS root-counting lemmas (Lemmas 4.7–4.8 and their footnotes, credited to Lenstra, Macaj, Kalai, Sahai and Sudan), and the constants and auxiliary prime are chosen within the appendix. (3) Uniformity is defined per bit length, but the proofs of Lemma 'quarter' and of the theorem write V_N for each N and speak of 'fixed classical input N'. The text covers this in one sentence (a circuit for a fixed bit length with the input bits as controls is polynomial-time uniform), so the per-N and per-length readings are asserted to coincide rather than separately proved. (4) The polynomial degree is never stated, and the parameters are large (see 'delivers'). The text notes this itself.
can-integer-factorization-be-done-in-pol.direction: proves the quantum case exactly (zero error, fixed gate set); classical case not addressed
can-integer-factorization-be-done-in-pol.object: The explicit object is the uniform quantum circuit family itself. For each bit length it is a circuit with N in classical basis input bits, generated by a deterministic polynomial-time classical algorithm (Section 2 and the proof of the theorem in Section 6). This is an explicit construction, not an existence argument. Its classical subroutines (the primality test, the factor-tree verification and the classical controller) are compiled into the same gate set. It is not a classical factoring algorithm.

baum-connes-conjecture.what_happened: Three manuscripts in this family bear on the coefficient-free reduced assembly map (target C*_r(G), coefficient algebra C). (1) 'A torsion-free counterexample to reduced Baum-Connes injectivity' (dated 23 September 2026) constructs a finitely generated torsion-free discrete group Γ, an injective homomorphism i: Z^2 -> Γ, and a class c in H^2(BΓ; Z) with <(Bi)^*c, [T^2]> = 1, such that i_*(β) = 0 in K_0(C*_r Γ), where β is the rank-zero Bott generator of K_0(C*_r Z^2). Hence h = (Bi)_*[D_{T^2}] in K_0(BΓ) has infinite order, while its reduced assembly image is zero: a nonzero degree-zero kernel element of the reduced assembly map. (2) 'An irrational-trace counterexample to reduced Baum-Connes' (23 September 2026) constructs a finitely generated discrete group Γ_sur = V ⋊ Γ, with V a finite-field module, and a projection b_0 in C*_r(Γ_sur) whose canonical trace is the series sum over i of p^(-k_i), which the manuscript shows is irrational. Every class in the image of degree-zero assembly has rational trace (Lück's trace theorem, as recalled in the text), so [b_0] in K_0(C*_r Γ_sur) lies outside the image: a failure of surjectivity in degree zero. The manuscript states this refutes the coefficient-free reduced conjecture for countable discrete groups. (3) 'A torsion-free counterexample to the Kadison-Kaplansky projection conjecture' (23 September 2026) is about projections, not assembly: it constructs a finitely generated torsion-free Γ_proj = Γ_base * F_N and a projection e in C*_r(Γ_proj) with 0 < τ(e) < 1/2. Its introduction and conclusion add a remark, not a numbered theorem, that the same small trace places [p_0] in K_0(C*_r Γ_base) outside the image of degree-zero coefficient-free reduced assembly for the finitely generated torsion-free Γ_base, citing Baum-Guentner-Willett Prop. 10.3. That is a second, remark-level surjectivity failure in degree zero. (The same manuscript also disproves the Kadison-Kaplansky projection conjecture, which is not a matched problem here.)
baum-connes-conjecture.delivers: Injectivity fails in degree zero for the coefficient-free reduced assembly map, witnessed by one finitely generated torsion-free group (manuscript 1). Surjectivity fails in degree zero, witnessed by one finitely generated discrete group (manuscript 3, stated as a theorem); manuscript 2 gives the same kind of failure for Γ_base as a remark. Because the bullet asks that the assembly map be an isomorphism in every degree, a failure in degree zero alone refutes it as stated, under the bullet's reading (every discrete group, coefficient C, both injectivity and surjectivity). The manuscripts say so: manuscript 1 says it disproves rational injectivity of the coefficient-free reduced assembly map for torsion-free groups; manuscript 3 says the coefficient-free reduced Baum-Connes conjecture for countable discrete groups is false. Their statement of the conjecture matches the bullet's coefficient-free reading: assembly from equivariant K-homology of the proper classifying space to K_j(C*_r G), for j = 0, 1, with trivial coefficient C. Restrictions: manuscript 1's counterexample is torsion-free and fails only injectivity, in K_0. Manuscript 3's group is not claimed torsion-free; V is an F_p-vector space, so Γ_sur has elements of finite order. The bullet does not require torsion-freeness, so this does not weaken the refutation of the bullet as stated. Manuscript 3's failure is shown in K_0 only.
baum-connes-conjecture.remains: Nothing is left to refute in the bullet's stated reading: degree zero already refutes it. Not addressed by any of the three manuscripts: (i) degree one, K_1, of the coefficient-free reduced map; (ii) the version with coefficients in a separable G-C*-algebra, which the bullet does not name and which these manuscripts do not treat; (iii) the maximal assembly map, which manuscript 1 says still detects its class (mu^max(h) tensor 1 is nonzero), so it does not refute the maximal version; (iv) the status of the surjectivity failure for Γ_base in manuscript 2, which is a remark-level claim and not a numbered theorem.
baum-connes-conjecture.doubts: (1) Manuscript 1's group is a finitely generated subgroup obtained from an infinite construction by a finite-witness lemma, so the text establishes existence of the group rather than exhibiting it. (2) Manuscript 1's abstract says rational injectivity is disproved for torsion-free groups; its theorem gives one group, which is enough for the universal statement, and the kernel element has infinite order, so the abstract and theorem agree. (3) Manuscript 1's maximal-side discussion records a gap in the all-groups version of the cited Antonini-Buss-Engel-Siebenand result and says it uses the corrected, finitely presented version; the authors say the reduced claim does not depend on it. (4) Manuscript 3's group is not claimed torsion-free, although the abstract's phrase 'for countable discrete groups' suggests a general scope; the theorem gives one group. (5) Manuscript 3's surjectivity conclusion depends on Lück's trace theorem, which is cited, and not on the paper's own analysis. (6) Manuscript 2's surjectivity claim for Γ_base is a remark with a citation, not a proved theorem in its own right. A search of the section files for hedges (sketch, conjecture, assume, erratum, and similar) found no step flagged as sketched in the BC-relevant claims, beyond the items listed here.; conditional on: No unproven hypothesis is assumed in manuscript 1's reduced theorem or manuscript 3's surjectivity theorem, beyond their own constructions and cited published results. Cited results used but not reproved: manuscript 1 uses the twisted spin Dirac index theorem [AS63], in the dimension-two form of [BvE16, Thm. 1], the Emerson-Hudson assembly formula for the torus [EH20, Thm. 1.3], which identifies the assembly image of the torus Dirac class with the rank-zero Bott generator, and the geometric-to-analytic K-homology comparison [BHS07, Thms. 6.1-6.2]. Its maximal-side remark (μ^max(h) tensor 1 nonzero) rests on Hanke-Schick and on a corrected statement of Antonini-Buss-Engel-Siebenand; the reduced claim does not use these. Manuscript 3 uses Lück's trace theorem (Theorem 0.3 of Lück 2002) as a black box for rationality of traces on the assembly image, with the direct-limit domain convention stated in the text; it also uses Osajda's labelling theorem (Theorems 2.7 and 3.2) and Lubotzky-Phillips-Sarnak expanders. Manuscript 2's surjectivity remark depends on Baum-Guentner-Willett Prop. 10.3 and on Lück's integrality result; its projection theorem does not depend on them.
baum-connes-conjecture.direction: disproves the conjecture: injectivity fails in degree zero (manuscript 1); surjectivity fails in degree zero (manuscript 3; remark-level in manuscript 2)
baum-connes-conjecture.object: No explicit group is written down. In each case the group comes from an existence argument: expanders with large girth, codes over F_p or sampled voltages, Osajda-type labellings, and, in manuscript 1, a finite-witness lemma that extracts a finitely generated subgroup of an infinite construction. The manuscripts say finite presentation is not part of the conclusion. The explicit objects are: in manuscript 1, the degree-zero class h = (Bi)_*[D_{T^2}] in K_0(BΓ), of infinite order and in the kernel of reduced assembly; its vanishing is shown by proof, not by formula. In manuscript 3, the projection b_0 = 1_{0}(T), the spectral projection at zero of an explicit finite-field-module operator T in C*_r(Γ_sur), with trace sum over i of p^(-k_i), where the k_i are chosen with increasing gaps. In manuscript 2, the projection e is given by an explicit compression formula from p_0, but its base group Γ_base is existence-selected.

invariant-subspace-problem.what_happened: Two manuscripts by OpenAI bear on this problem; neither claims to settle it. (1) 'Invariant-projection counterexamples for every irrational rotation' (27 Sept 2026): for each irrational θ in (0,1) it constructs a continuous f: circle to [0,1] with f^{-1}(0) = {1} and ∫log f dm = −∞, so the Fuglede–Kadison determinant is 0. The operator T_f = U f(V) in the hyperfinite II₁ factor R_θ has no projection p in R_θ with 0 < τ(p) < 1 and (1−p)T_f p = 0. This answers negatively the Zhu–Fang–Shi question about affiliated invariant subspaces, with the angle fixed in advance. Its quasinilpotence corollary gives T_f nonzero and norm-quasinilpotent. Its transitive-commutant corollary derives, on every separable infinite-dimensional complex Hilbert space, a nonzero norm-quasinilpotent operator with no nonzero proper closed hyperinvariant subspace, whose commutant is a proper strongly closed transitive unital algebra. (2) 'Backward intertwiners and a transitive commutant' (27 Sept 2026): by a separate construction on H_0 = L²(Z₂, μ; ℓ²(Z)), it gives a bilateral weighted shift S with fibre weights β_j(x) = exp(−a_j(x)), where the a_j are explicit functions of the 2-adic residues of x; ‖S‖ = e^{−10}; ‖Sⁿ‖ ≤ exp(−10⌊(n+1)²/4⌋); and a commuting contraction V with (Vf)(θx) = V_x f(x). The algebra generated by S, V and all scalar multipliers is transitive, so the commutant of S is transitive. Its abstract presents the result as a negative answer to the hyperinvariant-subspace problem on every infinite-dimensional separable complex Hilbert space.
invariant-subspace-problem.delivers: Does not settle the problem as frozen, and the manuscripts do not claim to. The frozen problem asks whether every bounded operator on every complex Banach space has a nontrivial closed invariant subspace. The family gives negative answers to two neighbouring questions. (a) Paper 2 answers the hyperinvariant variant: on every infinite-dimensional separable complex Hilbert space there is a nonzero quasinilpotent operator with no nonzero proper closed hyperinvariant subspace. Paper 2 frames the question as whether every nonscalar bounded operator on such a space has one, so its statement of that variant is matched by this construction. A hyperinvariant subspace is in particular invariant, so having none is a weaker property than having no invariant subspace; the operator here does have invariant subspaces. (b) Paper 1 answers, for each irrational θ, the narrower question whether T_f has a nontrivial invariant projection inside R_θ. Its own introduction says invariant subspaces of the Hilbert-space representation need not be affiliated with R_θ, so these are not excluded. Both operators have ordinary invariant subspaces: paper 2 names the tails L²(X; K_{≥h}) as closed, nonzero, proper and S-invariant, and says the invariant and hyperinvariant problems 'must remain distinct'; paper 1's appendix notes the same kind of tail invariance for its product model. Hence neither manuscript gives an operator on a Hilbert space lacking nontrivial invariant subspaces, and neither proves that every operator has one. The matching pass's 'variant' label is accurate: the hyperinvariant result bears on a variant, and the frozen problem is not touched.
invariant-subspace-problem.remains: Everything in the frozen problem remains open: the question over all complex Banach spaces, including the separable infinite-dimensional Hilbert case, since every operator built here has nontrivial invariant subspaces and so is no counterexample to it. Paper 1's result covers only irrational θ, and its invariant-projection conclusion concerns only the factor R_θ.

machine_checked.scope:
For every irrational rotation angle $\theta\in(0,1)$, the formalization constructs a continuous nonnegative circle weight with a single zero and logarithmic integral $-\infty$ whose weighted rotation is nonzero and quasinilpotent. In its associated hyperfinite type $\mathrm{II}_1$ factor, the operator has no nontrivial invariant projection: $(1-p)Tp=0$ forces $p=0$ or $p=1$. The linked statements also include an earlier existence construction, a product realization, and the selected product model's Brown measure $\delta_0$.

The formalization for the companion paper [Backward intertwiners and a transitive commutant](../../preprints/Backward-intertwiners-and-a-transitive-commutant-September-27-2026/paper.pdf) gives, on every separable infinite-dimensional complex Hilbert space, a nonzero quasinilpotent operator whose commutant is transitive, proper, and closed in the strong operator topology. Thus no nontrivial closed subspace is invariant under every operator in the commutant.

The hyperinvariant-subspace problem asks whether every bounded operator on a complex Hilbert space has a nontrivial closed subspace invariant under every operator that commutes with it. The formalization gives a negative answer on every separable infinite-dimensional complex Hilbert space: there is a nonzero quasinilpotent operator with a transitive commutant. Its commutant is a proper unital operator algebra closed in the strong operator topology. The construction therefore has no nonzero proper closed hyperinvariant subspace.

invariant-subspace-problem.doubts: Paper 1 says its hyperinvariant corollary contradicts a hyperinvariant-subspace assertion of Cho, Ko and Lee (Corollary 2.8, p. 801) at μ = 1 (its Remark rem:ckl). That is the manuscript's own claim about a published result, which I have not checked. I found no sketched steps, hedges, or abstract-versus-theorem mismatches in either text; the search for such language matched only routine uses. Paper 1's obstruction argument is asymptotic ('for sufficiently large j'), and its constants are stated but I did not recheck them.; conditional on: Paper 2 uses two lemmas from paper 1, the scalar-multiplier field lemma (its Lemma 3.1) and the commutant lemma (its Lemma 1.2). Paper 1 proves both in its text, and paper 2 says so, so this is a dependency on a manuscript rather than an unproven hypothesis. Paper 1 depends on no other manuscript. Neither result assumes an unproven hypothesis.
invariant-subspace-problem.direction: disproves the hyperinvariant-subspace variant (paper 2, and paper 1 by a route through its factor result); disproves, for each irrational θ, the variant asking for invariant projections in R_θ (paper 1); does not decide the invariant-subspace problem
invariant-subspace-problem.object: Paper 2: an explicit bilateral weighted shift S on L²(Z₂, μ; ℓ²(Z)) with weights β_j(x) = exp(−a_j(x)), where the a_j^± are given by formulas in the residues x mod 2^m, and an explicit contraction V built by a recursion normalised by its supremum. Paper 1: a continuous weight f on the circle with f(1) = 0, built in stages (divisible frequencies, ordered couplings, smoothing and relocation of logarithmic drops, a background cost at the zero). Its construction is not a closed formula. The measurable model f_* = exp(−Σ c_i ⌊{q_i x} + {q_i θ}⌋) is explicit but is not the continuous operator the theorem concerns.

hilbert-smith-conjecture.what_happened: The family is one manuscript, 'The Hilbert–Smith conjecture in every finite dimension' (OpenAI preprint dated 23 September 2026). It claims a proof of the stated theorem: every locally compact, second-countable, Hausdorff group acting faithfully and jointly continuously on a connected, Hausdorff, second-countable topological n-manifold without boundary (n ≥ 1; the 0-dimensional case is trivial) is a Lie group. Its main technical theorem (the 'p-adic exclusion', §5–§6) is that for every prime p, every jointly continuous action of ℤₚ on such a manifold has nonzero kernel, so it factors through a finite quotient of ℤₚ. The group statement is then deduced from this via the classical Hilbert–Smith reduction, which the manuscript cites to Pardon (2013) rather than proving. The argument runs as follows. (i) Newman's periodicity theorem reduces to a faithful, orientation-preserving action of an open copy of ℤₚ on a connected invariant open subset O of one chart in ℝⁿ (Prop. 'chart-reduction', §5). (ii) For an odd d > n, O × ℝ^(d−n) is compactified, the orbit space Y is formed, and a degree-one map a: Y → Sᵈ is averaged out (§5). (iii) For each finite partition of the group of p-power roots of unity, integral classes z_i(t) are defined in a Witt group E_d(X) of real sheaf complexes generated by proper direct images of constant sheaves on finite polyhedra, using eigensheaf projectors of the orbit sheaf (§6). (iv) Σ_i z_i(t) = 2[A_t, α_t] and the classes are covariant and homotopy invariant (§6). (v) Finite quotient sheets plus a degree-s map that is constant off a region force all m = pᵏ classes z_i(a) to have equal rational images, which are then (4/m)ū_d. (vi) A fixed integrality lattice on E_d(Sᵈ), with denominator L_d = 2^(e_d) independent of the action (thm:sphere-lattice, §4), forces 4L_d/m to be an integer, contradicting m = pᵏ > 4L_d. The lattice is obtained by comparing the Witt groups of semialgebraic and continuous sheaf complexes with a bounded exponent-2 comparison (§4), using a dense-doubling homomorphism (thm:dense-doubling, §3) that the manuscript proves itself.
hilbert-smith-conjecture.delivers: If correct, it establishes the Hilbert–Smith conjecture in the restricted form stated in its theorem: for second-countable Hausdorff locally compact groups acting faithfully and jointly continuously on connected, second-countable, Hausdorff manifolds without boundary of any finite dimension, the group is a Lie group. It also gives the ℤₚ exclusion for the same class of manifolds, which is the input the list's own reduction (via Gleason–Yamabe and Newman) needs. The manuscript's abstract presents this as a proof of the conjecture 'in every finite dimension', and the introduction calls it 'a positive resolution in every positive finite dimension'. The statement of the list does not match the statement proved. The list does not assume the group is second-countable; the manuscript does. The list does not assume the manifold is connected, second-countable, or without boundary; the manuscript assumes all three. Dimension is handled as the standard finite-dimensional convention. So the result proves the conjecture for the restricted class, and says nothing about groups or manifolds outside it.
hilbert-smith-conjecture.remains: If the claim is correct, the following parts of the list's problem are still open. (a) Locally compact groups that are not second-countable (the text assumes second-countability throughout the group argument). (b) Topological manifolds that are not second-countable; the long line is a connected, Hausdorff, 1-dimensional topological manifold outside the class treated. (c) Manifolds with boundary; the theorem states 'without boundary'. (d) Disconnected manifolds; the theorem assumes connectedness and the text gives no reduction from the disconnected case. The problem_asks clause (1), about all locally compact groups with no Hausdorff or second-countability assumption, and clause (2), about all topological manifolds, are therefore only partly addressed.
hilbert-smith-conjecture.doubts: (1) The proof of the dense-doubling theorem (§3) derives y ⊕ y[1] ∈ 𝒜 from density by writing 'If density is expressed by a split inclusion, its cone supplies such a complement', and does not separately argue the non-split case. The exponent-2 bound used in the lattice depends on this step. (2) In the odd-sphere lemma (§5) the text says it will 'verify [the telescope's] homotopy type directly', but the key step, that a long enough product of degrees kills an element of πⱼ(Sᵈ), is compressed into a few sentences and rests on Serre's degree statement as cited. (3) The integral-signature and neutrality claims in the generic-signature proposition (§4) are argued in a few paragraphs, with local finiteness and locality of cohomology asserted from cited semialgebraic facts. (4) The appendix on duality signs says reversing the orientation or changing cone normalizations 'may negate both entries', and only one convention is fixed. The text does not check the main contradiction under other normalizations. (5) The text calls the result 'a positive resolution' of the conjecture. The theorem carries hypotheses (second-countable group, connected, second-countable, boundaryless manifold) that the classical statement does not, and the text does not discuss the excluded cases. (6) The claim is very strong: a dimension-free resolution with no regularity assumption, where the introduction itself describes earlier partial results that needed low dimension, regularity, or symplectic hypotheses. The decisive integrality step is a few pages long and depends on the compressed steps above.; conditional on: No unproven hypothesis beyond the stated restrictions, but the text relies on several results it cites rather than proves. (1) Newman's theorem on periodic homeomorphisms (Newman 1931; the modern statement is cited to Pardon 2019, 'author manuscript'). (2) The classical Hilbert–Smith reduction from locally compact groups to ℤₚ, cited to Pardon 2013, Introduction; the proof of the group statement uses it without proof. (3) Serre's results on odd spheres (Serre 1951, 1953): finiteness of higher homotopy groups, and the statement that a degree-2q map kills an element of order q; these drive the odd-sphere lemma. (4) Balmer–Walter 2002, Theorem 2.1, for the Witt localization sequence. (5) Hardt 1980 and Hardt–Lambrechts–Turchin–Volić 2011 for semialgebraic triviality and cohomology finiteness. (6) Woolf 2008 for the interval argument. (7) Dranishnikov–Ferry–Weinberger 2003 for the telescope argument. (8) Schapira's notes, Kashiwara–Schapira, Verdier, Stacks Project, and Bergfalk–Lupini–Panagiotopoulos for sheaf-theoretic foundations. Hornbostel–Schlichting's cofinality theorem is cited for the dense-inclusion bound, but §3 gives a direct proof (thm:dense-doubling), so it is not a dependency of the argument. No other OpenAI manuscript is cited.
hilbert-smith-conjecture.direction: proves a restricted case: the conjecture for second-countable groups acting on connected, second-countable, boundaryless manifolds (presented by the authors as the conjecture in every finite dimension)

hopf-conjecture.what_happened: One manuscript, 'The Singer conjecture in dimension four' (OpenAI, dated September 25, 2026; the only manuscript in this family). Its main theorem (thm:main, introduction) says that for any finite connected aspherical integral Poincaré complex Q of formal dimension four, with arbitrary orientation character, the L²-Betti numbers b_p⁽²⁾(Q̃) vanish for every p ≠ 2. Corollary cor:singer-manifolds applies this to closed connected aspherical topological four-manifolds M, which the paper calls the four-dimensional Singer conjecture. The consequences section (cor:euler) adds χ(Q) = b₂⁽²⁾(Q̃) ≥ 0 for the same class, with χ(Q) = 0 exactly when all L²-Betti numbers vanish. For manifolds this is the statement χ(M) ≥ 0 for closed aspherical topological four-manifolds, which is the dimension-four, aspherical case of the Euler-characteristic sign question. The paper also proves χ(M) ≥ |σ(M)| for closed oriented ones (cor:signature) and a growth statement for covers along a descending chain of finite-index normal subgroups with trivial intersection (cor:betti-growth). The main proof is by contradiction. A positive first L²-Betti number yields a nondegenerate continuum boundary with dimension at most one and vanishing Čech H¹ mod 2; the path-pushing section makes it locally connected, and conclusion.tex then contradicts Lemma end:continuum, which says such a continuum has a cut point. The manuscript says nothing about sectional curvature.
hopf-conjecture.delivers: Within the Hopf list, the claim bears only on part (e), Thurston's aspherical sign statement, and only in dimension four. It establishes χ(M) ≥ 0 for every closed connected aspherical topological four-manifold, with no smoothness, orientability or geometric-structure assumption, and more generally χ(Q) ≥ 0 for finite aspherical integral Poincaré complexes of formal dimension four, which need not be manifolds. This is the k = 2 instance of (e), which the list states as (−1)ᵏ χ(M^(2k)) ≥ 0 for closed aspherical manifolds in every even dimension; the manuscript's statement is therefore narrower in dimension and broader in the class of spaces. Parts (a) and (b) (positive and nonnegative sectional curvature) and the curvature-sign parts of (c) are not addressed. Since a closed nonpositively curved manifold is aspherical (Cartan–Hadamard, my note, not the text), the nonpositive case of (c) in dimension four falls under the claim, but the manuscript does not state or prove it, and the problem_asks records dimension four as the already-known case of the curvature conjectures. The product conjecture (d) is not addressed. The manuscript's own statements are not about the list's 'higher-dimensional' scope.
hopf-conjecture.remains: If the claim is correct, the dimension-four aspherical sign statement is settled for closed topological manifolds and for finite Poincaré complexes. Still open for this problem: (a) and (b), the positive and nonnegative curvature sign conjectures in every even dimension; (c), the negative and nonpositive curvature sign conjectures in dimensions 2n ≥ 6; (d), the product conjecture; and (e) for closed aspherical manifolds in dimensions 2k ≥ 6. The paper's Singer-type concentration would give the sign in higher even dimensions only if the vanishing were proved there, and the manuscript proves it only in dimension four.
hopf-conjecture.doubts: (1) The new steps are the authors' own extensions beyond their sources, and the text says so: the finite-interval reduction in the all-parabolic case (pretree.tex: Bowditch's Theorem 6.1 'does not itself produce' it, and 'we now prove that assertion'); the block graph and continuous retraction onto a block (blocks.tex: 'extensions established here, not an invocation of a retraction theorem'); and the separation counts, which the introduction says 'adapt' Bowditch's annulus method. These are the parts a reader must check against the text. (2) The boundary argument runs under standing hypotheses stated at the start of pretree.tex: a finitely presented, torsion-free, one-ended group acting minimally as a convergence group with no nontrivial splitting over a finite or two-ended subgroup. The text says these 'have been established for the boundary constructed above'; I did not check that in foundations.tex or compactification.tex. (3) The four-dimensional model step is compressed. Lemma found:model cites Wall's dimension theorem, justifies finiteness in one sentence ('It can be chosen finite because Q is finite, so its reduced finiteness obstruction vanishes'), and cites West for manifolds. (4) The text presents χ(M) ≥ |σ(M)| as 'the Euler–signature inequality discussed by Gromov and Lück', citing Conjecture 1.3 of Albanese–Di Cerbo–Lombardi, which that source states as a conjecture. The manuscript presents it as a corollary, and says the equality of ordinary and L² signatures is 'an additional input' that is proved only for manifolds. (5) Abstract and main theorem agree: both cover arbitrary orientation characters and both state the manifold case; I found no inconsistency. (6) Reading depth: I read the abstract, introduction, main statements, the conclusion, the consequences, and the openings and flagged passages of foundations, pretree, blocks, annuli and path-pushing. I did not check the full ~3,400 lines of the build, and I did not check the local-connectivity argument in path-pushing beyond its final assembly.; conditional on: No hypothesis is assumed for χ(M) ≥ 0 itself. The proof takes cited literature results without reproving them: Wall's dimension theorem and West's homotopy-dimension estimate for the four-dimensional model, topological Poincaré duality (Sun 2017), Bowditch's pretree package, and Lück's L²-Euler–Poincaré formula. It depends on no other OpenAI manuscript for the main theorem. The companion papers are cited only as an application (the PD4 nonmanifold example) and as a remark on complex surfaces, which the text says is not an input. The corollary χ(M) ≥ |σ(M)| additionally needs Lück–Schick's topological L²-signature theorem, and the growth corollary assumes a descending chain of finite-index normal subgroups with trivial intersection. Neither is relevant to the curvature parts of the list.
hopf-conjecture.direction: proves a case: the dimension-four aspherical instance of the Euler-characteristic sign (χ ≥ 0), plus χ ≥ |σ| for oriented topological four-manifolds as a side result; no curvature statement

borel-conjecture.what_happened: One manuscript, 'Nonhomeomorphic closed aspherical four-manifolds with the same homotopy type' (OpenAI, dated October 4, 2026). Theorem 'pair' (thm:pair): there are closed connected aspherical topological four-manifolds M and N that are homotopy equivalent but not homeomorphic, with a common word-hyperbolic fundamental group Π. Theorem 'self-map' (thm:self-map): for the same M there is a homotopy equivalence f: M → M such that no homeomorphism M → M is homotopic to f. Construction in outline: a four-dimensional Poincaré chamber (D, P, S) whose double cyclic cover S₂ has a marked filling, while every odd cyclic cover S_d (d ≥ 3) has none. Reflection quotient Q of P by an elementary abelian label group A = (ℤ/2)^𝒱 / C, where 𝒱 is the vertex set of a flag-no-square triangulation of S with at least 5000 vertices and C is an explicit 8-dimensional subspace; Q₂ is the double cyclic cover of Q, and Π = π₁(Q₂). M = M₀ and N = M_ℓ are two closed manifold models of Q₂, obtained by gluing copies of a topological filling of S₂ with boundary twists given by a linear functional ε on A (ε = 0 for M, ε = ℓ ≠ 0 for N). Self-map: a cyclic-cover criterion realizes the outer automorphism δ of Π by a self-homotopy equivalence of M and rules out any homeomorphism inducing δ. Non-homeomorphism: a Sylow-type criterion for Out(Π) (Proposition 'A Sylow criterion for manifold models'), using that A and B_ℓ are 2-subgroups of equal order, that the normalizer of A in Out(Π) is A × ⟨δ⟩, that δ is not realized on M, and that A and B_ℓ are not conjugate in Out(Π).
borel-conjecture.delivers: Dimension four only. The objects are closed connected aspherical topological (not smooth) four-manifolds. The pair M, N has one common fundamental group Π, which the text shows is word-hyperbolic, torsion-free, infinite, one-ended, and of finite index in the reflection extension W ⋊ H. Out(Π) is finite. The text claims a disproof of the homeomorphism-existence formulation of the Borel conjecture in dimension four, for this one group. Against the list's bullet, which asks for aspherical closed manifolds with isomorphic fundamental groups to be homeomorphic and does not restrict the dimension, the paper's existence form matches the bullet's wording, and the dimension-four pair falsifies that bullet as worded. The manuscripts do not claim to settle the Borel conjecture as a whole. Their statement is narrower than the bullet in dimension, and the bullet's part (3), the homotopy-realization form, is not the paper's headline. Reading the stated Theorem 'self-map' against the introduction's definition of the topological Borel conjecture (every homotopy equivalence between closed aspherical manifolds is homotopic to a homeomorphism), it also refutes that stronger form in dimension four. The text does not state that consequence in its abstract or introduction. It is my reading of the stated theorem. The text notes that Bartels and Lück prove the prescribed-class formulation in dimensions at least five for a class containing word-hyperbolic groups. The counterexample is in dimension four, so it does not conflict with that.
borel-conjecture.remains: If the claim is correct, the family does not touch these parts of the problem. (a) Dimensions other than four. The text treats dimensions at most two as classical, and dimension three for closed orientable aspherical manifolds via geometrization. It cites Bartels and Lück for dimensions at least five for a class containing hyperbolic groups. It says the cyclic-cover criterion 'works in every manifold dimension', but applies it only at n = 4. (b) Dimension four for other fundamental groups. The text does not characterize which dimension-four groups admit such pairs, and it gives only this one group. (c) The homotopy-realization form for other manifolds or groups. It is refuted only by the single self-map of M. (d) Goodness. The introduction presents goodness as the hypothesis of the dimension-four rigidity results it cites (Bartels–Lück, Freedman–Quinn), and the text does not say whether Π is good. The claim's conclusion is in tension with the good case, and the text does not discuss this.
borel-conjecture.doubts: (1) The two load-bearing inputs are imported, not proved here. Theorem 'Reflection and marked fillings' is presented as extracted from [PD, Sections 3–5]. The odd-cover non-filling (Proposition 'Odd covers do not fill') takes its edge-level input unchanged from [MT, Proposition 4.5 and Theorem 5.1], and the text says that what it verifies is only the assembly at vertices with both kinds of endpoint and the conversion of the four-slot laws. (2) The endpoint-assignment theorem is said to be argued 'in full', yet the same paragraph says its truncated differential forms and its two successive homologies come from [MT, Section 3]. (3) The introduction cites Khan's rigidity up to topological s-cobordism for closed aspherical four-manifolds with torsion-free word-hyperbolic fundamental group, and says the five-dimensional product theorem needs a good group. Theorem 'pair' concerns exactly torsion-free word-hyperbolic Π. The text never says whether Π is good and does not reconcile this with Khan's result. It says only that 'the dimension is essential to their topological conclusion'. (4) Finiteness of Out(Π) is obtained by citing the Bestvina–Feighn splitting theorem and applying the paper's own no-splitting lemma. The cited theorem is not proved in the text. (5) A search of all section files found no step flagged as sketched, conditional, or omitted, and no hedging beyond the imported inputs.; conditional on: Yes. (a) Two companion OpenAI manuscripts, neither read here: 'A marked tensor obstruction to four-dimensional disk embedding' ([MT]) and 'A PD4 group without an aspherical manifold model' ([PD]), both OpenAI Math Release preprints dated September 24, 2026. The reflection input (Theorem 'Reflection and marked fillings') is stated by the authors as extracted from [PD, Sections 3–5] and uses [PD, Propositions 3.2, 4.6, 5.5]. The parity chamber data and the odd-cover non-filling use the plumbing blocks of [MT, Section 2.2], the chamber and cut constructions of [PD, Section 2], the marked algebraicity theorem [MT, Theorem 5.1] with [MT, Proposition 4.5 and Lemma 4.4], and the universal-development argument of [PD, Section 3]. (b) That Out(Π) is finite rests on a splitting theorem of Bestvina and Feighn (using Paulin's construction), cited and not proved in the text. (c) Standard results cited without proof: Davis's reflection-group framework, Chepoi's median-graph facts, Przytycki–Świątkowski's flag-no-square triangulations, Stallings's ends theorem, and the Švarc–Milnor lemma. The argument does not use Khan's results.
borel-conjecture.direction: disproves the homeomorphism-existence form of the Borel conjecture in dimension four, for one hyperbolic group; the self-map result also refutes the homotopy-realization form in dimension four
borel-conjecture.object: Two closed aspherical topological four-manifolds M = M₀ and N = M_ℓ, and a self-homotopy equivalence f: M → M. M and N are built explicitly as gluings of copies of one compact topological four-manifold V with boundary S₂ (the double-cover filling, obtained from the smooth chamber double cover D₂ by replacing finitely many punctured S² × S² neighborhoods with four-balls), along a flag-no-square triangulation of S and a choice of linear functional ε on the label group A. Once these choices are fixed, the gluing recipe is explicit. The chamber D itself comes from the plumbing constructions of the companion manuscripts. The non-homeomorphism is proved by contradiction, and no invariant is exhibited. The self-map f is not written down: it is obtained by realizing an outer automorphism through the classification of maps between Eilenberg–MacLane spaces.
