crouzeixs-conjecture.what_happened: Two OpenAI preprints, each citing the other, both claim the complete numerical-range inequality with constant 2: for a matrix-valued F = Σ B_k z^k, ‖F[A]‖ ≤ 2 max over z in W(A) of ‖F(z)‖, where F[A] = Σ A^k ⊗ B_k. A scalar f is the m = 1 case. (1) "A direct proof of the complete Crouzeix inequality" (dated 26 September 2026) proves this for every finite base dimension n, coefficient dimension m and degree d, for matrix polynomials only. Its route: for a bounded convex domain Ω containing W(A), with regular real-analytic boundary, any matrix polynomial F with ‖F‖ ≤ 1 on ∂Ω satisfies ‖F[A]‖ ≤ 2 (Theorem 'domain'). This uses singular-vector duality, Faber-coefficient estimates, and a positivity comparison of a 2×2 block built from the resolvent of A. Analytic convex outer approximations (Lemma 'approx') then shrink Ω to W(A), which covers point and segment ranges. (2) "The complete Crouzeix theorem: optimal similarity and a common positive boundary representation" (dated 23 September 2026) claims the same inequality for matrix polynomials over finite matrices (Corollary 'polynomial') and for every bounded operator on an arbitrary complex Hilbert space, with no separability assumption (Corollary 'hilbert'). It extends the bound to matrix-valued F holomorphic on an open neighbourhood of K = closure of W(A), with ‖F[A]‖ ≤ 2 max over K of ‖F‖, and to rational functions with poles outside K, which it calls a complete 2-spectral set. The Hilbert case reduces to a finite-dimensional compression, with W(A_E) ⊂ W(A). The holomorphic case uses Runge approximation and a contour form of the holomorphic calculus. Its polynomial bound runs through its structural theorems: for an analytic convex Ω containing W(A), it constructs a metric whose similarity S has ‖S‖‖S⁻¹‖ = κ ≤ 2, making S f(A) S⁻¹ a contraction, and a continuous positive density Λ of mass I representing v[A'] for every matrix-valued v holomorphic near Ω̄ (Theorems 'structural' and 'representation'). Both manuscripts give the same 2×2 nilpotent example to show that the constant 2 cannot be lowered.
crouzeixs-conjecture.delivers: For the list's statement (operator norm of f(A), A any complex square matrix, supremum over W(A) of |f|, constant exactly 2): the second manuscript claims all of it for f holomorphic on an open neighbourhood of W(A). In finite dimensions W(A) is compact, so this is the same as a neighbourhood of its closure. The scalar case is m = 1, and the claim is stated uniformly over n, m and d. The second manuscript's claims also reach infinite-dimensional operators, which the list does not ask for. The first manuscript delivers only the polynomial case: for every finite matrix A and every matrix polynomial P, ‖P[A]‖ ≤ 2 sup over W(A) of ‖P‖, with 2 sharp. It does not state the holomorphic or rational cases. Neither manuscript covers the list's full class, 'every function for which f(A) is defined'. Both restrict to polynomials, rational functions, or functions holomorphic near W(A). Both abstracts say the result 'resolves the complete Crouzeix conjecture', meaning the matrix-valued form, which contains the scalar conjecture. The manuscripts attribute the scalar constant-2 proofs to earlier 2026 preprints by Jin, by Lorist and Schwenninger, and by Luo.
crouzeixs-conjecture.remains: If the claims are correct, the list's inequality is covered for holomorphic f on a neighbourhood of W(A). Not covered: functions for which f(A) is defined but which are not holomorphic (or rational) near W(A). The matrix-valued, completely bounded form is claimed but is not part of the list's statement. The similarity and common-density results are claimed only for analytic convex domains containing W(A), not for W(A) itself, and they are not needed for the list's inequality. The first manuscript leaves the holomorphic and rational cases and infinite-dimensional operators open; the second manuscript addresses them.

machine_checked.scope:
The complete Crouzeix inequality bounds a matrix-valued polynomial evaluated at a matrix by its maximum norm on the numerical range. The formalized result proves the bound with constant $2$ for every positive matrix and coefficient size, every polynomial degree, and arbitrary complex coefficients. It also proves that no smaller universal constant works. Normality of the matrix and nonempty interior of its numerical range are not assumed.

The formalization proves the complete Crouzeix inequality with sharp constant two for every bounded operator on an arbitrary complex Hilbert space. For every matrix-valued polynomial, its operator evaluation has norm at most twice its supremum norm on the numerical range. The same bound holds for finite matrix-valued functions holomorphic near the closure of the numerical range and for rational functions with poles outside that closure. No separability assumption is required.

For finite matrices in a bounded convex domain with regular real-analytic Jordan boundary, the structural result gives an attained optimal similarity with condition number at most two and one continuous positive boundary density of mass the identity representing every matrix-valued analytic test. The linked supporting statements include numerical-range geometry and finite-compression identities.

crouzeixs-conjecture.doubts: (a) The first manuscript does not write out the step from polynomials to holomorphic functions, which the list's f requires. The second manuscript does write it out. (b) The second manuscript's polynomial bound, and so its Hilbert-space and holomorphic bounds, depends on its structural chain: the κ ≤ 2 comparison (Lemma 'comparison'), fed by the endpoint extremal (Proposition 'extremal'). Two steps there are compressed. One is the removal of apparent poles on the circle for the disk function F_D. The other is the unitary realization, which the text attributes to classical interpolation and colligation results while saying its endpoint data and realization are 'established here'. The first manuscript gives a separate route to the polynomial inequality, which the text says is a separate complete proof path. (c) The rational-function claim in Corollary 'hilbert' is argued in one paragraph (resolvent identity, differentiation in the pole, partial fractions), not in full. (d) The Gaussian outer approximation (Lemma 'gaussian') and the conformal reflection and patching appendices in both manuscripts are compressed. They cite Ahlfors, Pommerenke and Carathéodory's theorem for the classical steps. (e) The two manuscripts cite each other. The first cites the second for 'counterparts' to its calculations. The second cites the first for an alternative outer approximation and for calculations it says it re-proves. Each says its own proof path is complete. (f) The sharpness and holomorphic claims are stated for the same constant 2 as the polynomial claim, so any doubt about the polynomial bound carries over to them.
crouzeixs-conjecture.direction: proves the conjecture (constant 2 holds and is sharp); the first manuscript proves the polynomial case only
crouzeixs-conjecture.object: A sharpness witness, not a counterexample to the inequality: the 2×2 nilpotent matrix A = [[0,2],[0,0]] with f(z) = z (scalar, m = 1). Here ‖A‖ = 2, while the maximum of |z| over W(A) is 1, so no constant below 2 works. The matrix is explicit. Both manuscripts give it.

cartan-hadamard-conjecture.what_happened: Two manuscripts, both dated 23 September 2026. (1) 'Generalized Cartan-Hadamard isoperimetry and Euclidean equality rigidity' claims that for a complete simply connected smooth Riemannian n-manifold (n >= 2) with sectional curvature at most kappa <= 0, every measurable set E with finite volume and finite ambient perimeter P_g(E) satisfies P_g(E) >= I_{sqrt(-kappa)}(vol(E)), where I_b is the isoperimetric profile of the model space of curvature -b^2 (Theorem 1.1). At kappa = 0 this is P_g(E) >= n omega_n^(1/n) vol(E)^((n-1)/n), equivalently P^n >= n^n omega_n vol^(n-1). It also claims an equality classification at kappa = 0 (Theorem 1.2): for bounded E with 0 < vol(E) < infinity and P_g(E) < infinity, equality in the Euclidean bound holds if and only if E agrees up to null sets with an open region whose induced metric is that of a round Euclidean ball, and the ambient manifold outside that region need not be flat. (2) 'Sharp integral fillings in CAT(0) spaces' claims that every compactly supported integral n-cycle T (n >= 2) in a proper CAT(0) space bounds a compactly supported integral current S with M(S) <= c_n M(T)^((n+1)/n), where c_n = 1/((n+1) s_n^(1/n)) and s_n = area of the unit n-sphere, and that this coefficient is optimal (Theorem 1 of that paper). Its Cartan-Hadamard corollary says that for a Cartan-Hadamard manifold of dimension d >= 3 and a bounded smooth domain Omega, area(boundary of Omega) >= d omega_d^(1/d) vol(Omega)^((d-1)/d). The filling theorem is applied to the integration current of Omega, and top-dimensional constancy gives S = [[Omega]]. The text says the same inequality extends to relatively compact finite-perimeter sets with ambient perimeter, and it handles d = 2 separately by the classical disk inequality (Section 8).
cartan-hadamard-conjecture.delivers: Part (1) of the problem, the inequality for subsets of a Cartan-Hadamard manifold: manuscript 1 covers every measurable set of finite volume and finite ambient perimeter, with no boundedness, smoothness or connectedness assumption, in every dimension n >= 2. At kappa = 0 this is the Euclidean bound in the form the problem asks. Manuscript 2 covers bounded smooth domains and relatively compact finite-perimeter sets in every dimension d >= 2 (d >= 3 from the filling theorem, d = 2 from the classical disk inequality). Part (2), all dimensions: both manuscripts assert it. Part (3): both manuscripts assert the inequality holds, so the answer to the problem is 'yes'. Part (4), equality: manuscript 1 gives it for bounded sets of positive volume, with equality exactly for a Euclidean ball. Manuscript 2 says nothing about equality. Settlement: manuscript 1 says 'We resolve the generalized Cartan-Hadamard isoperimetric conjecture in every dimension'. Manuscript 2's abstract says 'we prove the Euclidean Cartan-Hadamard isoperimetric conjecture in dimensions at least three', and its body extends this to d = 2. Match to the list: the inequality is the kappa = 0 case of the claims, and the set class is wider than the bullet's smooth-domain reading, as the problem's own note on bounded finite-perimeter sets anticipates. Manuscript 1 also proves a kappa < 0 model comparison that the bullet does not ask for.
cartan-hadamard-conjecture.remains: If the claims hold, the inequality is covered in every dimension, and the equality case is covered for bounded sets of positive volume. Two gaps remain against problem_asks item (4). Neither manuscript classifies equality for unbounded sets of finite volume, since the rigidity theorem assumes boundedness. Manuscript 2 makes no equality claim at all. Nothing else in the problem is left open by these claims.

machine_checked.scope:
The formalization proves the sharp Euclidean filling inequality for every compactly supported integral $n$-cycle in a proper $\mathrm{CAT}(0)$ space, for $n\ge2$. It constructs a compactly supported integral filling whose mass is at most $C_n$ times the boundary mass to the power $(n+1)/n$, where $C_n$ is the Euclidean isoperimetric coefficient. Integer multiplicities and the ambient dimension are unrestricted.

A second statement proves that this coefficient is optimal by giving, in Euclidean space, a cycle for which every compactly supported integral filling has at least that mass. This yields the selected integral-current form of the Cartan–Hadamard isoperimetric conjecture.

cartan-hadamard-conjecture.doubts: Manuscript 2's abstract restricts the Cartan-Hadamard claim to dimensions at least three, but its introduction and Section 8 extend it to every d >= 2 by the classical disk inequality, so the abstract understates the body. Its extension of the domain corollary to finite-perimeter sets is said to follow 'verbatim' from the smooth case, with citations and no separate check. Its foundations theorem (Theorem 'current-background') is recorded from the literature, not proved. Manuscript 1's introduction summarises key steps (the completed square, 'balancing ... forces a first-order identity', the spherical-coordinate variations) in prose, and the full arguments are in the body. In its dimension-two equality argument (Section 8), the periodicity of a boundary component is justified in part by the remark that it 'can also be seen by continuing an oriented arclength chart', with no full proof. Manuscript 1's dimension-three comparison rests entirely on a 1992 citation, not on argument in the paper.; conditional on: Manuscript 1 relies on cited results for the n = 2 and n = 3 cases: the Weil-Bol disk inequality in the Chavel-Feldman form (n = 2) and Kleiner's Theorem 2 (n = 3, cited with page 38). It also uses Gueneysu-Pallara's strict smooth approximation, cited as 'Theorem 2.12 in the author preprint'. Its regularity steps use Ghomi-Spruck Lemma 7.2(i),(ii) for obstacle regularity, Antonelli-Pasqualetto-Pozzetta Corollary 1.6 for almost-minimizer regularity in the equality part, and Brezis-Lieb splitting, with the Aubin-Talenti constant. The hypersurface Sobolev inequality, the confined profile, the n >= 4 comparison, the cutoff passage to infinite volume and the equality rigidity are proved in the paper. Manuscript 2's domain corollary depends on its own integral filling theorem, which is proved by induction on the cycle dimension. That theorem's foundations are Ambrosio-Kirchheim, Wenger, Kirchheim and Sturm's CAT(0) variance inequality, which the text records as standard and cites. The integration-current representation of finite-perimeter sets is cited to Simon 2014, and the d = 2 case is cited to the classical disk inequality (Izmestiev 2014). Manuscript 2 does not depend on manuscript 1.
cartan-hadamard-conjecture.direction: proves the conjecture in all dimensions (kappa = 0 case); equality classified for bounded sets
cartan-hadamard-conjecture.object: No counterexample and no explicit object for the Cartan-Hadamard problem. Euclidean balls are the extremal sets; manuscript 2 (Section 8) checks that the boundary of a Euclidean ball B_R in R^(n+1) attains the filling coefficient. That concerns the filling constant in Euclidean space, not a construction on a Cartan-Hadamard manifold.

arnold-givental-conjecture.what_happened: Five manuscripts; none treats Lagrangian intersections. (a) 'A nondegenerate counterexample to the Morse-number Arnold bound': for a closed symplectic 4-manifold X with π₁(X) = A₅ᵏ (k large; X from Gompf's existence theorem), M = X×(S²)⁴ is a closed symplectic 12-manifold, not Kähler. It carries a smooth one-periodic Hamiltonian whose time-one map has χ(M)+128 fixed points, all nondegenerate, all with contractible orbits. The paper proves Morse(M) ≥ χ(M)+4d(π₁M) (Lemma morse-lower) and states that d(A₅ᵏ) is unbounded (Lemma group-gap), so Morse(M) − #Fix is unbounded over the family. (b) 'Three fixed points on the symplectic quadric threefold': a smooth Hamiltonian diffeomorphism φ of the quadric Q³ ⊂ CP⁴ with the restricted Fubini–Study form, with exactly three fixed points, at least one degenerate. φ = A∘B_ε, where A[z] = [z₀:−z₁:…:−z₄] is a Hamiltonian involution with fixed set S²×S², and B_ε is the time-ε flow of an A-invariant extension of an explicit function f(x,y) = e·x + (x−p)·y on that surface; then Fix(φ) = Crit(f). The paper shows Crit(Q³) = 4 and that the unit-inclusive rational cup-length is 4, so three fixed points violate both the critical-number bound and the cup-length bound. (c) 'Hamiltonian Fixed Points Below the Stable Morse Number in Dimension Twenty-Two': for each m ≥ 1, a simply connected closed Kähler M_m = X_m×Y of real dimension 22 (X_m a blow-up of CP⁹ along m disjoint copies of each of two centres; Y a blow-up of CP¹×CP¹ at four points), with stable Morse number 80+1968m and a Hamiltonian with 80+1952m nondegenerate fixed points, all with contractible orbits. (d) 'Hamiltonian Fixed Points Below the Stable Morse Number' (the companion manuscript, cited as OpenAI2026Stable in (e)): a simply connected closed Kähler M = X×Y of real dimension 1412, with SM(M) = 318968 and a Hamiltonian with 318952 nondegenerate contractible fixed points (deficit 16). (e) 'Sharpness of the Cyclic Integral Floer Bound Below the Stable Morse Number': a simply connected closed Kähler M of real dimension 3332 and minimal Chern number 1, with a Hamiltonian having 1,872,232 nondegenerate contractible fixed points, against SM(M) = 1,872,264; the count equals the cyclic integral expression β_cyc(M). For (c) to (e) the mechanism is a Hamiltonian involution id_X×g_Y with four fixed components, each ≅ X×CP¹; an invariant perturbation turns a Morse function on each component into exactly its critical points as nondegenerate fixed points, so #Fix = 4λ(X×CP¹). Each of these papers states and proves SM ≥ λ in its Morse section and uses Smale's theorem for attainment.
arnold-givental-conjecture.delivers: Refutes list item 1 (nondegenerate, Morse-number form) on specific manifolds: (a) the closed symplectic 12-manifolds X×(S²)⁴ with π₁ = A₅ᵏ for large k, where the deficit is unbounded; (c) to (e) the simply connected Kähler manifolds of real dimensions 22 (one for each m), 1412 and 3332. For (c) to (e) the fixed count lies below the stable Morse number, and since Morse ≥ SM always, #Fix < SM ≤ Morse as well, so they refute item 1 on these manifolds too. Refutes the degenerate forms, item 3 (contractible count against cuplength(M)+1) and the critical-number form, on one manifold, Q³: the total count is 3, while cuplength(M)+1 = 4 (the paper's unit-inclusive cup-length, equal to the list's convention). Since the count includes all fixed points, the contractible count is also at most 3. Because Q³'s map has a degenerate fixed point, this example does not bear on the nondegenerate items 1 or 2. Item 2 (homological form) is not contradicted: the 12-dim count χ(M)+128 exceeds the total Betti number χ(M) (homology torsion-free and in even degrees); the dimension-22 paper's Remark counts:field-bounds shows its total Betti numbers over characteristics 0, 2 and 3 all lie below its count; the 3332 count equals the integral cyclic bound. No counterexample to item 2 is claimed. Not settled: each claim is for specific manifolds. Statement match: the 12-dim introduction's Morse-number form (nondegenerate maps) matches item 1; the Q³ paper addresses the unrestricted critical-number and cup-length bounds, which cover all fixed points and are therefore stronger than item 3's contractible form.
arnold-givental-conjecture.remains: If the claims are correct: (i) items 4 to 6 (Lagrangian Arnold–Givental forms) are untouched; no manuscript treats Lagrangian intersections. (ii) Items 1 and 3 remain open for closed symplectic manifolds outside the constructed examples. The examples fall outside the positive case the papers cite (Dimitroglou Rizell–Golovko, where symplectic area and c₁ vanish on π₂): the 12-dim sphere factors have positive area, and the Kähler examples have c₁ = 1 on an exceptional sphere. Whether the bounds hold under that or other hypotheses is not addressed. (iii) Item 2 is not addressed as a general statement. (iv) For Q³ the paper asserts only that at least one of the three fixed points is degenerate; it does not say whether the other two are nondegenerate.

machine_checked.scope: The critical-number form of Arnold's fixed-point conjecture predicts at least as many fixed points as the minimum number of critical points of a smooth function. The formalized counterexample is a Hamiltonian diffeomorphism of the complex quadric threefold with exactly three fixed points, while every smooth function on that manifold has at least four critical points. At least one fixed point is degenerate. The separate nondegenerate Morse-number construction is not included.

arnold-givental-conjecture.doubts: (e): the equality #Fix = β_cyc(M) is proved, but the lower bound it is said to attain is only cited (Bai–Xu). (c) and (e) state the same classical Smale theorem with different dimension hypotheses (at least 9 in (c), at least 6 in (e)); (e) does not prove the handle step. (c): the simultaneous embedding of all centres in CP⁹ (Lemma geo:projection) is argued in one paragraph by secant and tangent measure-zero counts, with Hartshorne cited only for comparison. No hedge or sketched step is flagged by the authors in the 12-dim paper, the Q³ paper, or (d). The arithmetic of the counts in (c) to (e), recomputed from the stated torsion profiles, agrees with the stated totals.; conditional on: Kähler (c) to (e): Smale's classical theorem for attainment SM = λ (cited; (c) includes an appendix handle proof for dimension at least 9; (e) cites Smale 1963 and Cerf 1962 for dimension at least 6 and gives no handle proof). (e): the framing 'attains the cyclic integral Floer bound' rests on Bai–Xu's lower bound (cited, not proved), and on the identification of Bai–Xu's expression with β_cyc when the minimal Chern number is one, which the text asserts. (c) and (e) take their surface computations and mechanism from the companion (d), reproduced in part. 12-dim: Gompf's existence theorem for a symplectic X with π₁ = A₅ᵏ (Gompf 1992, Theorem 3.1). Q³: none beyond the in-text arguments; the Palais symmetric-criticality principle is cited, but the text verifies the needed case directly.
arnold-givental-conjecture.direction: disproves the nondegenerate Morse-number form on specific manifolds, and the degenerate critical-number and cup-length forms on Q³; consistent with the homological form; Lagrangian forms untouched
arnold-givental-conjecture.object: Q³: the Hamiltonian diffeomorphism φ = A∘B_ε. Its three fixed points are explicit, being the critical points of the explicit function f on S²×S²: q₀ = (p,−e), degenerate, with f = 0; and q_± = ((±√3/2, 0, −1/2), (1/2, 0, ∓√3/2)), with f = ±3√3/2. The A-invariant extension K of f (by averaging) and the small time ε are existence constructions and are not written out. 12-dim: H is built from a Morse function F on X×ℝ⁸ with χ(X)+8 critical points, equal to (|v|²−|u|²)/2 for r ≥ 3; X comes from Gompf's theorem and is not explicit. Kähler (c) to (e): the involution, the blow-up centres and the bielliptic surfaces S_p are explicit, but the Morse functions on the fixed components come from Smale's theorem and are existential, so the Hamiltonians are not written out.

regularity-of-solutions-of-vlasov-maxwel.what_happened: The manuscript 'Global classical solutions of the three-dimensional relativistic Vlasov–Maxwell system' (the only manuscript in this family) claims global existence and uniqueness of classical solutions of the one-species relativistic Vlasov–Maxwell system in three space and three momentum dimensions, for every smooth admissible datum (Theorem 1.1, thm:global). A datum is a nonnegative smooth particle density f0 with compact support, and fields E0, B0 with all spatial derivatives bounded and finite energy, satisfying the two Gauss constraints (div E0 = rho of f0, div B0 = 0). Nonzero total charge is allowed. For each finite T the solution has f smooth on [0,T] x R^3 x R^3, E and B smooth on [0,T] x R^3, f with compact phase-space support on [0,T], and the constraints hold for all time. The proof has two parts. (i) A signed momentum-increment estimate along characteristics (Proposition 1.1, eq. bootstrap): |V_X(t2) - V_X(t1)| <= M P sqrt(t2 - t1) + A (t2 - t1) S(w), with S(w) = P^2 log(2+P)/w, proved by a bootstrap and continuity argument (setup.tex, direction.tex, selection.tex, closure.tex). Since the resulting lower bounds on the time needed to double the maximal momentum have a divergent sum, finite-time growth of momentum is excluded. (ii) A local-theory and bounded-momentum continuation statement (Proposition 1.2, continuation.tex). The manuscript obtains it from the Glassey–Strauss criterion as quoted by Luk and Strain, after a finite-horizon modification of the initial fields: the Coulomb field is kept and a vacuum Maxwell solution vanishing on the particle region is subtracted.
regularity-of-solutions-of-vlasov-maxwel.delivers: Global existence, uniqueness and smoothness on each finite time interval for the relativistic one-species Vlasov–Maxwell system in three space dimensions, with no restriction on size, symmetry or total charge. The restrictions that come with it: (a) the initial particle density must be smooth and compactly supported, so noncompact particle data are not covered; (b) the fields must have all spatial derivatives bounded and finite energy (in L^2), so fields without finite energy are not covered; (c) uniqueness holds only in the class of classical solutions as the manuscript defines it (C^1 solutions with E, B continuous into L^2); (d) the bound on the momentum support is available on each finite interval only and may grow with that interval; (e) the equations are written in a normalization with the usual 4 pi absorbed into the fields and charge density. The manuscript says the result 'resolves the large-data global classical regularity problem for this model'. Its own statement of the problem is narrower than the list's wording: it concerns the one-species relativistic system, compactly supported initial particles and finite-energy fields, whereas the list's bullet names no species, no relativistic or classical variant, and no data class. The manuscript says nothing about the non-relativistic, multi-species or radiation-reaction variants.
regularity-of-solutions-of-vlasov-maxwel.remains: If the manuscript is correct, these parts of the problem are not addressed: (i) particle data that are not compactly supported (the introduction notes that Bigorgne and Wang treat noncompact particle data, but only under smallness, and Wang's 2026 result handles noncompact data only for cylindrically symmetric large data with H^s fields and a weighted density); (ii) field data outside finite energy, or fields whose derivatives are not all bounded; (iii) other variants of the system: multi-species, non-relativistic, other spatial dimensions, radiation reaction, and weaker solution classes; (iv) bounds that are uniform in time, since the manuscript proves momentum and regularity bounds only on each finite interval.

machine_checked.scope: The formalized result gives global existence and uniqueness for the three-dimensional one-species relativistic Vlasov–Maxwell system. The initial particle density is nonnegative, smooth, and compactly supported; the initial fields have bounded derivatives of all orders, finite energy, and satisfy both Gauss constraints. The solution is smooth on every finite time interval, has compact particle phase support there, and is unique among classical solutions. No smallness, symmetry, or neutrality assumption is imposed.

regularity-of-solutions-of-vlasov-maxwel.doubts: The argument is long, and the text itself abbreviates several steps. The small-sector sigma partition is 'omitted' (direct.tex near the small-sector definition; occupation.tex lines 90-93). The justification of differentiation at the cone tip rests on a short argument with the 'omitted potential and cutoff errors' and 'omitted kernel integrals' bounded in a few sentences (retarded.tex lines 268-278). A 'deficit exception' in the spatial-transition lemma is disposed of in one paragraph (selection.tex lines 387-393), and one case in direct.tex (around line 239) is 'omitted'. The key selection lemma (sel:exponents) is an exponent-bookkeeping argument with fixed decimal constants (epsilon = 10^-5, beta = 1.16) and thresholds, and the text presents it as exact without any computer check. The abstract's 'arbitrary smooth admissible initial data' is qualified by the definition of admissible data (compact particle support, finite-energy fields). The abstract's 'resolves the large-data global classical regularity problem for this model' is stronger than the list's wording. The text is an unsigned preprint attributed to 'OpenAI', and it does not say it has been reviewed.; conditional on: The theorem itself assumes nothing beyond the datum class. The proof relies on the Glassey–Strauss bounded-momentum continuation criterion in the form quoted by Luk and Strain (their Theorem 1.1 and Footnote 1, arXiv version). The manuscript applies this criterion to its modified data (continuation.tex, 'The bounded-momentum criterion') and does not prove it. The retarded-field and characteristic-change formulas are attributed to Glassey–Strauss, Luk–Strain, Pallard and Lazarovici; the text says it derives them again in its own normalization. As far as the text shows, it depends on no other OpenAI manuscript for any step; its citation of Wang's 2026 papers is for comparison.

navier-stokes-existence-and-smoothness.what_happened: Nine manuscripts in the family each take the 3D incompressible Navier-Stokes equations with zero initial velocity and a prescribed smooth external force f built by an effective algorithm from a Turing machine M and input w. Each shows that a fixed particle (or, in one case, a fixed velocity test) detects whether M halts, and each gives a unique classical solution in a stated class, which is smooth and global. Per manuscript: (1) Finite Instructions and Solenoidal Shear Flows: unit flat torus T^3, force divergence-free and mean-zero, periodic only after a one-unit loading interval; particle (1/8,3/8,1/2) enters {1/2<x<1} iff M halts; derivatives globally bounded, kinetic energy bounded. (2) A Fixed Particle Test for Computation in a Forced Viscous Flow: unit torus, mean-zero force (a divergence-free variant with the same velocity is also given); particle (1/8,3/8,0) enters {1/2<x<1} iff M halts; force and velocity derivatives bounded and in L^2 in time in sup norm. (3) Universal Computation with Eventually Stationary Navier-Stokes Forcing: unit torus, mean-zero force, time-independent for t>=1 via a ramp from rest; particle (1/4,1/4,0) enters {1/32<Y<1/8} iff M halts. Also a periodic-from-time-zero corollary, and a slow-clock variant with force and velocity derivatives O((1+t)^{-1-h}). (4) Geometric Programs for Solenoidal Forcing: unit torus, divergence-free mean-zero force periodic from time zero; particle (1/4,1/2,1/4) enters {1/2<x_1<7/8} iff M halts. Separately, a general sheet theorem realizes diagonal maps on T_10^3 with no halting event. (5) Prefix Instructions and Incompressible Flows: unit torus, mean-zero force (divergence not asserted zero), period one after t>=1 following a loader; particle (1/8,1/4,1/4) enters {1/2<x_1<1} iff M halts; alternative realizations use boxes, normal compensation, invariant planes. (6) Computation under Rapidly Vanishing Navier-Stokes Forcing: three memory constructions. Addressed: force on R^3 supported in a fixed compact box, all derivatives decaying faster than any power of (1+t); origin particle enters {X_1<-1} iff M halts. Alternating: fixed compact spatial support, same decay with (1+t+|X|); particle (-1,0,0) reaches {X_1>0} iff M halts. Lattice: unit torus, mean-zero force, derivatives decaying faster than any power; particle (1/4,1/2,1/2) enters {1/2<x_1<1 mod 1} iff M halts; a solenoidal variant has the same velocity. (7) Velocity-Field Detection of Computation in Forced Navier-Stokes Flows: no particle. On the unit torus, the event is that u_3 exceeds 1/2 somewhere on {1/32<y<1/8} at some time; the force is supported in K x T with K compact in (0,1)^2 and its derivatives are bounded only on finite time intervals. On R^2 x T, the event is that the integral of u_3 over {X_2>0} x T exceeds 1/2 at some time; the force has globally bounded mixed derivatives and compact horizontal support on each finite interval. (8) Scalar Potentials and Slow Clocks for Forced Fluid Computation: R^3 force with one compact spatial support for all time and derivatives O((1+t)^{-1-j}); origin particle enters {x_1<-1} iff M halts. Torus variant: particle (1/4,1/2,1/2) enters {1/2<x_1<1} with the same decay. Expanded-plane variant: observation u_3>1/2 on a fixed set, via the velocity-field theorem of entry (7). (9) Incompressible Box Transport and Finite Computation (October 6 version): a balanced three-stack recorder gives an R^3 force with one compact spatial support, bounded mixed derivatives, one-periodic after a one-unit loading interval, affine in viscosity (f = f_0 + nu f_1, with one velocity U); particle (4,0,0) enters (-1,2)^3 iff M halts. Further variants: torus charts, periodicity from time zero, bounded or slab observers, and slow clocks giving L^2-in-time forces.
navier-stokes-existence-and-smoothness.revisions: 1 earlier edition(s) kept in the repository: Incompressible-Box-Transport-and-Finite-Computation-September-27-2026
navier-stokes-existence-and-smoothness.delivers: Nothing toward the Clay problem. The common result is a computability statement about forced flows: for a prescribed force, the zero-data equation has a unique smooth global solution in a stated class, and a particle event is equivalent to halting. Against the four alternatives: (A) and (B) ask about zero forcing and smooth data for all data on R^3 and T^3; every force in the family is nonzero and is defined as the residual of a chosen velocity, so none addresses zero-force global existence. (C) and (D) ask whether smooth data with smooth finite-energy forcing can lead to finite-time breakdown; no manuscript proves or constructs a singularity, and each asserts global smooth solutions for its own forces. The manuscripts disclaim regularity for arbitrary data: Finite Instructions says its existence result concerns 'this constructed family of forces, not regularity for arbitrary Navier-Stokes data', and Scalar Potentials says it makes 'no assertion about arbitrary-data regularity'. The matching pass's description ('a computability result about the equations though not a regularity or blow-up result') is accurate. The family does not claim to settle the problem, so no statement-match check arises.
navier-stokes-existence-and-smoothness.remains: All four alternatives remain open. The family says nothing about: whether smooth global solutions exist for all smooth finite-energy data with zero force on R^3 or T^3 (A, B); or whether some smooth data and smooth finite-energy forcing produce finite-time breakdown on R^3 or T^3 (C, D).

machine_checked.scope:
The formalization realizes finite families of prescribed positive diagonal maps on coding sheets by smooth incompressible flows on a flat three-torus. At every positive computable viscosity, it supplies a solution starting from rest with zero pressure and a force that is divergence free, has spatial mean zero, and is one-periodic from time zero. Each map acts on every point of its source sheet, and the construction provides effective bounds for all mixed derivatives.

This selected statement covers the sheet programs. The paper's fixed-particle halting detector and its reciprocal maps on solid boxes are outside its scope.

The formalization proves that a fluid particle can detect arbitrary finite-machine halting using alternating-coordinate memory in smooth incompressible Navier–Stokes flows whose velocity and force decay faster than every inverse power of time, including every mixed derivative. For each fixed positive computable viscosity, the construction starts from rest and provides effective forces, unique material trajectories, and an exact equivalence between entering a fixed open detector and halting.

The velocity and force share one compact support for every machine and input. The solution-uniqueness assertion uses the stated energy comparison class.

The formalization constructs smooth forced three-dimensional Navier–Stokes flows from rest whose velocity fields detect whether a prescribed machine halts, at any positive computable viscosity. On the unit flat torus, halting is equivalent to the vertical velocity exceeding $1/2$ somewhere in a fixed observation strip. On $\mathbb R^2\times\mathbb T$, it is equivalent to the integral of the nonnegative vertical velocity over the observation half-plane times the circle exceeding $1/2$.

The torus force is confined to a fixed horizontal region. The cylindrical force has globally bounded mixed derivatives and compact horizontal support on every finite time interval. Both constructions have effective descriptions and uniqueness within their respective smooth solution-comparison classes.

The formalization realizes finitely many positive diagonal affine maps of determinant one between rational solid boxes by a smooth compactly supported divergence-free flow. Source boxes are pairwise disjoint and target boxes are pairwise disjoint, while overlap between the two families is allowed. Each map holds on a neighborhood of the entire source box, and the velocity is supported in the middle half of the time interval.

It also encodes every finite machine and input in a smooth, compactly supported incompressible Navier–Stokes flow on $\mathbb R^3$ starting from rest: the particle initially at $(4,0,0)$ enters the fixed open box $(-1,2)^3$ exactly when the machine halts. One velocity works for every viscosity $\nu>0$, with zero pressure and force $f_0+\nu f_1$. Velocity and force have bounded mixed derivatives and are one-periodic after time one; the repeated velocity depends only on the machine. The force is computable for computable $\nu$. Velocity is unique among smooth zero-data solutions with $u\in C_tH_x^2\cap C_t^1L_x^2$, bounded $u$ and $\nabla u$ on finite time intervals, and pressure modulo a function of time in $C_tH_x^1$.

navier-stokes-existence-and-smoothness.doubts: Points from the text: (1) Finite Instructions does not quantify the radius of the positive neighborhood in its period-map statement, and it does not assert periodicity from time zero. (2) Velocity-Field Detection: torus derivative bounds may grow with the time interval, and its thresholds rest on heat-kernel constants of 10^9 or 10^8 and a total horizontal mass below 10^-11, proved in a lemma I did not read. (3) Universal Computation with Eventually Stationary: the autonomous clock argument asserts that each planar segment stays in the corridor J* where the spatial clock equals one. That assertion comes from the processor theorem, which I did not read. (4) Scalar Potentials: its stationary expanded-plane choice has nonzero mean force during startup, and its u_3 corollary asserts no large-time amplitude bound. (5) Rapidly Vanishing: observation is exact with no uniform margin; in the addressed construction the nonhalting first coordinate sits exactly on the boundary of the open detector, and the paper disclaims finite-precision robustness. (6) Geometric Programs' general sheet theorem is stated on T_10^3, not the unit torus.; conditional on: No unproven hypothesis bears on the Clay alternatives. Internal dependencies: the torus and R^2 x T velocity-field theorems of Velocity-Field Detection use the planar processor of Universal Computation with Eventually Stationary (its Theorem 4.1 and Lemma 3.1) and the uniqueness and projection lemmas of A Fixed Particle Test (Lemmas 3 and 1, cited as entry2026 and CompanionA). Scalar Potentials' expanded-plane corollary imports Velocity-Field Detection's Theorem 3.1. Box Transport's input-offset corollary imports Universal Computation with Eventually Stationary's planar processor and spatial clock. Rapidly Vanishing's realization, uniqueness and projection lemmas are cited from A Fixed Particle Test (Lemmas 3 and 1).
navier-stokes-existence-and-smoothness.direction: none toward the problem; constructs globally smooth forced solutions whose particle paths encode halting (no regularity or blow-up result)
navier-stokes-existence-and-smoothness.object: No counterexample or blow-up object. Each construction effectively builds an explicit smooth global solution (U, p) for its own forcing from (M, w). These are algorithmic constructions, not closed-form objects, and none is a counterexample to any Clay alternative.
