origin.family_title: Universal computation in forced Navier–Stokes flows

rejected.because: The family proves that rational numbers obtained by pairing specialized Hodge classes with divisor products agree across ℓ-adic and crystalline realizations, and that those classes are algebraic over F̄ₚ. It neither states nor proves any of the four standard conjectures: algebraicity of the Lefschetz inverse, algebraicity of the Künneth projectors, equality of numerical and homological equivalence, or the sign in the Hodge standard conjecture. Its only Lefschetz input, that hard Lefschetz and its inverse restrict to divisor-generated subspaces, is cited from Milne (1999) as a known result.

None of the three manuscripts says anything about ζ(1/2+it) as t → ∞. The zero-free half-planes (Re s > 7/8 in 'The Quasi-Riemann Hypothesis: A Zero-Free Half-Plane Re s>7/8'; Re s > 11/12 in 'The Quasi-Riemann Hypothesis') lie strictly to the right of the critical line and give no growth bound there. The only growth estimate on the critical line in the family is a crude Hecke strip bound, |L(σ+it,ψ)| ≪ Q^(3/5)(3+|t|)^2 for −1/10 ≤ σ ≤ 11/10 (Sept 30, Lemma 'Hecke strip growth'), used as an internal technical input; its t^2 exponent is far from the o(t^ε) claim.

Carmichael's question asks whether some value n has exactly one preimage under φ, which is a lower-end multiplicity question. The family proves only the upper-end statement that infinitely many n have more than n^(1-ε) preimages (Erdős's largest-fiber conjecture, Theorem 1 of 'Weighted dilation graphs, smooth shifted primes and totient fibers'). A large fiber at some n says nothing about whether any fiber has size one. None of the three manuscripts mentions Carmichael's totient conjecture, singleton fibers, or minimum fiber size; the matching pass's link through 'multiplicities of Euler's totient values' is a shared topic, not a shared question.

The manuscript proves that the primes cannot differ by finitely many elements from a sumset A+B with |A|, |B| at least 2 (Ostmann's inverse Goldbach conjecture). It never studies P+P or asks which even numbers are sums of two primes, and the binary Goldbach conjecture does not appear in the text. The only link is the name 'inverse Goldbach problem', which the introduction gives to Ostmann's question.

The manuscript proves that the primes cannot differ by finitely many elements from a sumset A+B with |A|, |B| at least 2 (Ostmann's inverse Goldbach conjecture). It never studies P+P or asks which even numbers are sums of two primes, and the binary Goldbach conjecture does not appear in the text. The only link is the name 'inverse Goldbach problem', which the introduction gives to Ostmann's question.

The three manuscripts prove equidistribution of torus packets and use measure classification only as a cited black box: Einsiedler–Katok–Lindenstrauss (2006, Theorem 1.3, and Corollary 1.4 for prime degree) makes positive-entropy ergodic components of the full diagonal group on SLₙ(ℝ)/SLₙ(ℤ) homogeneous. None of the manuscripts states or proves a classification theorem of its own, so none bears on whether every ergodic higher-rank diagonal-invariant measure on a homogeneous space is algebraic without an entropy hypothesis.

The manuscripts concern only π: they prove its irrationality exponent is 2 and derive the Flint–Hills convergence from that. None of the fourteen numbers asked about (γ, π+e, π−e, πe, π/e, π^e, π^√2, π^π, e^(π²), ln π, 2^e, e^e, Catalan's constant, Khinchin's constant) is π or is treated, and the irrationality measure of π is not one of the requested measures; the matching pass's link runs only through π.

The margulis-conjecture entry asks for classification of ergodic A-invariant probability measures for higher-rank diagonalizable actions on homogeneous spaces G/Γ, with the conclusion that each such measure is algebraic. Both manuscripts concern a different conjecture that carries Margulis's name: the Margulis–Platonov conjecture, which says that noncentral abstract normal subgroups of G(k) are pullbacks of open normal subgroups of the finite product of anisotropic local groups. Neither manuscript mentions ergodic theory, invariant measures on G/Γ, Cartan or diagonal actions, or the Furstenberg, Katok–Spatzier, Einsiedler–Katok–Lindenstrauss or Einsiedler conjectures; a keyword search of both build folders found only arithmetic uses of 'homogeneous space' (torsors and the Hasse principle). The only probability-measure material is an auxiliary translation-invariant law on finite colourings of unitary elements, built to prove the normal-subgroup result, not a classification of A-invariant measures. The matching pass's 'other' flag was right: this family is the Margulis–Platonov normal subgroup conjecture, not the measure-classification conjecture.

The family proves asymptotic densities for k-power-free values (k = d-2, so squarefree for quartics) of irreducible integer polynomials at positive integers, a sieve-type count that never asserts any value f(n) is prime and cannot yield prime values, since primes have density zero among the integers and the manuscript contains no prime-value claim.

The family's only manuscript, 'The Weak Inhomogeneous Duffin–Schaeffer Conjecture', proves that for one fixed real shift γ and a weight ψ, almost every real x satisfies ‖qx−γ‖ < ψ(q) for infinitely many q whenever Σ φ(q)ψ(q)/q diverges. It is a one-variable, inhomogeneous, weighted statement about a single real number. It says nothing about a pair of reals α, β, about the product n‖nα‖‖nβ‖, or about its liminf being 0. The word 'Littlewood' appears in the text only in the bibliography title of Chow–Technau (references/main.bib), which is cited for the weak conjecture, not for Littlewood.

The family's one manuscript, 'An asymptotic formula for the number of totients', counts distinct totient values V(x) and proves V(x) ~ (x/log x)·G_m·A(1;θ) and V(cx)/V(x) → c. It never asserts that some value has exactly one preimage under φ, nor that every value has at least two. Its nearest fibre statements do not decide the question: (i) the introduction cites OpenAITotientFibers2026, Theorem 1.1, for infinitely many v with more than v^(1-ε) preimages, describing it as concerning large individual fibres and as not an input to the proof; (ii) companion.tex's Ford inverse-fibre propagation lemma takes a given totient d with its full inverse fibre and shows that many v = dφ(b) inherit a fibre of the same size, which presupposes d and says nothing about whether a singleton fibre exists; (iii) the 'exactly one' in collisions.tex concerns tuples in the prefix map, not preimages of values under φ.

The manuscript bounds the minimum number of distinct unit fractions summing to a/b, for any 1 <= a < b, by O(log log b) with unrestricted denominators; it never treats the case 4/n with exactly three terms and does not mention the Erdos-Straus conjecture, so it gives no information on whether 4/n is a sum of three unit fractions.

The manuscript's greedy step (Lemma lem:greedy in elementary.tex) is the ordinary greedy algorithm applied to arbitrary rationals, and nothing in the family restricts to odd denominators or studies whether an odd-denominator greedy procedure terminates, so it does not bear on that question.

The one manuscript, 'Positive lower density of large prime gaps', proves that for each fixed C > 0 a positive proportion of indices n up to N have p_{n+1} - p_n > C log p_n. The gaps it counts grow without bound with p, so beyond some point they can never equal a fixed even n. The result therefore says nothing about whether any fixed even n occurs as a prime gap infinitely often, which is what Polignac's conjecture asks.

The family proves Uchida's conjecture: a continuous open homomorphism between absolute Galois groups of solvably closed Galois extensions of number fields is induced by a unique equivariant field embedding. That concerns Galois groups of number fields, not the fundamental groups of complete smooth curves over finitely generated fields, not splittings of the map from such a fundamental group to G_k, and not k-rational points on curves. A search of the remaining sections and the references finds no mention of curves, sections, splittings, Grothendieck, or fundamental groups of curves; the word 'splitting' occurs only in Kummer and exact-sequence contexts. The shared anabelian background is thematic and does not make the family bear on the section conjecture.

Neither manuscript treats the canonical bundle of a klt projective variety. The SYZ manuscript (The-Strong-Hyperkahler-SYZ-Conjecture-September-23-2026) proves that a nonzero nef isotropic line bundle on a compact IHS Kähler manifold is semiample; on such manifolds Kₓ is trivial and c₁(L) ≠ 0 excludes it, so the abundance hypothesis is never instanced. The projective-space manuscript (Projective-Space-Bases-of-Lagrangian-Fibrations-September-23-2026) proves the base of a projective Lagrangian fibration is ℙⁿ, uses -K_B ample only as background, and claims nothing about nef canonical bundles or semiampleness of K. The matching pass's 'abundance-type' label reflects only the shared pattern 'nef implies semiample'; the SYZ bibliography entry titled 'The abundance and SYZ conjectures in families of hyperkähler manifolds' is a citation of a different result, not a claim here.

The manuscript proves only the generalized Mukai bound ρ(ι−1) ≤ n and its equality case (ρ(ι−1) = n iff X ≅ (P^{ι−1})^ρ); it does not treat any of Hartshorne's candidate conjectures A–G (subvarieties of P^n and their complete intersection property, rank-2 bundles, the ample-tangent-bundle conjecture, local algebra, or curves in P^3), and its nearest contact, the ρ = 1 equality case recovering P^n from pseudoindex n+1, rests on a different hypothesis from ample tangent bundle and is not presented as extending Mori's theorem, which the text never cites.

The manuscript proves that a holomorphic one-parameter family of isolated surface singularities in C^3 with constant Milnor number is topologically right-trivial, which is the direction from constant Milnor number to topology; the Zariski conjecture asks whether topological equisingularity forces equal multiplicity, and the manuscript neither assumes topological equisingularity nor states or proves any multiplicity conclusion, with multiplicity entering only as a cited input (Fernández de Bobadilla–Pełka: constant Milnor number gives constant multiplicity) that already covers the μ-constant families it studies and so adds nothing to the Zariski question.

All seven manuscripts concern the anticanonical side: nonvanishing of H^0(X,-mK_X) (or of a positive multiple of -(K_W+D)) under semipositivity or nefness of -K_X; none proves that a nef K_X on a klt variety is semiample. The only semiampleness step touching a nef adjoint is in Integrable-metrics-and-effectivity-with-controlled-boundary (fano-auxiliary, the model theorem), where a klt pair with big boundary and nef K+Delta is made semiample by citing BCHM Corollary 3.9.2 as an input to a Fano-type model construction; that is a cited known result, not a claim about abundance.

The only sphere result in the family is the 'Spherical logarithmic energy' corollary of 'Triangular minimality for planar Coulomb renormalized energy', which concerns the logarithmic interaction −Σ log‖yᵢ−yⱼ‖ on the unit sphere S² and gives only the asymptotic linear term of the minimal value as n→∞ (settling the d=2 case of the Brauchart–Hardin–Saff conjecture). It does not treat the 1/r Coulomb interaction that the Thomson problem asks about, and it identifies neither the minimizing configuration nor the minimal energy for any particular n.

The family's packing result, 'A sharp Fourier certificate for planar circle packing', concerns only dimension 2, which the list excludes as already solved; the other three manuscripts are also planar (universal optimality of the triangular lattice in R²), so none determines the densest packing in any dimension other than 1, 2, 3, 8 and 24 or its high-dimensional asymptotics.

The manuscript 'A cubic lower bound for border determinantal complexity of the permanent' proves that the border determinantal complexity of the m×m complex permanent is at least c·m³ for m ≥ 1408 (c = 1/(5529600e)), and the same cubic bound for exact determinantal complexity and for vertex and edge counts of affine-linear algebraic branching programs. Everything is in the algebraic model over ℂ with affine-linear determinant representations. The text never mentions Turing machines, polynomial-time decision procedures, certificates, or the classes P and NP. Its only link to the problem is Valiant's algebraic framework (VP versus VNP), where a superpolynomial determinantal complexity of the permanent would separate the algebraic classes. A polynomial bound does not do that, and the manuscript itself says that whether the permanent has superpolynomial determinantal or border determinantal complexity 'remains open'.

The one manuscript, 'Beyond the Square-Root Exponent for Depth-Three Boolean Circuits', proves that a single language decidable in deterministic polynomial time has n-bit membership functions needing more than 2^(A√n) gates in depth-three OR–AND–OR circuits for every A > 0, at all sufficiently large n. This is circuit-complexity progress of the kind sometimes cited in the P versus NP programme, but it separates no complexity classes: the language lies in P, and the text never mentions NP or any problem in NP, so it does not decide or bear on whether P = NP.

Both manuscripts concern the Goemans–Linial SDP and uniform sparsest cut on complete graphs with arbitrary nonnegative capacities, with the gap witnessed by a general negative-type semimetric on a finite vertex set, not by the shortest-path metric of a graph; they neither treat graphs from any proper minor-closed family nor bound the ℓ1 distortion of such metrics, so they say nothing about whether that distortion is bounded.

The family is a deterministic factorization algorithm over F_p and says nothing about which integers are primitive roots modulo which primes. Its only contact with primitive roots is that its auxiliary-prime step cites Theorem 1.2 of the companion paper for a zero-free strip of Hecke L-functions; the generators it builds (of the 2-primary subgroup of F_p^* and of q-primary subgroups of K_q^*) are not statements about orders of integers modulo primes.

The family makes no claim about the set of primes p for which a given integer a is a primitive root, so nothing in it addresses whether that set is infinite for any a. Its only link is the citation of the companion's Theorem 1.2, a zero-free statement for Hecke L-functions that it uses to find auxiliary primes ℓ ≡ 1 mod 12q with p not a q-th power modulo ℓ, not primitive roots of any a.

The list bullet asks for the possible configurations of the connected components of M-curves, i.e. the first part of Hilbert's sixteenth problem for nonsingular real plane curves of maximal component count, with realisation and exclusion for every degree n. Both manuscripts concern only the second part, limit cycles of planar polynomial vector fields. 'Uniform bounds for planar polynomial limit cycles' proves that a degree-dependent bound B(d) on limit cycles exists, and 'Two limit cycles for quintic Lienard systems' shows that one Lienard family has at most two cycles, with the bound attained. Neither mentions real algebraic curves, M-curves, ovals or nests, or the arrangement of their components. The word 'components' in the uniform-bounds text refers to fibres of an analytic map in the proof, and 'ovals' appears only in a cited result on Hamiltonian ovals and limit cycles. The family's bearing is on the separate second-part question (a finite bound H(n) on limit cycles), which the problem_asks says is recorded as a different question, not on this bullet.

The family concerns translational tiles of Z^3 and R^3 and the periodic tiling conjecture in dimension three. It constructs no two-dimensional prototile and says nothing about aperiodic-only tilings of the plane. Its only planar content is cited positive results: every finite tile of Z^2 admits a periodic tiling (Bhattacharya), and Greenfeld and Tao's structure theorem for tilings of Z^2 by one finite tile. The manuscript does not address whether any statement of the Einstein problem holds in R^2.

The family never mentions spectral sets, spectrality, or Fuglede's conjecture. Its subject is the periodic tiling conjecture for translational tiles of Z^3 and R^3. Tiling by translation is the only shared notion, and the manuscript does not connect it to spectrality of nonconvex sets in R or R^2. Its planar material is cited positive results on tilings of Z^2 and of rational polygonal sets, not spectral results.

The list manuscript (A linear list-coloring bound in terms of the Hadwiger number) bounds the list chromatic number of vertices by a multiple of the Hadwiger number, and none of the three manuscripts mentions edge colourings, the chromatic index, the list chromatic index of edges, or line graphs (checked by search), so nothing in the family bears on whether ch'(G) = chi'(G) for edges.

The problem asks for the exact values of W(r,k) (and the off-diagonal numbers w(r; k_1,...,k_r)) across all r and k. The family's manuscript, Quantitative Superexponential Bounds for van der Waerden Numbers, proves only growth bounds: W_r(k) > k^(ck*floor(log_2 r)) for k at least an absolute K_0 and all r >= 2 (c = 10^-5), and W_r(k) > exp((log r)^2/(64 log 2)) for r >= 256 and k >= 3. It also gives a recursive finite upper bound. None of these fixes a value of any nontrivial W(r,k), and the only exact values it states (W_1(k) = k, W_r(1) = 1, W_r(2) = r+1) are the trivial cases the problem does not ask for; the manuscript does not treat off-diagonal numbers.

The manuscripts concern crossing numbers of complete bipartite graphs drawn in the plane, not the extremal function z(m,n;s,t). Neither states, bounds or uses the maximum number of edges in a bipartite graph with no Kₛ,ₜ, and neither gives any asymptotic for z(n,n;s,t). The shared name belongs to Zarankiewicz's crossing-number conjecture, a different problem, as the matching pass itself noted. The dimension-counting lemmas in the bipartite manuscript do not concern forbidden subgraphs.

The manuscripts determine cr(Kₙ) = Z(n) for complete graphs and cr(Kₘ,ₙ) for complete bipartite graphs, and they claim nothing about cr(G) for any other graph G. Albertson's conjecture is the inequality cr(G) ≥ cr(Kχ(G)) over all finite graphs. The only instances the family covers are G = Kᵣ, where the inequality is an equality, so the family does not bear on the inequality. The matching pass's link runs through the value cr(Kᵣ) on the right-hand side, which the problem does not ask for. The complete-graph manuscript states its cycle-pairing lemma for every finite simple graph, but uses it only to bound crossings of complete graphs.

The manuscript 'The higher-dimensional Erdős distinct-distances conjecture' (Sept 23 2026) proves only that every finite set of n ≥ 2 distinct points in R^d (d ≥ 3) has at least c_d n^(2/d) distinct distances, a cardinality bound on the distance set of a finite set. Falconer's question concerns the Lebesgue measure of the distance set of an infinite set of Hausdorff dimension above d/2, and nothing in the paper passes from the finite-set count to that measure; a search of all its TeX sources finds no mention of Falconer, Hausdorff dimension, Lebesgue measure of a distance set, or infinite sets, so any link between the two problems is only the heuristic analogy the matching pass noted.

Neither manuscript in this family mentions Falconer's conjecture, Hausdorff dimension, or distance sets of positive Lebesgue measure: 'The weak pinned planar distance theorem' bounds pinned distinct distances in finite planar point sets, and 'A power saving for planar unit distances' bounds unit-distance pairs. The matching pass's link is an analogy that neither manuscript proves or uses.

The sole manuscript, 'Combinatorial invariance of Kazhdan--Lusztig polynomials', proves only that the equal-parameter P_{u,b}(q) is determined by the abstract Bruhat interval poset; it makes no statement about the values P_{y,w}(1), about representations (Verma modules, category O, characters or multiplicities), or about the positivity of KL coefficients, and its only link to the problem is that it concerns the same polynomials, which the matching pass itself called a separate conjecture.

The manuscript classifies finite Euclidean Ramsey configurations in arbitrary high dimension D, with D chosen after the number of colours, and never treats the plane, the chromatic number of ℝ², or the colour count of unit-distance graphs; its Ramsey statement for the two-point set would only say that χ(ℝ^D) exceeds any fixed r for some large D, which it does not state and which is not the planar question of whether χ(ℝ²) is 5, 6 or 7.

The manuscript proves only that a real circulant Hadamard matrix has order 1 or 4, so it is a non-existence result restricted to circulant matrices. It constructs no Hadamard matrix of any order and gives no obstruction to non-circulant ones, so it neither proves nor disproves existence of a Hadamard matrix of any order 4k with k > 1.

The family proves Lech's inequality e(R) ≤ e(S) for flat local maps of Noetherian local rings. Along the way it proves a Dutta-multiplicity bound for short complexes over complete local domains of characteristic p (the domain case of Iyengar–Ma–Walker Conjecture 8.1), which is not among the named items. None of the fourteen named items is proved, stated or addressed: no zero-divisor, Bass, intersection, new or improved new intersection statement; no direct-summand, strong direct-summand, canonical-element, big Cohen–Macaulay, weakly functorial big Cohen–Macaulay, or Tor-vanishing statement; no Serre multiplicity vanishing or positivity (the only 'Serre' in the text is 'Serre subcategory'); and no small Cohen–Macaulay module result. Its nearest contact is a background citation to a companion OpenAI preprint, 'A Complete Local Domain without a Small Cohen–Macaulay Module' (cited as SmallCM, Theorem 1.1). This manuscript describes that result as a complete normal 3-dimensional C-domain with no nonzero finitely generated maximal Cohen–Macaulay module, though the cited title names small CM modules; the family claims nothing about small CM modules itself.

The manuscript never mentions the monomial conjecture or powers of parameter ideals. Its result refutes the existence of a finitely generated maximal Cohen–Macaulay module over one ring, but such a module is only a sufficient route to the monomial conjecture, so its failure does not decide the conjecture. The manuscript cites big Cohen–Macaulay algebra existence for Noetherian local rings as known, and makes no claim about the monomial conjecture for R.

The only manuscript, 'A Torsion-Free Group Algebra with Zero Divisors', constructs a finitely presented torsion-free group G with nonzero zero divisors in F₂[G], disproving Kaplansky's zero-divisor conjecture. It says nothing about surjunctivity, cellular automata, injective G-equivariant self-maps of full shifts, or Gottschalk's formulation; a text search of the paper and all of its \input sections finds no such term. Group algebras and torsion-freeness are shared vocabulary, but the claim does not bear on whether every group is surjunctive.

The frozen problem asks about the homological conjectures of commutative algebra (problem_asks items 1–14, such as the intersection theorems, Serre's multiplicity conjecture and the direct summand conjecture), but the manuscript works only with finite-dimensional complex, non-commutative algebras and proves only that the little finitistic-dimension conjecture fails for one of them; it does not touch items 1–14, and it does not discuss the Nakayama, Tachikawa or Auslander–Reiten conjectures that problem_asks flags as possibly in scope.

The bullet's list is the commutative-ring conjectures (zero divisor theorem, Bass's question, intersection and new intersection theorems, direct summand, canonical element, balanced big Cohen–Macaulay modules, Serre's multiplicity conjectures, small Cohen–Macaulay modules, and related). Both manuscripts, 'An explicit counterexample to the Auslander-Reiten conjecture' and 'A counterexample to Tachikawa's second conjecture', work with finite-dimensional, noncommutative algebras over the characteristic-two field F₂(q,H₁,H₂) in the Artin-algebra setting. The Auslander-Reiten manuscript says of its construction that 'the commutative restriction is not resolved by either construction', and none of the listed commutative problems is addressed. The Artin-algebra forms of the Auslander-Reiten, Tachikawa and Nakayama conjectures are a different target, not this commutative bullet.

Neither manuscript mentions Fröberg's conjecture or generic forms: both prove Hilbert-function comparisons (the Betti paper also graded Betti numbers) for quotients by arbitrary homogeneous ideals containing a regular sequence, which is the Eisenbud–Green–Harris and lex-plus-powers setting; for k > n forms the only bound they yield is the complete-intersection Hilbert function of the first n of them, which does not determine the Fröberg series for generic forms, and the k = n case is just the Hilbert series of a regular sequence, which they use as a standard input.

The family is a single preprint, 'A Counterexample to Kurosh's Division-Ring Problem', which constructs a countable characteristic-zero division ring that is algebraic over its center, generated by two elements over it, and infinite-dimensional over it. Its subject is local finiteness of algebraic division rings (Kurosh's problem), not nil one-sided or two-sided ideals of arbitrary rings as in the Köthe conjecture. A text search of the build/ sources finds no mention of Köthe or of one-sided or two-sided nil ideals; the only nil-related remark (introduction, Golod's nil algebras) concerns non-division algebras and is set aside as not answering the division-ring question. Division rings have no nonzero nilpotent elements, so the Köthe implication holds trivially for them and the construction says nothing about the general ring-theoretic statement.

The manuscript proves only the numerical blockwise Alperin weight count l(B) = |Wₚ(B)|, which compares simple modules of a block with weights, and never mentions Dade's conjecture or its counts of ordinary characters of blocks of G against blocks of local subgroups; the problem's own wording treats the Alperin weight conjecture as a neighbour, not part of Dade's conjecture.

The manuscript never mentions McKay's conjecture, and its only local-global count against a Sylow normalizer is the inequality |IBrₚ(G)| ≥ |IBrₚ(N_G(P))| for irreducible Brauer characters, which counts simple modules rather than the p′-degree complex characters McKay equates and is not an equality, so it does not bear on McKay's statement.

Both manuscripts prove Donovan's finiteness: for a bound on defect-group order, blocks of finite groups fall into finitely many Morita equivalence classes, over an algebraically closed field of characteristic p ("Donovan's Conjecture over Algebraically Closed Fields") and over W(F̄ₚ) and fixed complete DVRs ("Integral Donovan Finiteness over Witt Vectors"). Neither states or proves a counting identity between the irreducible characters of blocks of G and those of blocks of local subgroups, and neither mentions Dade's conjecture. The character-theoretic inputs they use (the Brauer–Feit bound on simple modules, Cartan entries, cones of projective characters) serve Cartan and Morita bounds, not a Dade-type identity.

Both manuscripts prove only that particular Kronecker coefficients are positive: 'Universal Tensor Squares for Symmetric Groups' gives g(λ,λ,ν)>0 for every ν⊢n for one chosen self-conjugate λ per degree n, and 'A Cyclic Polytabloid Proof of Saxl's Conjecture' gives g(ρ_m,ρ_m,λ)>0 for the staircases ρ_m. Positivity is obtained by showing that a cyclic module contains each irreducible, and the Cyclic paper states that its objective is 'support, or positivity, rather than a formula for Kronecker multiplicities.' No family of objects whose count equals g(λ,μ,ν) is constructed for any triple, so neither manuscript gives the combinatorial interpretation the problem asks for.

Both manuscripts (The ℓ¹-Bass Conjecture for Discrete Groups, 5 October 2026; The Bass trace conjecture and the characteristic-zero Kaplansky idempotent conjecture, 24 September 2026) concern the Hattori–Stallings trace on K₀ of group algebras (ℓ¹(G), ℂG, ℤG) and its support on conjugacy classes. Their 'Bass conjecture' is Bass's trace conjecture (refs Bass1976, Bass1979 'Traces and Euler characteristics'), not the Wikipedia problem on finite generation of the higher algebraic K-groups Kᵢ(X) or K'ᵢ(X) of regular schemes of finite type over ℤ. Neither manuscript mentions finite generation of K-groups, regular schemes over ℤ, G-theory, or motivic/Chow groups; the family does not bear on this problem.

All five manuscripts concern two-dimensional O(n) spin models: lattice nearest-neighbour sigma models with global O(n) symmetry and no gauge field, and their continuum limits as 1+1-dimensional theories. Yang-Mills asks for a four-dimensional quantum gauge theory for every compact simple G, with nontriviality and a positive mass gap, and none of the five constructs a gauge theory, a four-dimensional quantum field theory or a glueball, or refers to Yang-Mills or the Clay problem; the only gauge reference is a citation to lattice gauge-theory variational methods. The matching pass's 'toy analogue' is a shared theme (a mass gap in a relativistic QFT), not a claim that bears on the problem.

Neither manuscript mentions NP, certificates, or the P versus NP question. Both concern whether choiceless polynomial time with counting (a logic over hereditarily finite sets) defines every polynomial-time query on unordered finite structures. The separating query is itself shown to be decidable in deterministic polynomial time, so the result separates P from a logic, not P from NP. The only link is that both are about descriptive-complexity capture, which the matching pass noted as adjacent.

Neither manuscript treats free Burnside groups B(m,n). Their periodic groups have no common exponent: the companion says the order of an element 'may depend on that element', and the residual paper says the orders in its group are unbounded. A group of unbounded exponent is not a quotient of any B(m,n), so these constructions say nothing about whether B(m,n), or B(2,5), is finite.

Köthe's implication concerns rings with no nonzero nil two-sided ideal. The companion's algebra R = F₂ ⊕ I has a nonzero nil two-sided ideal I, which the companion proves is nil (Corollary cor:nil-algebra, item 1), so R falls outside the hypothesis Köthe's question is about. Neither manuscript constructs a ring without a nonzero nil two-sided ideal, and neither addresses one-sided nil ideals in such rings. Their nil results concern Ufnarovskij- and Amitsur-type nilpotence questions and Kurosh-type algebraic finiteness, not the Köthe implication.

The manuscript disproves the Eilenberg-Ganea statement for one group and says nothing about whether connected subcomplexes of aspherical two-dimensional complexes are aspherical. Whitehead's question appears only as background in the introduction, which recalls the Bestvina-Brady dichotomy that at least one of the Eilenberg-Ganea and Whitehead conjectures fails for certain flag triangulations. The failure of Eilenberg-Ganea here is consistent with that dichotomy but does not decide the Whitehead side.

Both manuscripts concern mutually unbiased bases and complex Hadamard matrices in dimension six. 'The maximum number of mutually unbiased bases in dimension six' claims N(6) = 3, and 'Exact Fourier certificates for complex Hadamard matrices of order six' claims a Fourier-vanishing result and excludes seven MUBs. Neither constructs, bounds or excludes a SIC-POVM (d² unit vectors in ℂᵈ with all pairwise squared overlaps 1/(d+1)) in any dimension. Zauner's name enters only because the MUB conjecture is his; the MUB paper's introduction mentions his thesis's quantum-design conjecture as historical context, and its one SIC-titled reference (Grassl, 'On SIC-POVMs and MUBs in Dimension 6') is cited for a different result, that the standard-Fourier pair cannot lie in four MUBs.

The Hadamard conjecture asks for real ±1 matrices of order 4k for every positive integer k. In this family, 'Hadamard matrix' means a complex matrix with unimodular entries and H·H* = 6I, and every result concerns order six, which is not a multiple of four. Neither paper constructs or discusses a ±1 Hadamard matrix or any order 4k. The Fourier paper's Hadamard content is the classification of order-six complex matrices H whose entrywise square H∘2 is also Hadamard, which does not bear on the existence question.

The manuscript is about unital embeddings of C*-algebras into norm ultrapowers B^omega of nuclear C*-algebras (Kirchberg's norm-ultrapower embedding problem). It does not treat II1 factors, the hyperfinite II1 factor R, trace-preserving embeddings into R^omega, or tracial von Neumann algebras, and its introduction says the question is distinct from Connes' embedding problem.

The family proves that the microstates entropy χ and the nonmicrostates entropy χ* can differ by at least 1/2 for one bounded self-adjoint tuple whose two entropies are both finite. Neither manuscript mentions Connes embedding, embedding into the ultrapower R^ω, the hyperfinite II1 factor, II1 factors in general, or Kirchberg's QWEP property, and neither proves or refutes that any tracial von Neumann algebra embeds in R^ω. The only contact is that χ is defined through matrix approximations of moments, which is the shared technique the matching pass pointed to. The nearest fact the paper does prove is that χ(X) > −∞ for its tuple X, which gives matrix microstates for that one tuple. That is a statement about a single tuple's approximability, not about embedding the algebra it generates, and the paper says nothing about whether W*(X) embeds.

The manuscripts disprove the rational coarse Novikov assertion, that ordinary coarse assembly is rationally injective for uniformly discrete bounded-geometry spaces; this is a separate statement about coarse K-homology and the Roe algebra, while the listed problem concerns homotopy invariance of higher signatures <L(M) cup f*(x), [M]> over closed oriented manifolds M and all groups pi. The constructed spaces are coarse disjoint unions of finite graphs with no manifold or classifying-space structure, and neither manuscript draws any consequence for higher signatures or for any B(pi).

The listed problem is the group-level assembly map from the equivariant K-homology of the classifying space for proper actions of a discrete group G to K-theory of its reduced group C*-algebra, whereas both manuscripts state they concern the non-equivariant coarse assembly map on uniformly discrete spaces (the 'Failure of rational injectivity' paper: 'The present theorem concerns the non-equivariant coarse assembly map'; the 'counterexample' paper: 'maximal completions and coefficient-free group assembly are different questions'). The counterexample paper cites a separate companion, OpenAITorsionFreeBC2026, which it says constructs a finitely generated torsion-free group for which group assembly is not rationally injective; that companion is not one of this family's manuscripts and was not read, so it should not be credited to family 307.

The family's theorem is about whether a connective p-complete spectrum of fp-type two lies in the thick subcategory generated by BP<2>; it is a finite-generation counterexample to the Hahn-Wilson conjecture, not a statement about telescopes. Its only telescope content is Proposition scope:telescopes in the section 'The counterexample and its localizations': for the one spectrum X constructed (at sufficiently large primes), L_2^f X ≃ L_2 X and L_{T(2)} X ≃ L_{K(2)} X. That is a comparison for a single object, not a claim that L_n^f → L_n is an equivalence for all spectra, all heights or all primes, and the manuscript says these comparisons 'neither assume nor settle the general restricted telescope conjecture for fp-spectra'. The unrestricted telescope conjecture is not addressed; the introduction cites Burklund-Hahn-Levy-Schlank as having already disproved it at every prime and height at least two.

The manuscript settles Wall's finite D(2) problem: it builds a finite connected 3-dimensional complex X with infinite fundamental group that satisfies the D(2) homology conditions but is not homotopy equivalent to any finite complex of dimension at most two. The question concerns finite complexes and their finite 2-dimensional homotopy models. The Eilenberg-Ganea conjecture concerns groups G with integral cohomological dimension 2 and asks for a 2-dimensional K(G,1). Neither the abstract, the introduction, the tower or plus-construction sections, nor the construction section mentions cohomological dimension of a group, K(G,1), asphericity, geometric dimension, or Eilenberg-Ganea (checked by keyword search over all the manuscript's sources). The manuscript does not claim that pi_1(X) has cohomological dimension 2, and it does not claim that any group of cohomological dimension 2 lacks a 2-dimensional aspherical model. The matching pass's link is a shared theme of Wall-type dimension questions, not an overlap of the stated problems.

The manuscript disproves Pietsch's duality conjecture, which compares covering numbers N(K,L) with covering numbers of polar bodies; it never mentions volumes, the volume product vol(K)·vol(K°), the 4ⁿ/n! bound, or the cube and cross-polytope minimisers, so it does not bear on Mahler's volume-product conjecture.

Neither manuscript says anything about higher signatures, the L-class pairing ⟨L(M) ∪ f*x, [M]⟩, or homotopy invariance. 'Positive scalar curvature forces rational inessentiality' proves that the rational fundamental class maps to zero in H_n(Bπ;Q) for manifolds with positive scalar curvature, a conclusion about scalar curvature that does not involve L-classes. 'An integral scalar curvature bound for real simplicial volume' concerns the integral of negative scalar curvature against simplicial volume. The only occurrence of 'higher signatures' in either manuscript is a bibliography title.

Neither manuscript treats whether aspherical manifolds with isomorphic fundamental groups are homeomorphic, nor whether homotopy equivalences between them are homotopic to homeomorphisms. Their aspherical content is that closed aspherical manifolds admit no positive scalar curvature metric (Corollary 'The Gromov–Lawson aspherical conjecture') and that every nonnegative scalar curvature metric on one is flat (Corollary 'Aspherical nonnegative-scalar-curvature rigidity'). The flatness conclusion is a metric rigidity statement, not a topological one. The integral-bound paper does not discuss aspherical manifolds at all.

The family is "A counterexample to the nearby Lagrangian conjecture", which asks whether closed exact embedded Lagrangians in T*Q are Hamiltonian isotopic to the zero section, and it constructs a closed exact Lagrangian in T*(S^9 x S^{N-1}) that is diffeomorphic to the base but not Hamiltonian isotopic to the zero section. It proves no fixed-point count and no Lagrangian intersection bound for a Hamiltonian diffeomorphism (no Betti-number, cup-length or Morse-critical-point lower bound). The only intersection material is background in the introduction (Hofer and Laudenbach–Sikorav constraints on Hamiltonian deformations of the zero section), and the argument never counts L ∩ φ(L). The shared link is only that both are Arnold-type questions in symplectic geometry.

All three manuscripts are four-dimensional results about Einstein metrics (strictly positive sectional curvature, nonnegative sectional curvature with a zero-curvature plane, and a small trace-free Ricci L^2 energy forcing a diffeomorphism type); none states or proves a sign relation between sectional curvature and the Euler characteristic, and the only dimension they treat is four, which problem_asks records as the already-known case, so they leave the open higher even-dimensional statements untouched.

The manuscript proves a volume lower bound for closed, non-totally-geodesic minimal hypersurfaces of S^{m+1} (every such hypersurface has volume at least a_m, the least minimal Clifford product volume). It never bounds or computes the first nonzero eigenvalue of the Laplace–Beltrami operator on a minimal hypersurface, so the equality lambda_1 = n is not addressed. Its only spectral objects are the Jacobi operator L = Δ + m + P, used for the index bound and the index-(m+3) classification (Proposition index-rigidity), and Takahashi's bound is not used. Tang and Yan's isoparametric eigenvalue result is cited only as background in the introduction.

The manuscript proves a least-volume bound for non-equatorial closed minimal hypersurfaces of spheres, with Clifford products as the extremal examples. None of the listed parts of the Chern problem is addressed: the set of attained values of S (or of σ in higher codimension) is not studied, there is no isoparametric rigidity under constant scalar curvature, no second gap S > n ⇒ S ≥ 2n, no Lu variant, and no treatment of Bryant's S^4 conjecture for non-closed pieces. The only nearby statements are the average-curvature inequality ∫|A|² ≥ m|Σ| (Theorem curvature-average) and index-(m+3) rigidity (Proposition index-rigidity), which concern integrals and the Jacobi index rather than the spectrum of constant S. The averaged inequality would give S ≥ n for a closed non-totally-geodesic minimal hypersurface with constant S, but the manuscripts do not state this, and it is the classical first gap rather than one of the listed parts.
